articles.title: India's road rage: When cars become weapons
articles.summary: Road disputes are turning violent across India, raising questions about status and impunity behind the wheel for drivers of expensive cars.

image.caption: The number of cars on India's streets is rising, and over half of all cars sold are SUVs (file photo) Image: Vipin Kumar/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A road altercation in Gurugram, a suburb of New Delhi, went viral last week after a 27-year-old female biker was allegedly chased and hit by a car.
The two sides gave differing accounts of the initial dispute, with the car driver telling Indian media that the group of bikers overtook his car and slowed down in front of it.
In turn, the motorcycle rider, Shivani Chauhan, said the car was following her and the argument started when she asked the people inside to keep a safe distance.
Chauhan's motorcycle-mounted camera shows the car hitting her from the side and them speeding away as she falls and rolls on the road.
"I could have suffered serious fractures or internal injuries and even died. Due to such people, the roads of Gurugram and Delhi feel unsafe," Chauhan was quoted as saying by Indian news outlets.

According to reports, the driver claims that he lost control over his vehicle and left the scene because he feared reprisals from the biker group. Police have since arrested the driver on charges including attempted murder and stalking.
Road rage escalates to violence, shootouts
The case was only the latest example of how quickly a dispute on India's increasingly crowded roads can turn violent.
In March in Hassan, in the southern Karnataka state, young men reportedly shouted at the driver of a Toyota Fortuner SUV to slow down.
Police said the driver turned the vehicle around and rammed the group, killing one man and seriously injuring three others.
In the northern city of Dehradun that month, an argument over giving way between two SUVs, a Toyota Fortuner and a Mahindra Scorpio, escalated into a chase and gunfire.
The altercation cost the life of one man, a retired Army brigadier Mukesh Joshi, who was not involved in the initial dispute.

"The occupants of the Scorpio waited outside the club till early morning and then chased the Fortuner. During the firing, the brigadier, who was out on morning walk, was hit by a bullet in the chest,” said senior superintendent of police Pramendra Dobhal.

Concerns over road safety prompted the administration of Daman, a small coastal town north of Mumbai, to take an unusual step. On September 9, officials gathered owners of Mahindra Thar and Toyota Fortuner SUVs and made them take a public road safety pledge.
District Collector Saurabh Mishra, the district's top administrator, warned that these kinds of larger vehicles should not be used to intimidate others or display power.
More cars, less space on Indian roads

India's roads are notoriously dangerous, with government figures showing 485 people were killed in crashes on an average day in 2024. The data also indicates that the number of vehicles is currently growing much faster than the expansion of the road network.

Notably, SUVs accounted for about 2.63 million vehicles, or 56% of India's car sales, in the 12 months leading up to March 2026, according to industry data. While more SUVs on the road does not neccesarily mean more aggressive driving, the vehicles' size, height and presence can change the dynamics of a confrontation.
"For some drivers it is an expression of strength and domination," former police officer Yashovardhan Azad told DW.
"One drives with impunity to make an impression on smaller vehicles," said Azad.
He called for tougher policing using new technology, rigorous punishment and a nationwide programme to promote safer driving.
"Hitting a smaller vehicle intentionally is not rash driving. It is a measure of criminal intent," he said.
'SUV drivers have a beast in their hands'
Road safety expert Prince Singhal, founder of the Community Against Drunken Driving, sees both vehicles and drivers as parts of the problem.
"The issue of terror behind SUVs is not just a traffic challenge but also a behavioral issue," Singhal told DW.
"The SUV drivers have a beast in their hands and it's their mindset which decides the outcome."
How a start-up in India is turning old cars into EVs
Singhal notes that SUVs are a practical choice for bad roads and long journeys, but also points to issues in their design.

"High bonnets and elevated bumper heights increased the risk of fatal head and chest injuries for pedestrians, children, and cyclists and all other road users compared to traditional lower cars," added Singhal.
With an SUV at hand, drivers often experience "a psychological sense of invincibility," which can lead to hostile behavior, road bullying and rule violations, he said.
Are drivers taking traffic too personally?
Psychiatrist Ravi Prakash, who studies traffic behavior at Veditha Mind Care Clinic in Bengaluru, agrees that the driver "feels both powerful and protected inside a large, sturdy vehicle."
He also warned that there are other mechanisms at play.
"There is a psychological phenomenon called 'personalization,' where people interpret an ordinary act by a stranger as something personally directed at them," he told DW.

Someone cutting across a lane may be in a hurry. But the other driver may see it as an attempt to assert superiority. A perceived insult can then threaten a person's identity and trigger a spike of anger.
"Usually, hitting the other person is not the goal initially," Prakash said.
The driver first tries to assert superiority through speeding, honking, gestures or shouting. When that fails, a desire to punish can emerge, what Prakash calls an "illusion of retributive justice."
'Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture'
Sociologist Dipankar Gupta says road rage happens "because traffic rules are not strictly enforced," with the problem in no way limited to SUV drivers.
"Even motorcyclists get into road rage," he told DW.

"It's like a child who is not disciplined and throws a tantrum," Gupta said of the wider breakdown in road discipline. When rules are routinely ignored and people do not want to face the consequences, he added, it becomes similar to "a punch up" in school.
Why India will shape the car of the future
With cameras everywhere, however, such behavior has become harder to ignore.

"The anger is not new. What has changed is that everyone has a camera now, whether it is a dashcam, a helmet camera or a mobile phone," Deepanshu Gupta, cofounder of CrashFree India, a road safety nonprofit, told DW.
He warns that recording an incident is not the same as preventing it.
"Every driver knows that the odds of facing any real consequence are very low," he said.
"Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture. Aggressive driving is normalized here, but culture responds to enforcement," Deepanshu Gupta said.
He also noted that road rage is not a specifically defined offense in India, leaving police to choose between rash driving and far more serious charges such as attempted murder.
"There is very little in between," he said.
In such conditions, responsibility rests on the drivers, particularly when a large vehicle is in a confrontation with a more vulnerable road user.
"The bigger the vehicle you bring onto the road, the greater your duty of care has to be," he said.

articles.title: Fuel prices rise again with big hike on September 22
articles.summary: The upcoming hike marks the third straight week of substantial price increases at the pump

blocks.text: ADJUSTMENTS. A gas station in Paco, Manila, on January 12, 2026.
Rappler
The upcoming hike marks the third straight week of substantial price increases at the pump

items: Fuel prices in the Philippines will increase starting September 22, with gasoline rising by P4.88, diesel by P8.82, and kerosene by P6.47 per liter.
The price hikes are attributed to tight global supply and ongoing tensions in the Middle East, despite efforts by Saudi Arabia to restore export capacity.
The Philippine government is considering fuel tax relief due to rising crude oil prices, with a recommendation pending for approval from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Fuel prices are going up again starting Tuesday, September 22, continuing a run of pump price increases as tight global supply and continuing Middle East tensions keep petroleum markets under pressure.
In a press conference on Monday, September 21, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin announced the following fuel price adjustments for the week of September 22 to 28:

items: Gasoline – increase of P4.88 per liter
Diesel – increase of P8.82 per liter
Kerosene – increase of P6.47 per liter

blocks.text: The adjustments will take effect on Tuesday, September 22.

Before the latest adjustment, the Department of Energy’s (DOE) price monitoring showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P91.40 per liter for gasoline RON95, P83.10 per liter for gasoline RON91, P94.50 per liter for diesel, and P124.50 per liter for kerosene for the week of September 15 to 21.
The latest increase follows last week’s big fuel price hike, when gasoline prices rose by P5.68 per liter, diesel by P4.31 per liter, and kerosene by P4.62 per liter.

The continuing increases come as physical fuel supplies remain tight despite efforts by Saudi Arabia to restore some of its export capacity. Saudi Arabia has been working to bring part of its East-West pipeline capacity back online and offer additional cargoes to Asian refiners, helping ease some of the most severe price pressures seen earlier in the week.

But supply risks remain. Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continues to be constrained, while continuing tensions involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis threaten energy infrastructure and shipping through the Red Sea.

The government, meanwhile, is considering another round of fuel tax relief. Last week, the DOE formally certified that the one-month average price of Dubai crude reached $99.41 per barrel from August 13 to September 11, well above the $80-per-barrel threshold that allows the government to consider suspending or reducing excise taxes on petroleum products. (READ: DOE sees ‘no signs’ oil prices will fall as excise tax relief goes on table)

The Development Budget Coordination Committee is still finalizing its recommendation on possible excise tax relief, which will be submitted to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for approval. The Department of Finance earlier said it was prepared to propose a suspension of excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gas and kerosene.

Local pump prices also remain far above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com

articles.title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
articles.summary: Visitors stopping to take pictures of the 68m medieval embroidery were holding up others, prompting the rule change.

blocks.text: The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.
Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.
The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.
But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.
A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible.
"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."
The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.
British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux.
The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.
Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.
The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London.
Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.
Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.
Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum.

MANILA, Philippines – The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is now investigating Genesis88 Construction Inc., a construction firm whose owner is linked to the Duterte family.
“Yes, and case buildup,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag told Rappler on Monday, September 21, when asked for confirmation regarding the probe.
“Subpoena [was] served to DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways) officials in relation to this,” Matibag added.

blocks.caption: NBI probes Davao contractor linked to Dutertes; issues subpoena to DPWH

blocks.text: On September 8, Matibag had said his bureau was looking into the P1.9-billion flood control projects awarded to Genesis88, located in the district of Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte.
The Dutertes’ longtime friend, Glenn Escandor, is the owner of the said firm, based on Securities and Exchange Commission records obtained by Rappler in 2025.

A Rappler investigation revealed that one in four flood control projects in Davao City were awarded to Genesis88. The years when it bagged the contracts coincided with the time when Rodrigo Duterte was president and when the younger Duterte was the lawmaker representing the 1st District of Davao City.

Almost P2.9 billion (or P2,890,690,550.13) worth of contracts for flood control infrastructure from 2021 to 2023 went to the firm, based on figures from the Sumbong sa Pangulo website. This translated to a total of 35 projects — solo contracting and joint ventures with other firms included — in the region.

blocks.caption: Dutertes’ longtime friend is Davao’s top contractor for flood control projects

blocks.text: Escandor was former president Duterte’s assistant for sports. He also owns the Escandor Development Corporation, which donated P19.923 million for the ads of Vice President Sara Duterte during the 2022 national elections, according to the Vice President’s Statement of Contributions and Expenditures seen by Rappler.
On Monday, the NBI also announced that it had served subpoenas to Engineer Juby Blancaver Cordon, director of DPWH Davao Region.

The bureau invited Cordon to the NBI headquarters in Pasay City on September 24 for its investigation into alleged violations of Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code, Republic Act No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and RA 9160 or the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001.
It also asked for a list of documents related to the infrastructure projects secured by Genesis88.
Representative Duterte, in a statement on September 17, said he welcomed Matibag’s statement regarding the supposed probe.

“Walang selective investigation. Ebidensya ang dapat magsalita. Kaya welcome na welcome sa amin ‘yang Matibag investigation na ‘yan (There should be no selective investigation. Evidence should speak for itself. That is why this Matibag investigation is very much welcome),” said Duterte. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN
articles.summary: A report says the attacks, of which there have been at least 68, were not self-defence.

blocks.text: A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity.

The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people.

Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law.
The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean.

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video.

But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law".
"There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded.
BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people".
The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September.
However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking.
Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted.

However, Nicolás Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year.
Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election.

articles.title: Converse apologizes and pulls ad that critics said evoked racist imagery
articles.summary:
Sneaker company removes social media ad after backlash from critics who said it resembled KKK imagery

The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among…

blocks.text: The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan and lynching.

The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers. Critics lashed out online, saying that a white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a KKK hood – and that the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim.
Converse, owned by Nike, issued a statement apologizing and saying it removed the ad.

“We’re sorry,” said the statement, first released on Friday. “We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better.”
Converse, based in Boston, declined on Sunday to answer questions seeking additional information, including how the company screens ads before they are posted and how the ad was approved.
Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts.
Retailers and top fashion brands have issued a string of apologies over the years for products criticized as being racially insensitive.

In August, retailer Target pulled a children’s Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

The Converse photo sparked swift criticism, including calls for staff involved in the ad to be fired and for a boycott of the company. In a slew of comments on social media, posters questioned how the ad could have cleared the company’s advertising vetting process. Other commenters defended Converse, saying they didn’t believe it was intentional.
Lee Merritt, a Texas-based civil rights attorney, posted on Instagram that Converse’s apology “doesn’t undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step”.
“We keep having this conversation because corporations keep failing the same test,” he wrote. “Do better means catching this before it airs – not after we’re offended.”

Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in 1908, makes the Chuck Taylor All Star sneaker. It was first released in 1917 as a non-skid basketball shoe, adding the signature of Taylor – a basketball player who promoted the sneaker – in 1934, according to the company’s website.

articles.title: Fears over interest rate rise and jobs send UK consumer confidence to three-year low
articles.summary: Blow to John Healey before budget as UK households face ‘notable strain’ on their finances

blocks.text: Fears of a steep rise in mortgage payments and increasing job insecurity have sent UK consumer confidence tumbling to a three-month low, according to a leading survey.

In a blow to John Healey before next month’s budget, the S&P Global consumer sentiment index dropped to 42.7 in September from 42.9 in August, indicating “a notable strain on financial confidence across UK households”.
The chancellor could announce tax rises in his first budget to offset the rising cost of government borrowing, which has soared in response to the conflict in the Middle East.

S&P Global said consumers were concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England. More than 50% of 1,500 respondents said they expected a rise in the cost of borrowing over the next year.

Fixed-rate mortgage costs have already jumped to multi-year highs in the UK, while the threat of artificial intelligence and caution among employers about hiring new staff sent consumer confidence in the jobs market plunging to its lowest level in three-and-a-half years.

The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate rose to 5.88% on Monday, its highest since 16 April and up from 5.84% last Friday, while the average five-year is at its highest since October 2023, at 5.92%, up from 5.88%, data from Moneyfacts showed.
The rise in mortgage costs is expected to add about £150 to monthly mortgage payments, based on a typical loan of £250,000 over 25 years, since the start of March 2026.
Official figures have shown that the average direct debit to cover monthly mortgage costs has risen over the past four years from about £600 to £900.

Maryam Baluch, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a downbeat mood was spreading across UK households “as improved sentiment surrounding the new government is eroded by renewed worries over energy prices, the cost of living and job prospects”.

She said: “Against a backdrop of rising volatility in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East, households increasingly reported difficulties accessing credit, suggesting that expectations of tighter monetary conditions are beginning to feed through to borrowing conditions. Together, these factors point to cautiousness about both financial prospects and pose some downside risks to the broader economic outlook.”

Analysts believe the jobs market has proved resilient since the US attack on Iran and a steep rise in the cost of fuel and energy, but a steady decline in the number of payrolled employees over the past six months and a drop in vacancies to a five-year low have shown employers are worried about their profitability over the next year.

The British Chamber of Commerce has called for the government to give businesses extra support after a series of tax rises over the past two years, including an increase in employers national insurance payments.
after newsletter promotion
A survey by the business organisation of 5,000 companies in the second quarter of 2026 found that only 17% were planning to increase investment in the coming months, a post-pandemic low.
Last week, Andy Burnham said he will need to take “difficult decisions” on the economy to ensure that it “remains on track”.

In response to the growing clamour for tax cuts to support businesses and households hit by the cost of living crisis, the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, said at his party conference that the UK should cut fuel duty to offset some of the rise in petrol and diesel prices at the pumps.
The German government on Monday announced plans for a cut in tax on fuel of about 15p to take effect on 1 October.

Healey could limit his tax rises to wealthier groups, including a rise in capital gains tax. However, analysts say he is unlikely to raise sufficient funds from discreet tax rises to pay for higher defence spending and the rise in debt costs while preserving a reserve buffer, often referred to as headroom, of at least £20bn.

articles.title: [OPINION] ‘Difficult: The Life and Times of Etta Rosales’ — a big lesson in perspective
articles.summary: Perhaps this is the deeper lesson of 'Difficult': political commitment is not always about where you stand or what organization you belong to. Sometimes, it is about finding new ways to pursue the…

items: Difficult: The Life and Times of Etta Rosales, written by Carmela Abao, explores Etta's life and activism, emphasizing the importance of context in understanding historical events.
Etta's unwavering commitment to social justice and her transition from underground activism to mainstream politics highlight her adaptability and determination to effect change.
The book illustrates that political commitment can evolve and that finding new ways to pursue a vision for social change is crucial, as demonstrated by Etta's enduring influence and legacy.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Some biographies tell you what happened. Difficult: The Life and Times of Etta Rosales makes you stop and ask why. Written by Ateneo de Manila University political science professor Carmela “Melay” Abao, it is a very well-crafted book and, for me, a profound lesson in perspective — a reminder that events cannot always be understood on their own, but must be seen in the context of the times, the struggles, the choices, and the people who shaped them.

Reading Etta’s story made me look back at many events and people I thought I already understood and see them in a different light. What stays with me most is a deep admiration for Etta’s stubborn persistence — the refusal to give up on what she believed was right, even when the path was difficult and the odds were against her.

Her commitment to a more just and humane society, especially for the poor and marginalized, was not simply an idea she espoused; it was a conviction she carried throughout her life. Her vision remained the one constant in a life marked by difficult choices amid changing political, as well as personal, circumstances. That, perhaps, is what makes her story both difficult and inspiring.

Difficult is divided into six chapters, chronicling Etta’s life from childhood, through her years in the underground movement, her transition to parliamentary politics, and eventually her chairmanship of the Commission on Human Rights. There is also a chapter devoted to her marriage and family life. The book ends with her struggles with cancer, stroke, COVID-19, and the Duterte presidency.

Etta, now 87 years old, grew up in relatively comfortable circumstances. The daughter of a military officer, she received her early education at the University of the Philippines (UP) before attending Woodrow Wilson High School in Washington, DC. She later studied English Literature at George Washington University but completed her college education at UP Diliman after her father was recalled to the Philippines and promoted to the rank of commodore. She earned a degree in Foreign Service.

She was first “exposed to activism” while pursuing a master’s degree in Asian Studies at UP in the late 1960s. Later, she was recruited into the underground movement and became active after the suspension of the writ of habeas corpus in 1971, and the declaration of Martial Law in 1972.
She was captured twice, and during her second arrest in 1976, she was tortured and sexually harassed. Yet these experiences did not break her spirit.

She continued the struggle, eventually helping lead the teachers’ movement through the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT), the multisectoral organization Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), and other formations of the national democratic movement.

When the CPP-NDF [Communist Party of the Philippines-National Democratic Front] split into factions, she identified with the anti-Joma Sison group known as the Rejectionists (RJ), while the other faction became known as the Reaffirmists (RA). Yet Etta refused to join any formal RJ organization. As she explained to some of her underground comrades who mostly identified with the RJs, she wanted to explore new forms and ways of struggle, particularly parliamentary politics.

What makes Etta’s decision to shift the arena of struggle particularly significant is that her move from revolutionary politics to electoral politics was not simply a move from idealism to pragmatism. It was a choice about where political struggle could be most effective.

While many of her colleagues in the underground wanted to establish an alternative to the CPP, Etta was thinking about how to continue the struggle for social change outside the ideological, political, and organizational ambit of the CPP — or of any other alternative organization. This led her toward mainstream politics.

Yet her entry into mainstream politics did not mean a rejection of her activism or of the principles that had guided her life. Rather, it raised a larger question: Can political transformation be pursued only from outside the state, or must movements eventually find ways to enter, occupy, and use state institutions to advance their vision of social change?

Etta’s willingness to test this question by courageously entering mainstream politics is, for me, one of her greatest contributions to the broader movement for social change. She was willing to move beyond the familiar terrain of movement politics and into institutions she had once challenged from the outside. It was not necessarily a retreat from struggle, but an attempt to discover whether the state itself could become another arena for pursuing the changes she had spent her life fighting for.

That is one of the things I find most compelling about Etta’s story. Her circumstances, political affiliations, and arenas of struggle changed, but her underlying purpose did not. She kept searching for ways to make her vision relevant to the realities of the time. And perhaps this is the deeper lesson of Difficult: political commitment is not always about where you stand or what organization you belong to. Sometimes, it is about finding new ways to pursue the same vision.

A few months ago, Etta and I were exchanging emails about the difference between the personality cult surrounding Marcos Sr. and that of Duterte. At the end of the first email, she wrote: “Etta, not so cockeyed optimist anymore.”
I replied, and she wrote back:

“It just occurred to me while reading your response to not so cockeyed me, that what you term as the ‘qualitatively persuasive segment of our population that has consolidated in favor of the Duterte cult’ was a slow process of dismay and disappointment post-EDSA Revolt. This lineal process was largely met by complacency and inaction and opportunism…”
Then, in the final paragraph, she wrote:

“As you explicitly express, it will perhaps take generations after to provide the creative response. Our duty now is to plant the grains and hope that one of them will grow out of the withered weeds.”
I keep coming back to those words.

Etta may no longer consider herself a “cockeyed optimist,” but I still see in her life the stubborn optimism that made her keep fighting, changing course when necessary, and looking for new ways to make a difference. She spent 54 years of her life planting those grains — in the underground, in the teachers’ movement, in the human rights community, in Congress, and in the institutions of the state.

And perhaps that is what I take away most from Difficult. Etta herself is one of the grains she planted. So are the people she inspired, the movements she helped build, and the ideas she refused to abandon.
And I remain optimistic — not cockeyed optimism, but a quieter and more stubborn kind — that one of those grains will indeed grow out of the withered weeds. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [OPINION] Nepal landslides and recalling past Philippines events
articles.summary: As we commemorate the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law, we should also remember the lessons learned from past landslide disasters

blocks.text: On August 26, 2026, the day the Nepal landslides happened, the initial posts on social media claimed that “flash floods” had killed nine individuals and left hundreds missing. A quick review of these initial posts and other news feeds showed that the incident was not about flash floods per se, but debris flows and landslides instead. The flash floods were merely a consequential process.

The death toll and number of missing individuals would rise rapidly in the next days. Nearly a month since, more than 1,400 are now reported dead with more than 6,000 individuals missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals.
Nepal landslides and flash floods, August 2026

A landslide is a phenomenon that involves the downward movement of earth materials due to gravity. It is one among several types of what is generally referred to as “mass movement” in engineering geology. Certain areas are inherently prone to landslides, such as those with steep slopes and poor rock and soil integrity.
They can be triggered by several other phenomena. In the Philippines, the more common triggers are intense rainfall and earthquakes. In temperate and polar regions, avalanches are a common trigger.

Most post-event studies of the Nepal landslides now point to the collapse of a glacier in the Lantan National Park located high up in the Himalayan Mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border as the culprit. The glacier collapse triggered avalanches that mixed snow, rocks and soil scraped from steep mountain slopes turning into debris flows as the earth mass flowed down river to warmer elevations.

At this stage, the debris flows were estimated to be travelling at speeds peaking at about 180 km/hr. Further mixing with more river water allowed the debris flow to become more fluid and transformed into flash floods at the head of the onrushing rock-mud-water mixture. The first videos posted on social media showed footages of this fluid material, hence the initial captioning as flash floods. By then, the river gradient had become more gentle at lower elevations and the flow speed had decreased below 100 km/hr. The volume of eroded materials was so vast that the landslide travelled and filled the river channel of the Lende-Trishuli Khola river valley for more than 100 kilometers.
Allah Valley flash floods, September 1995

Sometime in late 1995, an investigative team climbed the active volcano Mt. Parker in South Cotabato with the objective of reaching the crater then called Lake Maughan (now Lake Holon). The climb was undertaken by a team consisting of government scientists and officials, escorted by a squad of Citizen Armed Force Geographic Unit and a couple of junior officers of the Philippine Army.

Today, Lake Holon is a tourist destination accessible through a 3-hour-hike trail, which otherwise required at least two nights and two days in 1995, not to mention that the region then was still a hotbed of insurgency.

The climb was in response to instructions from authorities at the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to investigate the cause of a massive September 1995 flooding at the northwest flank of Mt. Parker, causing the death of more than 50 individuals, and rendering hundreds of families homeless, damaging infrastructure and devastating agricultural lands in the Allah Valley.

Official reports indicated that the flooding resulted from the natural overflow of the crater lake after an artificial dam at the crater wall breached as it could no longer bear the weight of excess water impounded in the lake after days of heavy rainfall. Earlier reports indicated the possibility of blasting activities by treasure hunters wanting to drain the lake in search of the infamous Yamashita Treasure as the culprit.

Regardless of the real cause of the tragedy, the deadly Allah Valley floods resulted from the release of excess water impounded upstream after days of heavy rainfall that could no longer be contained by natural barriers.
Cherry Hills landslide, August 1999

In the first week of August of 1999, Cherry Hills Subdivision, a low-cost residential village in eastern Antipolo, a suburban mountain city east of Metro Manila, was engulfed by a landslide emanating from the collapse of a steep hillslope on the eastern flank of the village. Reports indicated that the subdivision was constructed over a former aggregate quarry. This hillside slope was an excavation left open at the edge of the quarry property.

More than 50 lives perished in this disaster, with the entire village left practically inhabitable. Prior to the landslide, eastern Antipolo and vicinity were battered by torrential rains for three days. It was classified as a freak rainfall event because the estimated amount of rainfall of almost 1,000 millimeters exceeded the two-month rainfall average during the rainy season of the region. There was no weather disturbance at the time, except for the southwest monsoon that was then commencing.

The already inherently slide-prone steep slope left by quarry excavation became extremely saturated by the three-day rains, adding to the weight of the slope that promoted its failure. The tragedy was exacerbated by the loose quarry materials upon which the village houses were built.
Guinsaugon landslide, February 2006

In early 2006, the village of Guinsaugon in the town of Saint Bernard in Southern Leyte was buried in debris flow emanating from the steep cliffs of the Southern Leyte mountain range transected by the active Philippine Fault. This landslide event killed more than 1,000 individuals, most of whom were elementary pupils in a school located nearest to the source of the debris flow.

Debris flows are a mixture of water, rocks and soil that slide down from high elevations, usually using river systems as the channel way. When debris flows reach low and flat elevations, they pile up and bury the area with boulders and thick mud that together usually form hummocky hills when they dry out.

The Guinsaugon landslide was preceded by at least a week of continuous heavy rains over southern Leyte. It deposited debris flows about three meters thick over an area three kilometers long and two kilometers wide. This is roughly equivalent to the area of the central business district of Makati City in Metro Manila.

Several other deadly debris flow and landslide events would occur later, including those that affected Baco, Oriental Mindoro and Gabaldon, Nueva Ecija both in 2015; Naga, Cebu in 2018; New Bataan, Compostela Valley (now Davao de Oro) in 2017; Baybay, Leyte in 2022, to name some. Like the Allah Valley, Cherry Hills and Guinsaugon disasters, all these events were preceded by extreme rainfall.

In the same way that, as we commemorate today the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law on Monday, September 21, we should not forget the lessons learned from this era marred by political suppression and extensive human rights abuses, we should as well remember the lessons learned from past landslide disasters.

The Nepal landslides were triggered by a glacier collapse high up in the Himalayas, generating deadly debris flows and flash floods as the rock-mud-water mixture traveled downstream for about 100 kilometers. While the Philippines is not expected to experience the same phenomenon due to the absence of glaciers in any of the Philippine mountain ranges, debris flows can emanate from landslides in steep mountain slopes at high elevations that may be induced by continuous heavy rains and/or earthquakes.

The Mt. Parker- Allah Valley flash floods taught us that crater lakes at the summit of volcanoes must be protected and monitored, to avoid breaches and collapses of the crater wall preventing uncontrolled overflow of lake water that can induce flash floods downslope.

When building subdivisions and housing villages, especially in places earlier meant for a different land use, slopes must be kept at safe gradients and protected, and the subsurface must be rendered capable of bearing the foundation of houses. Village design must integrate extreme weather conditions such as anomalous rainfall and intense ground shaking due to earthquakes. – Rappler.com

Mario A. Aurelio, PhD is a professor at the National Institute of Geological Sciences-University of the Philippines. Then a geologist of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, he was part of the team that climbed Mt. Parker to investigate the 1995 Allah Valley flash flood.

articles.title: Batanes congressman Ciriaco Gato Jr. dies
articles.summary: Gato chaired the House health committee from 2022 until his death

blocks.text: CONGRESSMAN. The late Ciriaco Gato Jr. in 2024.
House of Representatives
Gato chaired the House health committee from 2022 until his death
MANILA, Philippines – Batanes Representative Ciriaco “Jun” Gato Jr. has passed away, the provincial government announced on Monday, September 21.
He was 66.

“For Batanes, his passing is not merely the loss of a public servant. It is the loss of a son of the province who devoted his life, his profession, and his public service to the welfare of his fellow Ivatans,” the Batanes provincial government said on Facebook.
“As our congressman, he stood as a voice for our province and worked to ensure that the needs of our people were heard and given due attention at the national level,” it added.
The cause of death has not been specified.

Gato entered Congress in 2019, spoiling former budget secretary and Batanes representative Butch Abad’s comeback bid. Gato had been reelected twice and had been serving his third and final term prior to his death.

Gato was a native of Batanes, born in Sabtang and raised in Itbayat, where he finished basic education. He is a product of the University of the Philippines College of Medicine and was an ear, nose, and throat specialist prior to entering politics.
Gato was a member of the House health committee throughout his congressional stint and had been its chairperson from 2022 until his death.

As health committee chairperson, he played a key role in the passage of some priority measures of the administration. These include Republic Act No. 11959, which builds specialty centers in Department of Health hospitals in every region, and Republic Act No. 12290, which established the Virology and Vaccine Institute of the Philippines.
Gato is survived by his wife Jade and their two daughters. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Infected blood victims and their relatives are left struggling to claim compensation
articles.summary:
Claimants are asked to dig out decades-old medical records to prove they qualify despite inquiry’s recommendations

Suzanne Morgan will never forget the day her mother died. It was nine…

blocks.text: Suzanne Morgan will never forget the day her mother died. It was nine months after she had gone into hospital with gallstones, where she received a routine blood transfusion.
“She went downhill rapidly,” Morgan recalled. Her mother haemorrhaged in her liver, and the next day she was dead.

The family were astonished to be told that she had Hepatitis C, and doubly shocked to learn that they couldn’t see her because her body was sealed due to contagion risk, leading them to suspect she was HIV positive.
Morgan, who was pregnant at the time, said: “I went into full-blown miscarriage. I was in total shock. I was hysterical.”

That was 35 years ago, and the family now know Morgan’s mother died because she was given infected blood. Yet Morgan has found herself forced to “keep reliving” the horror through the infected blood compensation scheme.

Like many other victims of the scandal and their families, she has been asked to dig out decades-old medical records to prove she qualifies, despite the public inquiry’s recommendations that eligibility be determined “on the balance of probability”.

blocks.caption: Suzanne Morgan with her mother, Mari, who died after being given infected blood. Photograph: Family handout

blocks.text: “I have been everywhere to try and get medical notes of any sort. I cannot get them,” said Morgan.

Infected blood campaigners who spoke to the Guardian shared their fury that thousands like Morgan face being locked out of the Infected Blood Compensation Authority (IBCA) payment scheme due to its stringent approach.
Rachel Halford, the chief executive of the Hepatitis C Trust, said this was “placing an intolerable burden on people who have already endured decades of injustice”.

Victims and bereaved families had been asked to prove “even the most basic of things”, such as whether they lived with their deceased spouses or siblings, she added. Some have had to show old school records, tenancy agreements, utility bills or family photos.

“People feel they are being treated as potential fraudsters rather than victims of one of the greatest scandals in our history,” said Halford, adding that there have been complaints of unfairness after different compensation awards for people with similar experiences.

Halford said the community hoped that Andy Burnham, who has long campaigned for victims of the infected blood scandal to receive justice, would offer his support. “As prime minister, we need him to live up to that reputation and the promises he has made,” she Halford.

Yet Rosie McKearney, a policy specialist at the Hepatitis C Trust, said the community was “shocked” that Burnham had moved responsibility for the scandal from a cabinet-level secretary of state to a junior minister.

Research from the Haemophilia Society suggests that two years since the IBCA’s inception just 15% of projected compensation claims have been dealt with. In a letter sent to the IBCA’s chief executive, David Foley, the campaigners said they were “concerned and angry at the lack of progress”, especially its “unreasonable and sometimes impossible bureaucratic demands”.

The Haemophilia Society is calling for regulatory change to shift the burden of evidence from applicants to the state, meaning that all applicants with a bleeding disorder would be entitled to compensation unless proved otherwise.

Kate Burt, its chief executive, said that the current system was “putting haemophilia treatment centres under intolerable pressure”, with staff “asked to sift through patients’ medical notes to find evidence”, knowing that errors could cost the applicant thousands of pounds.

“This is highly technical work, relying on expert knowledge to find fragments of crucial information, yet centres are expected to fund this themselves,” she said, adding that one consultant told her they work unpaid on Saturdays to answer the IBCA’s inquiries.

blocks.caption: Suzanne’s mother, Mari, as a young woman. Photograph: Francesca Jones/The Guardian

blocks.text: Charlotte Evans, a lawyer at Leigh Day who is representing several victims and their families in their IBCA applications, said “the balance of probabilities” was the standard of proof for medical negligence claims.

She said it represented a comparatively lower threshold, which considers a risky procedure that took place at the same time as infected blood was used as indicative that a blood product had been administered.

Instead of assessing all the available evidence to build up a picture of what most likely happened, applicants are being asked to prove beyond reasonable doubt that they received a specific blood product.

“The scheme is supposed to provide a simpler process,” she said, adding that although the government and the IBCA had an obligation to ensure taxpayers’ money was properly spent, “the question is whether those obligations, and IBCA’s understanding of the same, go beyond what the regulations actually require”.
The reasons for this disconnect remained unclear, she said. “It may be that certain individuals [assessing claims] haven’t been given the appropriate guidance or training.”

Lynne Kelly, the chair of Haemophilia Wales, observed a “tick box” approach from the claims managers she had met. “The Cabinet Office is completely controlling the Infected Blood Compensation Authority scheme. It’s meant to be an independent, arm’s length body,” she said, adding that she believed the eligibility criteria was intended to “minimise the amount of compensation paid out”.
For Zena Whittaker, that extra compensation would both give closure and a comfortable retirement, enabling her to stop worrying about putting the heating on.
She is still haunted by the memory of asking a doctor how much longer her son Andrew had to live. He replied: “We don’t know, because it depends whether the Hep C takes him first, or the Aids.”
As a haemophiliac, Andrew received multiple blood transfusions, making it more likely than not that he also had hepatitis C. Yet medical records were destroyed when his hospital merged with another.
“It’s just coming up to the anniversary [of his death], which makes everything raw,” Whittaker said. “It’s 31 years since he died and it brought it all back again.”

Luke O’Shea is also struggling with a bureaucratic nightmare. He was given an infected clotting product as a three-year-old, but because he was not given a liver biopsy due to the risk of bleeding for haemophiliacs, he is unable to prove how bad his liver damage was, resulting in a shortfall in compensation he estimates at up to £1m.

“I wasn’t told I had hepatitis C until I was 15. So just as life was beginning to open up, I was suddenly told what had already been done to it,” he said. “My infection is my life, and it’s unrecognised in every way.”
A spokesperson for the IBCA said: “Missing or destroyed records will not prevent someone from making a claim. We will determine what is most likely from all available evidence.

“Our claim managers work with the person claiming to help them gather information from a range of sources to support their claim. We consider all evidence: medical records, witness testimony, and other family records can all be used to support a claim.
“Every compensation claim is unique, with individual circumstances, so they cannot be compared.”

A government spokesperson said: “The government has listened and learned through constant engagement with the community to make changes to the compensation scheme to ensure the community receive the compensation they deserve.
“The government will continue to be held accountable for its work in the usual ways across both Houses of Parliament.”

articles.title: Who is Jaime T. Cruz, Sara Duterte’s business partner?
articles.summary: Aside from connection to Sara Duterte through business, Jaime T. Cruz is also connected to former president Rodrigo Duterte

blocks.text: BUSINESS TIES. Vice President Sara Duterte (left) and businessman Jaime Tan Cruz (right)
Aside from connection to Sara Duterte through business, Jaime T. Cruz is also connected to former president Rodrigo Duterte
The business ties between Vice President Sara Duterte and businessman Jaime T. Cruz came under scrutiny during the Senate impeachment trial on Monday, September 21.
Cruz’s name appears in the corporate records of several companies linked to Duterte.

Testifying before the impeachment court in relation to allegations of Duterte’s unexplained wealth, Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Company Registration Director Gerardo del Rosario identified Cruz as an incorporator of the following companies:

items: City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation
Davao Bounty Times Foods Corporation
Davao Emerging Taipans Corporation
Davao New Royal Taipan Foods Corporation
Great Jolly Times Foods Corporation
JTC Group of Companies Philippines, Inc.
Metro City Chow Foods Corporation

blocks.text: The 2025 general information sheet of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation, as presented in the court, identifies Cruz as the company’s president and biggest shareholder.

Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) show that she has declared herself an “incorporator/stockholder” of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation since 2007. The company was previously named City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation, according to Duterte’s SALNs.

Another company, Davao New Royal Taipan Corporation, formerly known as Davao Emerging Taipans Corporation, also appears in Duterte’s 2022 and 2023 SALNs. She declared herself an “incorporator/stockholder” of the company since 2004.

Karen Batu, officer in charge of the Records Division of the Office of the Ombudsman, also testified that Duterte declared Davao Bounty Times Foods Corporation as a business interest in her 2010, 2011, and 2012 SALNs.
Cruz is also an incorporator and president of JTC Group of Companies Philippines Inc. The company’s name corresponds to Cruz’s initials.

blocks.caption: Who is Jaime T. Cruz, Sara Duterte’s business partner?

blocks.text: JTC is the biggest shareholder of Gencorp Industries Inc., another company declared by Duterte in her SALNs.
Gencorp’s corporate records, however, do not list Duterte as a corporate officer or shareholder.

A Rappler investigative report found that Gencorp secured millions of pesos worth of contracts from Davao City Hall while Duterte is sitting as vice president and her brother, Sebastian “Baste” Duterte, is the city mayor.

Article VII of the 1987 Constitution prohibits the vice president from participating “in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality.”

SEC records reviewed by Rappler also showed that Gencorp and JTC had the same shareholders. In an interview with Rappler, House prosecutor Terry Ridon said they may seek testimony from Gencorp executives and Jaime T. Cruz of the JTC Group.

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte trial: Can a VP have business interests?

blocks.text: Cruz’s ties to the Duterte family also extend to former president Rodrigo Duterte.
In 2019, then-president Duterte appointed Cruz as special envoy to the People’s Republic of China for trade and investments, according to a report by Malaya Business Insight.

Months before that appointment, Duterte had offered Cruz top positions at PhilHealth, including president and CEO. It is unclear whether Cruz accepted the offer. Months later, Duterte appointed Ricardo C. Morales to lead the state health insurer.

blocks.caption: Duterte asks doctor-businessman Jaime Cruz to be PhilHealth president

blocks.text: Cruz also joined the business delegation that accompanied Duterte during his working visit to Japan. Gencorp president Kimberly Cruz was part of the delegation as well.
During the trip, Jaime Cruz and Kimberly Cruz secured a deal to operate Dohtonbori and Karayama restaurants in the Philippines. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Firm of COA commissioner's wife issued notice of disallowance
articles.summary: A notice of disallowance has been issued against a construction firm owned by the wife of Commission on Audit (COA) Commissioner Mario Lipana, Davao del Sur Representative John Tracy Cagas said…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 7:23pm

A notice of disallowance has been issued against a construction firm owned by the wife of Commission on Audit (COA) Commissioner Mario Lipana, Davao del Sur Representative John Tracy Cagas said Monday.
Cagas made the statement while defending the COA’s proposed 2027 budget during the House plenary deliberations.
“COA conducted an investigation. In fact, there is already a notice of disallowance… referring to Mrs. Lipana’s construction firm,” Cagas said, quoting COA officials.
Cagas, however, said the notice has yet to become final.
“The case is currently on appeal before Cluster Seven,” he said, referring to COA’s Public Works, Transport and Energy auditing cluster.

During a House budget hearing in September 2025, questions were raised about Lipana’s links to government contracts, with his wife, Marilou Lipana, listed as the owner of Olympus Mining and Builders Group Phils. Corp.
Following this, ACT Teachers party-list Representative Antonio Tinio asked whether Lipana would take part in deciding the appeal if the case eventually reaches the COA en banc.
Cagas said Lipana would inhibit himself from the proceedings.
According to Cagas, Lipana is currently on sick leave due to cancer.
COA Chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba had previously confirmed that Lipana had been on medical leave while undergoing treatment abroad.
Cagas, meanwhile, said the two remaining commissioners are continuing to perform their duties.
The House later terminated the plenary deliberations on COA’s proposed P2027 budget.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: RappLearn’s masterclass: Professionals learn basics of vertical videos
articles.summary: 'Scrollproof,' RappLearn's one-day vertical video masterclass, equips professionals with practical tools to make their messages stand out in today’s fast-moving digital space

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – How do you make people stop scrolling when the message you need to share is competing with thousands of other videos for their attention?

That was the question at the heart of RappLearn’s Scrollproof: A Vertical Video Masterclass on Friday, September 18, as professionals from different industries explored how to make short-form videos more effective without losing the message they want to communicate.
Rappler journalist JC Gotinga told participants that the challenge is not simply producing video, but finding a way to make a message competitive in an environment built around constant scrolling.
“You have messages that you need to put out in public, but the question is: how?” he said.

The one-day masterclass at the Rappler newsroom introduced participants to the fundamentals of vertical video, including conceptualizing and scripting, storytelling, shooting, and the realities of a rapidly changing digital landscape.

Throughout the masterclass, participants connected these principles to the challenges they face in their own industries — from reaching younger audiences to finding new ways to make products and brands more memorable.

For Justin Pardo, a digital creative associate at a wires and cables manufacturing company, the decision to explore vertical video came as his company began seeing stronger performance from video content compared with static posts.

His team had been comparing the metrics of their educational content and found that videos were reaching more people. This year, they also began exploring TikTok, even though Pardo felt the platform was “quite far” from their field of wires and cables, which traditionally reaches electricians and customers aged 30 and above.
“Our current dilemma in marketing is how to get the attention of the younger generation, since our target market is electricians in their 30s and above,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Because of this, Pardo, whose work focuses on digital and graphic design, wanted to strengthen his own production skills. During the masterclass, he got a closer look at the different stages of production, from planning and lighting to directing and editing.

blocks.caption: CAMERA PRACTICE. Rosebie Panales participates in an on-camera lab exercise led by JC Gotinga during Scrollproof: A Vertical Video Masterclass on September 18, at the Rappler newsroom. Photo by Jake Gomez/Rappler.

blocks.text: One of his biggest realizations, however, was about the vertical format itself.

His team had been approaching vertical video mainly by repurposing content made for other platforms. They would take square videos made for Facebook, add a background, and export them in vertical format.
“We were just converting it so it would fit the platform,” Pardo said in a mix of English and Filipino. “[I realized] it’s more than just adjusting the video to fit a vertical format,” Pardo added.
He said that the masterclass led by Gotinga helped clear up these misconceptions by showing that creating for vertical needs to be planned right from the concept to filming stages.

This was also echoed by another participant, Franz San Diego, who works at a real estate company. He came to the masterclass with his colleagues wanting to better understand how to create vertical videos.

Before attending, he said he thought creating one was mainly about putting different scripts and shots together and stitching them into a finished video. But the session changed how he approached the process.
“Upon attending this workshop, [I realized] it really matters how you conceptualize it first,” San Diego said.
He realized that starting with the concept made the storytelling and production process simpler and more precise. It also made him see that content does not have to be complicated to work.
“Sometimes, keeping things simple is much, much better than overcomplicating it,” he said.
San Diego hopes to apply this approach to real estate marketing, using vertical video not only to generate engagement, but also to build familiarity with the brand among potential customers.
While it’s easy to sell to people already looking for property, he said his goal is to hook even the general public with his vertical videos.

“Making someone who isn’t interested pay attention…that’s what I want to achieve,” San Diego said. “You might not be interested today, but eventually, when you are at that time, I want our company or our brand to have an impact on you,” he added.
The September 18 masterclass was the second run of Scrollproof: A Vertical Video Masterclass since it was launched on July 10, 2026.

Designed for professionals, marketers, educators, and creators, the masterclass helps participants tell stronger stories through vertical video. Previous attendees included professionals from the corporate sector, government, academe, real estate, marketing, and non-government organizations. Learn more about Scrollproof here.

articles.title: Comelec exempts LTFRB's fuel subsidy from social services ban
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Monday said it has exempted the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) from the ban on public spending for social services ahead of the…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 7:20pm

The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Monday said it has exempted the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) from the ban on public spending for social services ahead of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).
"Na exempt na po namin ang fuel subsidy ng LTFRB sa social services (we exempted the fuel subsidy of LTFRB social services)," Comelec chairperson George Garcia said in a Viber message.
The exemption also covers the Libreng Sakay and monthly assistance under the Public Transport Modernization Program, Comelec spokesperson John Rex Laudiangco said.

However, the poll body pointed out that the exemption does not include the distribution of social assistance under the TUPAD, AKAP, AICS, and 4Ps from October 23 to November 2 except for medical and burial assistance.
Elective officials, candidates, nominees, and aspirants are also prohibited to be present during the distribution of social aid of the said programs.

The LTFRB is tasked to follow the guidelines set by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), Department of Labor and Employmen! (DOLE), and other relevant agencies during its aid distribution.
Any violation to the guidelines may result in the revocation of the certificate of exemption.
The LTFRB earlier suspended the distribution of the P12-per-liter fuel subsidy for PUV drivers due to the election ban.

During the election period, a certificate of exemption is given to a government agency to allow specific activities that fall under the elections ban, like releasing or disbursing public funds for social welfare, housing, or infrastructure projects and transporting firearms.
The release, disbursement, or expenditure of public funds is prohibited from September 18 to November 1 due to the upcoming BSKE scheduled for November 2. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
articles.summary: The US media outlets say they are defending "the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes".

blocks.text: CNN, Politico and MS NOW have said they will sue the Trump administration after the three US media outlets were barred from the White House.
President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the three organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his government.
The companies said their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized when attempting to access the building on Saturday.

In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes".

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
"Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," the CNN, Politico and MS NOW statement continued.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
BBC News has asked the White House for comment.
Announcing the ban last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".
The US president added that there "may be others to join them".
When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."
He has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

articles.summary: Ayala expects to receive around P20 billion in fresh capital from the transaction, which it will use to reduce debt and continue its buying spree of what it deems as undervalued shares of Ayala and…

blocks.text: DEAL. Executives from both Mitsubishi Corporation and Ayala Corporation pose for a photo after signing off on a P44.5-billion deal.
Ayala Corporation

Ayala expects to receive around P20 billion in fresh capital from the transaction, which it will use to reduce debt and continue its buying spree of what it deems as undervalued shares of Ayala and its listed subsidiaries

items: Mitsubishi Corporation is increasing its stake in Ayala Corporation through a P44.5-billion transaction, raising its economic ownership from 4.7% to 15%.
Ayala expects to receive around P20 billion from the deal, which will be used to reduce debt, buy shares, and support future growth.
The transaction will enhance Mitsubishi's influence in Ayala, increasing its voting interest to 20%, while Ayala plans to expand its board and conduct a tender offer for additional shares.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Japanese trading giant Mitsubishi Corporation is increasing its stake in Ayala Corporation through a P44.5-billion transaction that will bring in fresh capital to the Philippine conglomerate to reduce debt, buy shares, and support new developments.
Ayala said on Monday, September 21, that it had signed a definitive agreement with Mitsubishi covering a mix of primary and secondary shares priced at P650 apiece.
Once completed, Mitsubishi’s economic ownership in Ayala will rise from 4.7% to 15%.

Ayala expects to receive around P20 billion directly from the transaction. It said the proceeds would be used to reduce debt, continue buying shares of Ayala and its listed subsidiaries, and support future growth.

The amount is sizeable relative to Ayala’s parent-level balance sheet. As of end-June, the company had P19.9 billion in parent cash and P138.2 billion in parent net debt, meaning the expected proceeds are roughly equal to its cash balance and about 14% of its net debt.

Not all the money will necessarily go toward deleveraging. Ayala has also been buying shares it considers undervalued and still had P10.1 billion available under its share purchase program as of its April stockholders’ meeting. The program covers both Ayala and its listed subsidiaries.
The deal also gives Mitsubishi a considerably larger role in Ayala itself.

Its voting interest will rise to 20%, compared with 15% economic ownership. Ayala also plans to expand its board from seven to nine directors, subject to shareholder and regulatory approval, although it has not disclosed who will occupy the two additional seats.

The deal will not displace the Zobel family’s control of Ayala. As of end-2025, Mermac, Inc., the family’s holding company and Ayala’s controlling shareholder, held 47.84% of the conglomerate’s common shares and 57.79% of all voting shares.
As part of the transaction, Ayala will also conduct, on Mitsubishi’s behalf, a voluntary tender offer for up to around 30 million common shares at P650 each.

“Mitsubishi’s increased investment in Ayala Corporation is designed to grow value for Ayala’s shareholders by combining global reach and technology of one of Japan’s leading trading houses with the assets of one of the Philippines’ most diversified conglomerates,” Ayala president and CEO Cezar Consing said, describing the deal as “turbo-charging a 52-year relationship.”

blocks.caption: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday

blocks.text: The expanded alliance comes just as another Ayala-Mitsubishi investment prepares to enter the stock market. (READ: Stage set for GCash’s record P92.3B IPO, October 20 listing eyed)

While the P44.5-billion deal is not related to GCash specifically and spans a much broader set of sectors, from infrastructure and energy transition to real estate, mobility, logistics, and digital technologies, Mynt is a concrete example of the kind of collaboration Ayala and Mitsubishi are looking to deepen.

Mitsubishi already has an indirect stake in Mynt, the parent company of GCash. Mitsubishi acquired 50% of Ayala’s venture arm, now called AM50 Ventures, which holds an investment in Mynt. Before the joint venture, Ayala had built that vehicle’s Mynt stake to about 13%.

Mynt is now preparing for an October 20 listing on the Philippine Stock Exchange. The PSE approved an IPO of up to 8.03 billion firm shares at as much as P10 each, plus an overallotment option of up to 1.20 billion shares, with the offer period scheduled for October 6 to 12. – Rappler.com
