articles.title: ‘Incredibly encouraging’: healing the scars of traditional anchors in Dorset’s seagrass meadows
articles.summary:
Eco-moorings help to restore seagrass in just five years, boosting sealife such as seahorses, eels and crabs

One of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows –…

blocks.text: One of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows – is recovering thanks to “eco moorings” designed to prevent the seabed being ripped up, a study has revealed.
Scars caused by traditional anchors in some areas of seagrass in Studland Bay have almost entirely vanished, which is boosting the number of seahorses that thrive in the submerged meadows.

The Studland Bay Marine Partnership, which includes a wide range of organisations including conservationists and boating enthusiasts, hopes the findings could help protect and restore seagrass in other busy marine environments around the UK.
Seagrass meadows are considered one of the world’s most valuable ecosystems because, as well as supporting creatures such as seahorses, they store carbon and help protect coastlines from erosion.

blocks.caption: Corkwing fish swimming among the seagrass. Photograph: Pete Lightowler

blocks.text: They are declining globally due to pressures including pollution, coastal development and the climate emergency. The meadows at Studland Bay are particularly at risk because the spot is so popular with leisure boaters.
Research conducted by Kira Dunn, as part of her masters degree at the University of Southampton, analysed data collected since eco-moorings were installed by the partnership in 2021.

In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed five years ago, bare patches in the seagrass shrank by an average of 94% between 2021 and 2025. In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65%.

blocks.caption: Kira Dunn: ‘It’s incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate.’ Photograph: Valerie Mather

blocks.text: Dunn said: “The results clearly show that seagrass is recovering in areas where physical disturbance has been removed. It’s incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity.”

David Brown, the chair of the Studland Bay Marine Partnership steering group and lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: “The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it.”

blocks.caption: A spider crab in seagrass. Photograph: Jon Bunker

blocks.text: Studland Bay was designated a marine conservation zone in 2019 and is home to one of the UK’s largest seagrass meadows, supporting numerous marine species including the protected spiny seahorse and the occasionally recorded short-snouted seahorse.
after newsletter promotion

Since eco-moorings were introduced volunteer divers who monitor seahorses have reported increases in numbers. Other creatures spotted in the seagrass include conger eels, spider crabs and corkwing wrasse.

Eco-moorings consist of a 2-metre helical screw, which is drilled securely into the seabed. Attached to this is a 2-metre elasticated riser that connects to a surface buoy. As the tide rises and falls, the riser stretches and retracts, preventing any scouring of the seabed and seagrass.

blocks.caption: A boat tied to an eco-mooring at Studland Bay. Photograph: Brad Wakefield/National Trust

blocks.text: Ken Collins, emeritus research fellow and diving officer at the University of Southampton and supervisor of the study, said: “This research provides robust scientific evidence that eco-moorings are an effective tool for seagrass conservation and restoration.
“The findings support the continued use and expansion of eco-mooring schemes, not only in Studland but in other sensitive marine environments where seagrass habitats are under pressure.”

blocks.caption: A conger eel in seagrass. Photograph: The Seahorse Trust

articles.title: Starbucks baristas reel from surges in health insurance costs: ‘I’m considering a second job’
articles.summary:
Several workers say they’re opting to go without health coverage due to premium costs soaring this year

Starbucks workers say their health insurance premiums have soared this year, in some…

blocks.text: Starbucks workers say their health insurance premiums have soared this year, in some cases more than doubling, according to a recent survey conducted by Starbucks Workers United.

The survey of more than 130 Starbucks workers in both unionized and non-unionized stores, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found baristas are experiencing significant hikes in costs for their health insurance coverage starting 1 October.
Some workers reported their premium costs per paycheck nearly doubling, even as they struggle to afford other basic necessities andare scheduled to work enough hours to be eligible for the benefits.

The changes come as Starbucks Workers United launched a boycott last month against the company demanding a union contract, what would be the first since stores started to unionize in December 2021. Since then, more than 700 Starbucks stores have won union elections, with the union representing over 12,000 workers at the company.
Several workers said they are opting to go without health insurance coverage due to the costs and the price hikes are forcing them to worry about whether they need to find an additional job.

Kaye-Lani Story, who has been a barista in Edina, Minnesota, for nine years, said she took herself and her son to the doctor this month as their health insurance is set to lapse on 1 October. Her health insurance premiums were set to go from $130 a week to $170 a week, a 30% increase.

“That is another $40 each week that I am not going to have in my income, if I choose to go with it, and that’s just not something that financially I can afford,” she said. “I have to drop my insurance because the company will not cover those costs when it’s clear that they’re definitely making enough.”
In the past, Kaye-Lani was qualified to receive Minnesota’s state health insurance, but switched to the company’s health insurance plan when she made too much income to qualify.

“I make too much to qualify for coverage through the state. I don’t make enough to keep my medical coverage through work, and so at this point, I just have to drop it completely,” she added. “During the winter, the heating bill goes up. During the summer, the electric bill goes up from the AC. There are just all these wavering things throughout the year that I have to pull from to be able to apply to expenses just to be able to keep a roof over my head and food on the table and whatnot, and then this happens, and it’s too much.”
Cory Wagner has relied on Starbucks’s health insurance for five of the seven years he’s worked as a barista at Starbucks in Woods Cross, Utah, outside Salt Lake City.

“This is the first year that [premiums] nearly doubled,” Wagner said. “My insurance rates are going up to a point where I am now having to consider getting a second job, potentially leaving the company.”

Wagner relies on a heart medication to be able to work and noted the health insurance premium cost increases have made the out of pocket cost of his medication unaffordable. His health insurance premium cost went from $70 per biweekly paycheck to $122 per paycheck this year.

“Now I’m kind of left at a point where I am choosing between paying for this medication and paying for my utility bills, paying for my groceries, paying for the gas that I need to get to work,” he said. “The company has the money to keep our insurance premiums the same. They have the money to help the partners that are actively making them money.”

Starbucks Workers United has filed an unfair labor practice charge after the company did not respond to a request for information on health insurance coverage changes regarding what prompted the fee hikes and how Starbucks’s contribution to the healthcare costs were affected.

A Starbucks spokesperson did not comment on the unfair labor practice charge but said in an email “like employers across the country, we continue to face rising healthcare costs while remaining committed to providing quality, affordable healthcare coverage for full and part-time partners at Starbucks, beginning at just 20 hours per week.”

articles.title: Why Sara Duterte skips questions related to her impeachment
articles.summary: 'Masyado nang maraming problema ang mga abogado ko ayaw ko nang dagdagan 'yong kanilang problema with the contempt,' the Vice President says

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte, along with legal counsels, arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over a grave threats case, on September 5, 2026.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
'Masyado nang maraming problema ang mga abogado ko ayaw ko nang dagdagan 'yong kanilang problema with the contempt,' the Vice President says
Vice President Sara Duterte is at least taking notes from her ongoing Senate impeachment trial.
She is now aware and careful about possibly violating the sub judice rule that bars parties, including herself, from discussing the merits of her ongoing impeachment case.

“Mako-contempt ako, sir, eh kapag sumagot ako sa impeachment (I will be cited in contempt if I answer questions related to impeachment),” said the Vice President during an ambush interview with reporters in Banga, South Cotabato on Monday, September 21.

“Masyado nang maraming problema ang mga abogado ko, ayaw ko nang dagdagan ‘yung kanilang problema with the contempt (My lawyers have a lot of problems already and I don’t want to add to that list a possible contempt),” she added.

Under Rule 18 of the Senate impeachment rules, the presiding officer, senator-judges, prosecutors, members of the defense team, respondents, as well as witnesses, are barred from disclosing to the public matters related to the trial.

Presiding officer Chiz Escudero reminded the parties of this rule on August 26, and set the possible penalties against violators. This includes public reprimand or admonition for the first offense, and then a P30,000-fine for each subsequent offense.

blocks.caption: Can sub judice rule stop Sara Duterte from talking about her trial?

blocks.text: Apart from reiterating the rule to the prosecution and the defense, Escudero also reminded the Vice President’s camp that the sub judice rule also applies to Duterte.

Prior to Escudero’s August 26 reminder to the parties, Duterte talked about her impeachment trial in some of her media interviews. Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro also said in the past that Duterte allegedly violated the rule through a social media post where the Vice President defended her staff from the remarks of senators.
Defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa said in August that he would sit down with Duterte to discuss Escudero’s reminder.
On Monday, Poa confirmed that he had already talked to Duterte. He said that his client is “receptive” to his feedback.

“At hindi ko naman i-deny na nagkaroon na ng pag-uusap between myself and the Vice President on what I think is skirting sub judice, skirting contempt. At very receptive naman po ang ating Vice President,” Poa told reporters during his Monday briefing. “So may mga ganyan kaming pag-uusap…. At usually naman, she values our opinion.”

(And I won’t deny that the Vice President and I already discussed what I think is skirting sub judice, skirting contempt. And the Vice Presdient is very receptive. So we have already talked about it. And usually, she values our opinion.)
The prosecution is currently presenting evidence about Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth — the last articles of impeachment to be presented against the Vice President.

Simultaneously, the Vice President is also facing a criminal case, grave threats, at a Quezon City Regional Trial Court due to her alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data
articles.summary:
Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests

Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’…

blocks.text: Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones.
The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took.
Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations had complained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy.

The DPC inquiry was prompted by research by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018 which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars).
The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data.
It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests.

“Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC.
“Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals.
“It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added.

Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”

The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, which claimed Google used “various tricks” to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled.

“Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council.
BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”.

Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”.
The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020.
after newsletter promotion
Imposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months.
It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland.
It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m.

Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner.

“As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.
“The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle.
There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage.

articles.title: Trump accused of ‘manufacturing a national security justification’ to push arch plan – US politics live
articles.summary: President had said the triumphal arch he plans to build near Washington would double as a ‘military complex’

blocks.text: Key events

items: nowCNN, MS NOW and Politico to sue over White House ban
8m agoTrump accused of 'manufacturing a national security justification' to push arch plan

blocks.text: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to sue over White House ban

MS NOW, CNN and Politico said they were suing the Trump Administration ⁠to protect their First Amendment ​rights after ‌president Donald Trump’s ‌announcement that he would ban ‌them from the White House’s building grounds.

The three news outlets said they had notified the government that they were ‌filing their lawsuit in the US District Court for ​the District of Columbia and could see emergency hearings in the case as soon ⁠as this week, according to ​CNN.
All three news outlets had hinted at legal action, saying they would vigorously defend their First Amendment rights.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the outlets said in a joint statement posted on X. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”
Representatives ​for the White ​House did not immediately respond ​to ‌a request from Reuters ​for ​comment outside normal business hours.
Trump accused of 'manufacturing a national security justification' to push arch plan
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump was accused of “manufacturing a national security justification” to push forward his plans for a triumphal arch.

The president said yesterday that the planned structure near Washington would double as a “military complex” housing drones and snipers, making it ⁠the second major construction project he ⁠has sought to justify on national security ​grounds.

“The president’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nicolas Sansone, one of the attorneys representing litigants suing to stop the plan, said on Sunday. “Congress has not authorized the arch and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward.”

The ⁠arch and plans for the White House ballroom are part of Trump’s broader effort to remake the nation’s capital, including the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the redevelopment of a golf course in East Potomac Park and a push to add his name to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
The ⁠initiatives have drawn criticism from preservationists and others who argue they would alter some of Washington’s most prominent historic landmarks.

US representative Don Beyer, a Democrat whose Virginia district includes Arlington National Cemetery, posted on Sunday that operating drones so close to the airport would be dangerous and impractical, and suggested the move was aimed at bolstering the administration’s legal position.

“Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security,” Beyer, who has introduced legislation to block the arch’s construction, wrote in a social media post.

In a social media post, Trump said that at the “strong request” of the military he ​had agreed to turn the planned 250 ft (76m) arch “into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, ‌store, and have the rapid ability to use large ‌numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”
In other developments:

items: Trump refused to ​say whether he would attempt to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the iconic facility on Washington’s Potomac River. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump ​repeated his belief that the center should append ‌his name to the building ​in exchange for his work to raise money to ​renovate the facility.

Trump will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when Trump travels to the city for the upcoming UN General Assembly. The meeting is scheduled for later today and at Gracie Mansion, the official mayoral residence, according to Anna Bahr, Mamdani’s communications director.

Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan. As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry.

China’s leader Xi Jinping will visit the United States this week for talks with Trump, Beijing confirmed today, expressing hope they will strengthen “strategic stability” between the world’s two largest economies. Washington had already made clear that the leaders would meet in a bid to find common ground on trade disputes, artificial intelligence and broader strategic issues including Trump’s war in the Middle East.

A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and wounded a man on Sunday afternoon in Texas’s capital city of Austin, local authorities said, as protesters demonstrating against the Trump administration’s hardline anti-immigration campaign quickly gathered at the scene.

articles.title: Russia: Putin party retains majority in controlled parliamentary vote
articles.summary: Vladimir Putin's United Russia won just under 58% of the vote, the electoral commission said. Meanwhile, Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov won nearly 100% of the vote in elections in the Russian republic of…

image.caption: Putin has been in power since 1999Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Russian Gov/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that the ruling United Russia party has won the parliamentary election.

It's the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin has cast it as a referendum of support for what is termed in Russia, the "special military operation."
Parties that support Putin and the Kremlin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition was barred from taking part.
The polls took place amid rising prices, a crackdown on political opponents and the internet, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.
War anxiety casts shadow over Russia's election
What do we know about the Russian election results?
The Central Election Commission said that with 95% of ballots counted, the party of Russian President Vladimir Putin won 57.83% of the vote.

Commission chair Ella Pamfilova said that according to the preliminary results, United Russia would get 355 seats in the 450-seat Duma, giving the party around 20 more seats than it currently holds and marking the strongest result in its history.

The parliamentary vote was also the first to include residents of four regions in Ukraine — those being Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia — that were occupied and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year.
Voting was also held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.
Record Ukrainian attack leaves Moscow ablaze on election day
Chechen ally receives nearly 100% of vote
Russia's electoral commission also announced that close Putin ally, Ramzan ​Kadyrov, has been re-elected to a fifth term as leader of Chechnya, a Russian republic in the North Caucasus region.
Electoral officials said he achieved 99.85% of the vote, a slight improvement from the 99.73% garnered in 2021.
International observers have previously severely criticised electoral processes in the small region.
Kadyrov's government has been accused of widespread rights violations by human rights organizations, including targeting journalists and homosexuals, something he denies.

blocks.caption: Ramzan Kadyrov's forces have been part of Russia's full-scale invasion of UkraineImage: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP

articles.title: House ends plenary debates on proposed 2027 COA budget
articles.summary: The House of Representatives on Monday terminated plenary deliberations on the Commission on Audit"s (COA) proposed 2027 budget, bringing it one step closer to inclusion in the General Appropriations…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 6:47pm

The House of Representatives on Monday terminated plenary deliberations on the Commission on Audit’s (COA) proposed 2027 budget, bringing it one step closer to inclusion in the General Appropriations Bill.
Akbayan Party-list Representative Perci Cendaña moved to terminate the deliberations after less than two hours of interpellation.
Although he did not ask any questions, Cendaña expressed concern over the reduction in COA’s capital outlay.

“This is a critical part in their efforts to digitize and computerize the systems within this critical government agency. And I hope that at a certain point, we will be able to restore the necessary capital outlay for the COA,” he said.
Davao del Sur Rep. John Tracy Cagas sponsored COA’s proposed budget of P16.46 billion, inclusive of automatic appropriations.

Cagas said that, excluding automatic appropriations and considering only new appropriations subject to congressional approval, COA’s proposed budget totals P14 billion, 2.49% higher than its 2026 budget.

“The proposed budget is a vital investment in good governance. By equipping COA with the necessary resources, we are strengthening its capability to conduct rigorous audits, expand its workforce of dedicated state auditors, and adopt digital innovations that bring greater transparency to government transactions,” Cagas said.
“To starve COA of resources is to weaken our defenses against… corruption. To support COA is to fortify the integrity of our entire bureaucracy,” he added.

During the interpellation, Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco questioned COA about its audit report on the House of Representatives, the Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) of lawmakers, and the House’s allocation for supplies and materials.
Cagas said the plenary deliberations should focus on COA’s proposed budget.

“They are here to seek our support. As for the House budget as early as 2024 and 2023, to be fair to COA, their report is there and they have already provided it. If we have some speculation or suspicion, that’s not fair to COA, is it?” he said.
“They are doing their job, and it is reflected in the annual audit report. There is nothing being hidden there; it is open,” he added.
Tiangco clarified that he was not doubting COA and that he fully supported its proposed budget.
Cagas later said, however, that he would no longer answer questions regarding the House’s expenses in 2024 and asked Tiangco to submit his questions in writing.
Tiangco said his questions concerned COA’s audit report, which falls within the agency’s mandate.
“But if the distinguished sponsor no longer wants to answer any questions, then there is nothing we can do. Then we will stop asking questions,” he said.
Before the deliberations on COA’s budget, Tiangco had questioned why the plenary deliberations on the House of Representatives’ own budget were moved from September 24 to September 17.
His attempt to reopen the debate was denied.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Banished to alien lands – Trump’s secret deportation deals | First Thing
articles.summary:
Thousands of people deported from the US to countries where they have no connections. Plus, European spy chiefs warn of Moscow action against Nato

Good morning.

After a plane journey…

blocks.text: Good morning.

After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands of people deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US, intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

The Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Forbidden Stories. The consortium reviewed documents and interviewed more than 100 people on the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration.

items: At what scale are third-country deportations happening? Since returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own.
Which countries are people being deported to? The Trump administration has struck 35 deals allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to countries where they often have no connections.

Is this legal? A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration’s third-country removals policy was unlawful. A three-judge panel unanimously agreed that it violated due process. But the government has 90 days to appeal against the court’s decision, and is expected to do so.

blocks.text: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato

blocks.caption: There are fears Vladimir Putin’s regime is making preparations for more decisive action in Europe. Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP

blocks.text: European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”, the Guardian’s Shaun Walker reports.

The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months.
The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

items: How imminent is the threat? Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy. “It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said.

blocks.text: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign

blocks.caption: Smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saturday. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against it.

Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

items: What has Iran said? The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack did take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.

What has caused the outburst of sabre-rattling? It appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force.

blocks.text: In other news …

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz is facing growing calls to quit. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA

items: Friedrich Merz, Germany’s chancellor, has vowed to stay in office, despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.
Gavin Newsom, the California governor, has signed off on a package of bills aimed at bolstering election security, including measures to block federal political interference.
Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the assassination of the Haitian president, Jovenel Moïse, who was killed in July 2021, according to US officials.
Starbucks workers say their health insurance premiums have soared this year, in some cases more than doubling, according to a survey conducted by Starbucks Workers United.

blocks.caption: Fast-tracking vaccine development could massively cut death rates, say scientists. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

blocks.text: An extra 2.7 million lives could be saved in the next pandemic if countries share vaccines in a less selfish way, a new study has found – although the death toll in richer countries would rise. Researchers modelling a hypothetical global outbreak of flu found that fast-tracking vaccine development could cut deaths from 58.5m to 23.9m.

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation has summoned the Department of Public Works and Highways' regional director in Davao through a subpoena as part of its investigation into alleged anomalous flood control projects in the city.

The subpoena, issued on September 17 and served on Monday, September 21, ordered DPWH Region XI Director Juby Blancaver Cordon to appear before the NBI and submit documents related to the investigation.
Cordon was directed to appear before the bureau at 1 p.m. on September 24 and turn over records covering 51 flood control projects.

The summons follows NBI Director Melvin Matibag's disclosure last week that the bureau had obtained documents on nearly 50 projects in Davao City that had been flagged for possible irregularities, including alleged ghost or substandard projects.

Matibag also previously said P1.9 billion worth of flood control projects in the district of Davao City Rep. Paolo Duterte had been awarded to a contractor whose owner he described as close to the Duterte family.

articles.title: Second Philippine exporter ships Carabao mangoes to Canada
articles.summary: Weekly shipments are planned as exporters build a larger Canadian market.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 6:14pm
Stock photo of Philippine mangoes sold at a market.
Wikimedia Commons

MANILA, Philippines — A second Philippine exporter has begun shipping Carabao mangoes to Canada, flying one metric ton to Vancouver as the government looks for new overseas buyers for the iconic sweet fruit.
The 250 cartons from Mensch FilAm Corp. were flown to Vancouver on September 18 and are bound for Vancouver distributor Fresh Makers Ltd., the Department of Agriculture said Monday, September 21.
The cargo adds a second supply line into Canada after the first-ever shipment of Carabao mangoes in June.

The export of Carabao mangoes first entered the Canadian market in June, when the DA sent off 1 metric ton to Toronto supplied by Hi-Las Marketing Corp. and Castillo Import Export Ventures Inc. and imported by Ontario-based TSI Tropicals Inc.
That supply chain delivered 100 cases to T&T Supermarket in the Vancouver area on September 9, according to the Philippine Consulate General in Vancouver.

The consulate said Mensch FilAm is the second major exporter supplying the Canadian market and shipments would arrive weekly at retailers and Asian supermarkets in Greater Vancouver and the Pacific region, with distribution to central and eastern Canada to follow.
Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said the shipment is part of a wider government effort to open new markets for Philippine farm products and raise agricultural export earnings.
State of Carabao mango exports
Most Carabao mangoes are sold at home.

The country produced about 710,000 metric tons of mangoes in 2025, and about 92% of the fruit is consumed locally, with the rest exported mainly to Hong Kong, South Korea and Japan, according to the Department of Science and Technology's Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development (DOST-PCAARRD), citing Philippine Statistics Authority data.
Canada is one of several new markets the government has pursued for the Carabao mango. In June 2025, the DA announced the first commercial shipment of Philippine mangoes to Italy.

articles.title: Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows
articles.summary:
Chancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own party

•

blocks.text: Friedrich Merz called it a “disaster”, and that was even before the full scale of the catastrophe for himself and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came into view after Sunday’s state elections.

In what one outlet called a “power move”, the German chancellor made a highly unusual televised speech just minutes after polls closed in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, attempting to get ahead of the narrative with a pledge to stay on and fight for his economic recovery programme.

But as the results trickled in, it became apparent that the CDU had not only scored its worst-ever result in a state election, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it had crashed out of a regional parliament altogether for the first time in postwar history with just 4.9% of the vote in the region on the Baltic coast.
The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came out on top for the third time in a German state, drawing 38% against 35.5% for the centre-left Social Democrats, Merz’s federal coalition partner.

Although the AfD has little chance of taking power because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties, the anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly party could celebrate a further success in destabilising the German political establishment.

In Berlin, the CDU will almost certainly have to vacate city hall once the coalition negotiations wrap up after a stinging defeat to the leftwing Linke party, which is calling for the expropriation of corporate landlords to address a housing crisis.

Polls had been predicting the humiliating result for Merz’s conservatives, which came after a historic rout two weeks ago in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the CDU scored just 17% to the AfD’s nearly 44%.

But the cumulative effect of these losses, coupled with Merz’s dire approval ratings and a far right with clear momentum, can hardly be exaggerated. Despite his vow to stay the course, many regard the German leader to be on borrowed time.

“Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival,” said the Berenberg bank’s chief economist, Holger Schmieding. “Although Merz has vowed to stay on as chancellor to spearhead the much needed pro-growth reforms, it will not be easy for him to contain the unrest within his party.”

Speculation was already rife after the Saxony-Anhalt race about a Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap. But as long as none of the potential successors appears ready to wield the dagger, and Merz remains unwilling to step aside, a volatile deadlock will reign.
after newsletter promotion
Merz, 70, gathered the CDU leadership at the party headquarters in Berlin to watch the exit polls together late on Sunday.

Local media reported that some of those assembled loudly objected to the defiant, full-steam-ahead speech he planned to deliver regarding his programme, saying that it amounted to ignoring what voters were shouting from the rooftops with their choices.
Merz cancelled a planned trip to New York this week to speak before the UN general assembly, already anticipating he would need to be in Berlin to grapple with the state elections’ aftermath.
Now, more than ever, he will have his work cut out for him after just 16 months in office.

articles.title: When the Press Was Silenced, Who Kept the Stories Alive?
articles.summary: There was a time when the question was not whether you could find information, but whether you were allowed to

blocks.text: There was a time when the question was not whether you could find information, but whether you were allowed to publish it.

When Martial Law was declared in 1972, newspapers, radio stations, and television networks were shut down or placed under government control. Journalists critical of the government faced arrest and other forms of repression. Yet the press did not disappear entirely. An alternative press emerged — made up of journalists, student editors, religious groups, workers, and others who continued to put stories into the public sphere despite the risks.

They came to be known as the “Mosquito Press.” The name itself was meant to diminish them, as something so small and annoying can easily be clapped to death. But what made the metaphor powerful was precisely what it implied: even something small could be persistent enough to make itself heard.
Decades later, the way we tell and consume stories has changed dramatically.

We no longer have to wait for tomorrow’s newspaper or the evening news to know what is happening. A phone can bring us breaking news, livestreams, commentaries, vlogs, podcasts, and countless opinions within seconds. A student journalist can publish a story online and reach people far beyond their campus. A creator can explain an issue to millions from a bedroom. A single post can spark a national conversation.
But the same technology that has made information more accessible has also made it harder to determine what deserves our trust.

In the Philippines, social media remains a major source of news, while creators and influencers increasingly play a role in how people encounter current events. The 2026 Reuters Institute Digital News Report found that social media remains the dominant source of news in the country, while 36% of respondents said they consume content from creators or influencers who mainly focus on news. At the same time, overall trust in news fell to 28% in the report’s survey.

This does not mean that every vlogger is a journalist, or that every creator is spreading misinformation. In fact, creators can make complex issues more accessible and bring important conversations to audiences that traditional media may not always reach.
But it does mean that the responsibility of telling stories no longer belongs only to the newsroom.
We are all participants in the information ecosystem.
We share. We repost. We comment. We create. We screenshot. We forward messages to group chats. We decide, often within seconds, what deserves our attention and what deserves to be believed.
And that raises an uncomfortable question: In a world where everyone can tell a story, who is responsible for telling it truthfully?
This is where the lessons of the past continue to matter.

The struggle for press freedom during Martial Law was not simply about newspapers or journalists. At its heart, it was about the public’s ability to access information, question those in power, and hear stories that might otherwise disappear.
Today, the challenge may look different.

We may have more platforms, more voices, and more information than ever before. But abundance does not automatically mean truth. A story can be buried by an algorithm. A false claim can travel faster than a correction. A carefully researched report can compete for attention against a 30-second video designed to go viral.
For young people especially, this changes what journalism asks of us.

For student journalists, the responsibility is not only to produce the next issue of a campus paper. It is to ask better questions, verify before publishing, give context, listen to the people behind the story, and understand that every piece of information we put into the world can shape how someone understands an issue.
For audiences, it means becoming more critical of what we consume and share.
And for all of us, it means recognizing that press freedom is not only a concern for journalists. It is a public concern.
Because when the press is free, people have more space to question, scrutinize, participate, and make informed decisions. When information is restricted or distorted, everyone is affected.
This is why remembering Martial Law cannot simply be an exercise in looking backward. It is also an invitation to ask what we are doing with the freedom, platforms, and tools we have today.
Remembering through film

As we commemorate the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law this year, 2030 Youth Force in the Philippines Inc. is bringing this conversation to the screen through #SineSDGs, our youth-led film screening initiative that uses cinema to connect stories with issues that matter to young people and communities.

With the screening of Portraits of Mosquito Press, a documentary by JL Burgos that revisits the history and struggles of the alternative press during the Marcos dictatorship. The film draws from the experiences of Jose “Joe” Burgos Jr., his family, and the college editors who helped build an alternative newspaper while facing harassment, arrest, and raids.
For us, the film is not only an opportunity to remember a difficult chapter in Philippine history. It is an opportunity to pause and ask what that history means in the present.
What does press freedom look like when news can come from a TikTok video as easily as a newspaper?
What happens when misinformation can reach thousands before a journalist has the chance to verify the facts?
What responsibility comes with having the power to publish?
And perhaps most importantly: What stories will we choose to keep alive?

These are conversations we hope to open with young people, especially student journalists and aspiring storytellers who are growing up in an information landscape vastly different from the one the Mosquito Press navigated.
The tools may have changed. The platforms may have changed. But the responsibility to seek truth, tell stories with care, and protect the public’s right to information remains.
This is what #SineSDGs hopes to create: not simply a movie screening, but a space to watch, reflect, question, and talk about what stories mean for the world we are building today.
Join us for #SineSDGs: Portraits of Mosquito Press on September 25 at 7 PM at Basta Cafe, Quezon City, followed by a post-screening dialogue with Director JL Burgos.
Tickets are ₱300, with limited slots available. A portion of the proceeds will support youth-led activities of 2030 Youth Force in the Philippines.
Because sometimes, remembering the past is not about staying there.
It is about understanding what it asks of us now.

articles.title: Sara Duterte remained company director even after assuming VP post -- witness
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte remained one of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President, a witness from…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:56pm

Vice President Sara Duterte remained one of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President, a witness from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Monday.

SEC Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo Fernando del Rosario made the testimony during Day 27 of the impeachment trial of Duterte, saying the Vice President’s position in the said firm was reflected on Metro City Chow Foods Corporation submissions to the SEC.
“Ayon po sa GIS nila from 2022-2024, si VP Sara Duterte ay member pa rin po ng Board of Directors,” Del Rosario said, referring to General Information Sheet.
(Based on its GIS from 2022 to 2024, Vice President Duterte is a member of the Board of Directors [of Metro City Chow Foods Corp.)
Asked about the following year’s filing, the SEC official confirmed: “Member pa rin siya ng Board of Directors sa GIS ng 2025.”
(The GIS of the same firm showed the Vice President remained as one of the Board of Directors in year 2025.)

Asked by private prosecutor Erwin Matib to explain what a board does, Del Rosario described its authority over the corporation’s business and property, as well as its responsibilities to shareholders and government agencies.
On the board’s role in conducting the company’s business, Del Rosario replied, “Hindi po siya makakapag-conduct ng business kung wala po siyang Board of Directors.”
(A firm cannot conduct business without a Board of Directors.)
Prohibited under 1987 Constitution
Also on Monday, Del Rosario said the Constitution prohibits the Vice President from participating in any business as provided under Article 7, Section 13 of the Constitution.

During the same hearing, Del Rosario said that GenCorp. Industries Inc. (GenCorp), a firm declared by Vice President Duterte as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), did not list her as an incorporator or director based on the firm’s General Information Sheet and Audited Financial Statement submitted to the SEC.

Del Rosario made the confirmation when he was asked by prosecutor Eric Matib and later on by Senator Joel Villanueva if SEC records showed any involvement of the Vice President with GenCorp given that the Vice President listed it as one of her business interests in her 2023, 2024 and 2025 SALNs or during her term as Vice President.
“Wala po siya sa [company records ng] GenCorp,” Del Rosario said.
(Her name is not in GenCorp.)

Senator judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian then quizzed Del Rosario as to possible scenarios which would explain the Vice President’s declaration of the firm as one of her business interest even if the company’s SEC submissions does not say so.
“Ano po ang posible na nangyari rito?,” Gatchalian said.
(What possibly happened here?)
Del Rosario then said that possibly, the Vice President could be behind the largest subscriber of GenCorp.

“If GenCorp has a corporate subscriber with a controlling interest…based on its GIS, it has corporate subscriber, JTC Group of Companies, which holds 55% of the company’s equity. If I am to give an example [scenario], maaring ang may-ari ng JTC ay si VP Sara, para magkaroon siya ng control dito sa GenCorp na kung saan hindi mag-aapear ‘yung pangalan niya [sa corporate records].
Del Rosario said that based on SEC records, JTC Group of Companies is represented by a certain Jaime T. Cruz.
“Yun po ang isang scenario; kung talagang siya ay may control ng JTC,” Del Rosario added.
(That is one possible scenario, if she is in control of JTC," Del Rosario added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Weather tracker: Japanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon again
articles.summary:
Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet

Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding…

blocks.text: Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back into a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.

Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.

Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.

The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.

South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

articles.title: Kids' repeated online exposure to school violence magnifies fear, confusion --NCMH
articles.summary: Authorities warned the public about the risks associated with young people repeatedly viewing violent online content about school shootings.

blocks.text: Following the latest fatal school shooting incident in Banga, South Cotabato, authorities warned the public about the risks associated with young people repeatedly viewing violent online content about school shootings.

The National Center for Mental Health (NCMH) emphasized on Monday that while social media plays an important role in disseminating information, excessive availability of graphic content on school violence, especially misinformation, can harm students, even those who did not experience the event firsthand.

“Social media can help disseminate information… However, social media can also magnify. Napapalala niya ‘yung fear, ‘yung confusion, and ‘yung emotional distress, especially when young people are repeatedly exposed,” NCMH Medical Center Chief Dr. Noel Reyes said on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon.

(Social media can help disseminate information… However, social media can also magnify things. It worsens fear, confusion, and emotional distress, especially when young people are repeatedly exposed.)
“Lalong-lalo na ngayon ‘yung graphic video, photographs, ‘yung mga opinyon ng iba, speculations, and unverified reports,” he added.
(Especially nowadays with graphic videos, photographs, opinions of others, speculations, and unverified reports.)
Reyes said prolonged consumption of content related to school violence could foster a sense of ongoing threat that may trigger anxiety or intrusive memories in children.

“Even if the child is not present during the incident, repeated exposure may make that a threat. Parang ongoing pa [sa kaniya] ‘yung threat kasi parati siyang exposed doon. They may contribute to anxieties, sleep difficulty, and intrusive memories,” Reyes said.

(Even if a child was not present during the incident, repeated exposure can cause them to perceive it as an active threat. It feels as if the threat is still ongoing because they are constantly exposed to it. This can contribute to anxiety, sleep difficulties, and intrusive memories.)
The NCMH emphasized the importance of close parental monitoring and guidance, especially for children who spend significant time online.
Reyes advised parents to consider setting limits not only on screen time or internet access, but also on the platforms their children visit, engage with, and the content they consume.
He added that adults should be ready and willing to address questions or content that requires parental intervention, which includes explaining right from wrong and reporting harmful online content.
Preventive measures
According to the NCMH, while mental health literacy among Filipinos has noticeably increased, broader mental health promotion needs further reinforcement.

The agency pointed out that student-initiated school violence should not merely be addressed after a crisis occurs, but prevented beforehand by establishing a whole-of-community mental health support system.

“Unang-una po… there should be a mental health promotion for all students. This includes [having] a safe and nurturing school environment, school emotional learning, sustained anti-bullying programs, ‘yung mga responsible digital citizenship po, ‘yung mga parent education and training,” Reyes said.

(First and foremost… there should be mental health promotion for all students. This includes fostering a safe and nurturing school environment, social-emotional learning, sustained anti-bullying programs, responsible digital citizenship, and parent education and training.)
To promote mental health, the NCMH stated it is willing to launch school caravans to help expand mental health awareness and literacy across academic institutions.
Reyes noted that Filipinos are sometimes deterred from seeking help due to the stigma surrounding mental health in the country, which is often tied to shame.

“Sometimes kasi napipigilan ang pag-seek ng intervention because of stigma. Base po sa ating kultura na tinitignan po talaga nating mga kapwa Pilipino na ang karamdaman sa pag-iisip o kaguluhan sa pag-iisip ay senyales po ng kahinaan or kaya nagdudulot po sa kanila ng shame,” Reyes said.
(Sometimes, seeking intervention is hindered by stigma. Culturally, many Filipinos still view mental illness or psychological distress as a sign of weakness, or something that brings shame.)
“Hindi po ganon ang mental illness. Agaran po natin dapat tanggalin ang stigma upang ang intervention ay right time,” he added.
(Mental illness is not like that. We must immediately eliminate this stigma so that intervention occurs at the right time.)
In addition to the early identification of students in need of mental health assistance, the NCMH stated that schools must provide targeted support for these students.
This includes ensuring access to school counselors or caregivers, establishing preventive wellness programs, and maintaining partnerships with mental health institutions or referral centers.

The NCMH encourages individuals who need mental health support to call its 24/7 crisis hotlines (1553 or 0919-057-1553) or avail free online psychosocial support by scheduling sessions at www.ncmhusaptayo.com.
Parents, teachers, and peers are encouraged to closely monitor children and friends for significant physical and emotional behavioral changes that may signal emotional distress.
Emotional and physical red flags in children experiencing distress may include intense fear of school, nightmares, and stress-induced symptoms like headaches, tremors, or cold extremities.

Meanwhile, more severe indicators could include expressions of hopelessness, alcohol abuse, or self-harm, which all signal a critical need for immediate parental and professional intervention. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Toby Tiangco's attempt to reopen plenary debate on House budget denied
articles.summary: An attempt by Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco on Monday to reopen the plenary debate on the budget of the House of Representatives was denied.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:39pm
An attempt by Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco on Monday to reopen the plenary debate on the budget of the House of Representatives was denied.
During the plenary session of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, Tiangco questioned the changes of the budget hearing of the House from September 24 to September 17.

"Kaya po tayo nagbibigay ng schedule ng budget is para po makapaghanda yung mga members na magtanong. So kung ang budget ng House ay September 24 pa, natural po ang paghahandaan muna ay yung mga September 18, September 21. So mas logical kung doon po humugot," Tiangco said.

(The reason we provide the budget schedule is so that the members can prepare the questions they want to raise. So, if the House budget is scheduled for September 24, naturally, the members would first prepare for the September 18 and September 21 budget hearings. So, it would be more logical to draw from those instead.)
"So I'm asking for a motion for reconsideration to reopen the budget of the House and be presented to the plenary," he added.
However, Deputy Speaker Janette Garin denied Tiangco's motion, saying that Tiangco was unable to vote during the plenary debate of the budget hearing the lower chamber.

"Section 105 of our rules states, 'when a national report or motion is approved, adopted, or lost, a member who voted with the majority may move for its reconsideration on the same or succeeding session day'," Garin said.

"As we have conferred with the Secretary-General, the Honorable Toby Changco was on official travel abroad. Hence, with due courtesy, Hon. Toby Tiangco, your motion for reconsideration is out of order," she added.
The interpellation on the proposed P27.9 billion budget for Congress was terminated on Thursday, September 17.
The budget covers the Senate, House of Representatives, Commission on Appointments, and the House and Senate Electoral Tribunal. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Flights cancelled at airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland
articles.summary: British Airways and easyJet among those to cancel or delay services after air traffic control fault at Prestwick

blocks.text: Flights are being disrupted in parts of the UK after National Air Traffic Services was hit by its second technical issue in a fortnight.
A number of departing and arriving flights at Scottish airports have been severely delayed, with disruption affecting Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England.
The fault has been reported at Nats’s second control centre, at Prestwick in Scotland.

Airlines including British Airways and easyJet have reported immediate cancellations. A total of 24 flights have so far been cancelled across UK airports, according to the analysts Cirium. However, many flights continue to operate.

The issue comes less than two weeks after a major incident at Nats control centre in England disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers, and only three days after the release of an initial report into that incident by Nats promising to “continually improve the critical service we provide”.

A Nats spokesperson said: “Our engineers are continuing to investigate the issue at our Prestwick centre in Scotland. Airports south of Manchester are broadly unaffected, however flights heading north and flights departing Scottish airports are now subject to some delay.
“Passengers should check with their airlines. This is unrelated to the issue two weeks ago. We apologise for the disruption.”

An easyJet spokesperson said: “A Nats air traffic control system failure in its Prestwick centre is causing delays to flights with some unable to operate. This, once again, calls into question the resilience of Nats’s systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures.”

articles.title: Think Australia would be better off with less migration? The numbers tell a different story
articles.summary:
The population is ageing and we’re having fewer babies. Labor should keep that in mind as the migration debate rages

  • Get our

blocks.text: The intergenerational report lays bare how today’s growing anti-migration rhetoric clashes with a future where we need to attract people from overseas to help grow the economy and pay for our ageing population.
The “replacement” fertility rate is 2.1 children per woman – this is the average number of births to keep the population steady without migration and we’ve been below this level for 50 years.

The fertility rate is about 1.5 now and the IGR projects it will drop to 1.34 over the coming 40 years. This is how Treasury makes the alarming prediction that by the mid-2060s deaths will outnumber births for the first time.

There is no direct plan to reverse the trend for smaller Australian families, and Chalmers has made it clear Labor has no intention of repeating Peter Costello’s baby bonus or the former Liberal treasurer’s free advice on how many babies we should be having.

“When it comes to fertility rates, I do not and will not give people free advice about these very personal decisions that they make about whether to start a family and when to start a family,” the treasurer said on Monday.
Fair enough, but the seventh IGR tells a very familiar story that Australians are, on average, getting older – and this has big implications for the economy and the budget.
It means there is a smaller share of workers paying the taxes to fund the growing burden of paying for things associated with an ageing population, like healthcare and aged care.
Maintaining a healthy migration program has helped – and will help – Australia overcome these structural challenges.

As the IGR says: “Migration contributes to population growth and slows ageing, while supporting a multicultural society and strengthening the economy through skills, innovation and international connections.”
For those who think we would be better off with less migration, Treasury’s analysis provides some evidence that the opposite is true.
The IGR’s “baseline forecast” assumes a long-run net overseas migration (Nom) figure of 235,000 people a year.
This central case predicts real GDP per person – a reasonable proxy for average living standards – to grow from $99,200 in this financial year, to $157,300 in 40 years’ time.
Treasury economists then ran the numbers under a lower population scenario, where Nom was 50,000 a year less, and where the long-run fertility rate was 1.24, instead of 1.34.
Under this scenario, real GDP per person would be $400 lower in 2065-66 than under the baseline.
after newsletter promotion
That’s not much, but it’s working in the wrong direction.
The impacts of lower population growth are more stark when it comes to forecasts of what’s known as the “dependency ratio”.
In 2025-26, there will be 27.4 people aged 65 and over for every 100 working-age Australians. The IGR projects this ratio will soar to 40 by the mid-2060s; with lower migration it reaches 43.
That hits the budget.
The projected underlying cash deficit with lower population growth is 2.4% in 2065-66, instead of 1.8% under the existing assumptions.
Gross debt as a share of GDP is nearly 10 percentage points higher, at 32.2%.
These are the numbers that any responsible government has to keep in mind when trying to navigate its way safely through the shoals of migration politics.

articles.title: DOH debunks myths, shares facts about suicide
articles.summary: The Philippines observes Suicide Prevention Month every September to raise awareness about suicide prevention and help break the stigma surrounding mental health conditions.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:22pm
The Philippines observes Suicide Prevention Month every September to raise awareness about suicide prevention and help break the stigma surrounding mental health conditions.

The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday conducted the "Mindful Media: Capacity Development on Responsible Reporting and Ethical Portrayal of Suicide" in Quezon City to strengthen responsible and evidence-informed media practices and promote compassionate and ethical reporting on suicide.
Here are some of the myths about suicide debunked by the DOH:
MYTH: Talking about suicide with someone who is suicidal is a bad idea and can be interpreted as encouragement.
FACT: Talking about suicide can help a person explore options and prevent suicide.
MYTH: Someone who is suicidal is determined to die.
FACT: They may be ambivalent about living or dying. Access to support can help prevent suicide.
"We urge them to address the situation and we want them to have access to available support," said Jason Roque, officer-in-charge division chief of the DOH Health Promotion Bureau.
MYTH: Most suicides happen suddenly without warning.
FACT: Most suicides are preceded by warning signs.
Speaking to the media, Roque said there are warning signs that may indicate that a person is at risk of suicide.
These warning signs may be seen in a person's words, feelings and actions.
Words: Expressing hopelessness, wanting to die or asking about suicide methods.
Feelings: Severe sadness, mood swings, unexpected rage and loss of interest.
Actions: Withdrawal from usual activities and isolation.
MYTH: Once someone is suicidal, they will remain suicidal.
FACT: Heightened suicide risk is often short-term and specific to a situation.
"Suicidal thoughts are not permanent. It is short term and specific to a situation," Roque said.
"It's not permanent for an entire life of an individual because because a person can be triggered by different situations in their life," he added.
These situations may include relationship concerns, financial problems, conflict, disasters, violence, abuse and loss.
MYTH: Suicide is an appropriate means of coping with problems.
FACT: Suicide is not a constructive means of coping with problems.
Roque said it is better to talk to family members and peers when dealing with problems.
MYTH: Only people with mental disorders are suicidal.
FACT: Suicidal behavior can indicate deep unhappiness but does not necessarily mean that a person has a mental disorder.
"There are so many things that can lead to deep unhappiness that may trigger a suicide attempt or the act of suicide itself," Roque said.
MYTH: Suicidal behavior is easy to explain.
FACT: Suicide is complex and cannot be explained in simplistic ways.
"It's not easy. It's difficult to discuss because you cannot easily talk about it. Discussing it can feel like you're walking on eggshells," Roque said.
To help avoid the stigma surrounding suicide, the DOH also presented the following terms that the public may use when talking about suicide:

items: Instead of "committed suicide," use "died by suicide" or "dying by suicide."
Instead of "completed suicide" or "successful suicide," use "died by suicide."
Instead of "failed suicide attempt," use "suicide attempt" or "self-directed violence."
Instead of "non-fatal suicide," use "suicide attempt."

articles.title: Alleged 'ghost internet' scheme in DICT under Ombudsman probe
articles.summary: Did taxpayers pay for routers and internet that never worked?

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 5:20pm
Composite image shows Ombudsman Boying Remulla (L) photographed in April 2025 when he was still Justice secretary, and DICT Secretary Henry Aguda as seen in June 2025.
Senate PRIB; PNA / Yancy Lim, file

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman is investigating whether the government paid for internet connections that were never delivered and IT systems equipped with substandard or even fake software, in what investigators have dubbed a "ghost internet" scheme.
The fact-finding investigation centers on projects of the Department of Information and Communications Technology, including the government's Free Wi-Fi program.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said investigators are examining whether contracted internet sites were actually installed and functioning, whether the government was billed for connectivity that was never delivered, and whether prices for hardware, software and services were inflated.
One potential loophole, Clavano said, is that government inspections may have focused on physical equipment such as machines and routers without adequately checking the software installed in them.

"And there comes the loophole. A contractor can install cheaper, outdated, or even fake software while still charging the government full price for the real thing," Clavano said at a September 18 briefing.
"Because nobody verifies the software after the hardware is approved, the overpricing goes undetected."
Investigators are also looking into who approved, certified or authorized payment for projects that may not have been fully delivered.

"Were the contracted sites actually installed, and are they working? Was the government billed for connectivity and services that were never delivered? Were the prices of hardware, software, and services reasonable or were they inflated?" Clavano said.
Routers but no internet
The investigation also covers allegations that some sites under the government's Free Wi-Fi program had equipment installed but did not actually provide internet access.
"Kaya parang niloloko na lang ho 'yung taumbayan dahil sinasabi na may free internet, free Wi-Fi, 'yun pala naglalagay lang sila ng mga router na wala namang lumalabas na internet," Clavano said.
("So it appears the public is being fooled because they are told there is free internet or free Wi-Fi, when routers are installed but no internet service is actually coming through.")
The Ombudsman's inquiry remains at the fact-finding stage, and no findings of liability have been made.
The DICT said Sunday, September 20 that it has yet to receive formal notice of the investigation but is prepared to provide records, technical information and system data.
"Although no formal notice has been received from the Office of the Ombudsman to date, the DICT proactively welcomes the inquiry," the agency said.
The DICT said Secretary Henry Aguda has ordered tighter monitoring of the Free Wi-Fi program, including technical audits and contractual sanctions for reported inactive or non-performing sites.

The agency also said it upgraded its network monitoring system to provide real-time information on Free Wi-Fi sites and verify whether contractors are delivering the services for which the government is paying.

Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the three – a man and two women - as a "breakthrough".
Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice".
The three suspects are due in court on Monday morning.
Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday.

Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Published September 21, 2026last updated September 21, 2026
Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

blocks.caption: Plans for a highway toll (Maut) in Germany have so far failed Image: Bernd Wüstneck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.
Both of them deny the charges made against them.
What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.
The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.
But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.
The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.
Jail sentences possible
The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.
If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.
