articles.title: Rebel Wilson back in court as The Deb producers sue star over allegedly blocking film
articles.summary:
Hollywood actress appears in NSW supreme court in Sydney for the latest lawsuit over her directorial debut

  • Get our

blocks.text: Hollywood star Rebel Wilson had a “last chance” phone call with her film’s co-producers over a dispute about up-front costs and her $1m fee, a judge has heard.
The Pitch Perfect and Bridesmaids star appeared in the New South Wales supreme court in Sydney on Monday in the latest lawsuit over her directorial debut, a musical comedy named The Deb.
The film’s release was shelved in 2024 after Wilson fell out with co-producers.

Vince Holden, Gregor Cameron and Amanda Ghost claim Wilson and her company, Camp Sugar, breached consumer law concerning misleading conduct and breached various contracts when making allegedly defamatory statements about them to her 11 million Instagram followers in July 2024.
The producers claimed Wilson accused them of inappropriate conduct toward the lead actor in the film, embezzling funds and trying to block its release.
Wilson was accused of preventing the release by undermining negotiations with potential distributors and threatening an injunction against showing the film in Australia.

In a cross-claim, Wilson and Camp Sugar allege Ghost, Cameron and Holden’s involvement in the film was marked by “a troubling pattern of illicit egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct”.
Wilson claimed Ghost broke verbal agreements over writing credits and a soundtrack album deal and Cameron and Holden embezzled $900,000 from a joint venture company set up to make the film.
Wilson sat in the back row of the small courtroom, frequently typing on her phone, as her barrister, Dauid Sibtain SC, questioned one of the film’s producers.
Holden, part of AI Film Production Limited, which brought the lawsuit, was asked about a series of budget and financing emails regarding the 2024 film.
Holden agreed he asked for a “last-chance call” in October 2023 over AI Film’s requests for increased fees and Wilson’s offer to reduce her acting and directing fee to $1m.
Sibtain asked if Wilson had been incredibly upset and angry at AI Film’s proposed $300,000 fee rising to more than $650,000 plus finance costs without consulting her.
“I would not say upset,” Holden said.
“She didn’t like the fees being there.”
After he cut off further money towards the film, Holden told fellow producers: “the clock has stopped ticking and I’m waiting for the boom.”
“AI Film had advanced considerable funds to keep the production on time and we didn’t have a final agreement on fee levels,” he said.
AI Film had planned an “extremely bold investment” toward producing The Deb before securing a share of the rights to the film.
“You accepted that $15m was a lot of money to risk on a first-time director, do you agree?” Sibtain asked.
“Correct, yes,” Holden said.
after newsletter promotion
Holden agreed AI Film was “quite content to risk that money and see where it ended up” and that the risk increased when the budget “subsequently went up to over $20m”.
AI Film company directors claimed these alleged statements breached contracts and Wilson’s obligations as production company director.
That allegedly caused economic loss, a potential film distributor to withdraw an offer and reputational damage to the producers.
Wilson and her company had an initial fee of six per cent of the film’s budget, shared 50-50 with AI Film.
The Deb – eventually released in April 2026 – had multiple estimates for its potential worldwide revenue, starting from a predicted loss of $4.5m if it performed poorly.
If successful, the film could “break even” or make a multimillion-dollar profit, Justice Elisabeth Peden heard.
As a musical comedy with an Australian theme, The Deb’s predicted revenue was based on films Pitch Perfect, Muriel’s Wedding, The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and Strictly Ballroom.
“They were all breakout successes but some of them came out 15 to 30 years ago,” Sibtain said.
“When people went to cinemas, before streaming.”
The hearing continues.
The equity case comes after a blockbuster defamation trial in May involving Wilson and the star of her directorial debut.
Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes claimed she was defamed in four social media posts by Wilson but a judge in July dismissed the case.

articles.title: Sara Duterte declines comment on impeachment trial: I might be cited in contempt
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday declined to give any comment on the ongoing impeachment trial against her, saying she didn"t want to give her lawyers more problems if she is cited for contempt

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:01pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday declined to give any comment on the ongoing impeachment trial against her, saying she didn’t want to give her lawyers more problems if she is cited for contempt
Duterte balked at making any comment on the proceedings after two prosecutors were issued show-cause orders over comments they made regarding her trial.
“Mako-contempt ako sir, eh, kapag sumagot ako sa impeachment (I might be held in contempt if I talk about the impeachment),” Duterte said in an ambush interview.
“Masyado nang maraming problema ang mga abogado ko. Ayaw ko nang dagdagan yung kanilang problema with the contempt,” she added.
(My lawyers already have too many problems. I don’t want to add to their problems with the contempt.)
Duterte has yet to personally appear before the Senate impeachment court. She is represented by her defense team.
Her trial entered its 27th day this Monday, with the impeachment court tackling Article II, which accuses the Vice President of accumulating unexplained wealth.

The House prosecution panel has finished its presentation on Article I, which alleges misuse of confidential funds, as well as Article IV, which accuses her of making grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and others.
Receptive
Meanwhile, Michael Poa, the spokesperson of Duterte's defense team, said that he is always in constant communication with the vice president regarding statements on the trial.
"Hindi ko naman ide-deny na nagkaroon ng paguusap between myself and the vice president....Very receptive naman po ang ating vice president," he said in a press briefing.
(I won't deny that there were conversations between the Vice President and me.... Our Vice President is actually very receptive.)

"May mga bagay naman kaming napag-usapan na 'Kung sasabihin mo ito, palagay ko this will be covered by sub judice,' at 'Kung sasabihin mo man 'yung ibang bagay, I don't think naman sub judice 'yan.' So may mga ganyan kaming pag-uusap," Poa added.

(There were things we discussed like, 'If you say this, I think this will be covered by sub judice', and 'If you say other things, I don't think that's sub judice.' So we had those kinds of discussions.) –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Babies ‘will face almost twice as much’ extreme fire weather in Europe than great-grandparents
articles.summary:
Children born after 2025 will experience three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather as global heating intensifies

European babies will face almost twice as much extreme fire weather…

blocks.text: European babies will face almost twice as much extreme fire weather as their great-grandparents if climate action does not ramp up quickly, a study has found.

Global heating under current policies will expose a child born in Europe in 2025 to three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather over their lifetime than someone born in 1950, the researchers found.

The number of days with the most severe conditions for fires to burn hotter and spread further will rise fastest in the Mediterranean, where generation Beta, the demographic cohort born from 2025, is to face five more years of lifetime exposure to extreme fire weather than boomers, born in the two decades after the second world war.

The hot, dry and windy conditions that let small fires explode into raging infernos have been exacerbated by one-and-a-half centuries of fossil fuel pollution and the widespread destruction of nature, which has heated the planet by 1.4C. In Europe, which has warmed twice as fast as the global average, the worsening weather has increasingly fuelled monster infernos that overwhelm authorities.

Rosa Pietroiusti, a climate researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel and lead author of the study, said severe fire weather was a “necessary but not sufficient condition” for the kind of extreme fires that ravaged parts of Europe this summer. “The meteorological conditions are an important element of fire risk – the possibility of that fire happening, being super-destructive and difficult to control, and spreading very fast.”

The researchers combined demographic data with outputs from global climate models and tallied the number of days when fire weather was more severe than the worst 5% of days for that region in the reference period from 1985 to 2014. They considered 21 scenarios that resulted in 1.5C to 3.5C of global heating by the end of the century, a spectrum that roughly covers the best- and worst-case scenarios humanity is likely to face.

They found that under current policies, which will result in 2.6C of warming, children born today can expect to experience 84% more exposure to extreme fire weather than those born in 1950. They attributed 86% of the increase to climate change and 14% to people living longer.

If end-of-century warming is limited to 1.5C – a target likely to be crossed in just a few years – children born in 2025 would face 1.3 fewer years of extreme fire weather than under current policies, the study found.
Raúl Cordero, a climate scientist at the University of Groningen, who was not involved in the research, said it highlighted the “inherently intergenerational injustice” of climate breakdown.
after newsletter promotion

“Just one month ago, inhabitants of central Europe experienced fire-weather conditions that their parents or grandparents had never encountered. Unfortunately, these conditions materialised in record-breaking fires in Belgium and western Germany,” said Cordero, whose relatives were among the thousands who fled their homes in Germany in August. “An unstoppable fire engulfing a town? This kind of emergency would have been unthinkable for Germans of older generations.”

In southern Europe, the number of fires and the area burned have declined over decades as authorities have grown better at suppressing them, according to a study Cordero co-authored in July, but in recent years the trend has reversed. As well as hotter and drier weather, aggressive fire suppression – preventing even low-intensity fires – has led to buildups of flammable vegetation that has fuelled ferocious blazes in years when climatological conditions are ripe.

Relentless heatwaves and widespread drought plagued Europe this summer and led to explosive wildfires across France, Spain, Italy and several other countries. Across the EU, the severity of fire weather this year broke records, while the area burned is shaping up to be the third-worst on record.

The EU’s civil protection mechanism was activated nine times as countries scrambled firefighting planes and crews to assist overwhelmed neighbours. In her annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, paid tribute to a Danish firefighter pilot who died with a colleague in Greece last month, and announced plans for the creation of a European firefighting fleet.
“I am so proud of Europe’s response, of our European assets flying across the continent,” said von der Leyen. “But clearly, we need to think bigger and learn faster.”

articles.title: Identifying unclaimed ashes at N.S. funeral home through DNA ‘very challenging,’ says expert
articles.summary: DNA expert Dean Hildebrand says that getting DNA from ashes is very challenging due to the high heat and prolonged duration of cremation. This comes as families in Annapolis Valley struggle to…

image.caption: When East Coast Memorial recently took possession of Serenity Funeral Home in Coldbrook, N.S., the new staff discovered a 'significant number' of cremated remains. The company has been calling families so they can retrieve them. (Angela MacIvor/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

DNA expert Dean Hildebrand says that getting DNA from ashes is very challenging due to the high heat and prolonged duration of cremation. This comes as families in Annapolis Valley struggle to identify buried ashes that aren't who they thought they were.
Heat from cremation destroys all genetic material

While some families in the Annapolis Valley grapple with uncertainty after discovering they may not have buried the actual ashes of their loved ones, an expert in DNA testing says the technology only offers a faint hope of positively identifying the remains.

Several families who used the services of the former Serenity Funeral Home were informed by the home's new owners earlier this month that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones were found in storage.
Michelle Carey had used Serenity when her father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, died in 2018. Hank had specific instructions for his funeral arrangements, including dealing with the funeral home.

Now, having to go through the burial process all over again and being unsure whose remains the family actually buried, she says she’s skeptical that they’ll ever be sure of the identity of the remains.

“Well, my sister and I talked and did a little bit of research and it would be very, very difficult to do any sort of DNA testing,” says Carey. “How do we know for sure that what we're going to get is, in fact, our father's remains this time?”
Dean Hildebrand, who manages the Forensic DNA Laboratory at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, says it’s very challenging to get enough DNA from ashes to make an identification.

items: More stories from Annapolis Valley

blocks.text: “It's not to say that some people or some scientists have reported that you can still find trace amounts of DNA,” he says. “But finding trace amounts of DNA is different from being able to use that [DNA].”
Hildebrand says that DNA is surprisingly robust, noting that labs very often get full DNA profiles from human remains that were in car or building fires, despite the damage done.
But the conditions of a crematorium, 900 C for up to three hours, result in a total breakdown of all organic matter.

items: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating

blocks.text: "[It’s] kind of a worst-case scenario for isolating,” said Hildebrand.

He says throughout his career he’s dealt with identifying remains of ashes being mixed up involving other funeral homes. But in this case there are a significant number of remains, according to the new owners of Serenity funeral homes, East Coast Memorial.
While the odds of making an identification are low, Hildebrand says he wouldn’t say it’s impossible.
He said that it’s worth testing in case a fragment of bone could yield useful DNA.
“I think it's worth the effort,” he says. “But of course, you have to set expectations.”
Michelle Carey says she was told that the ashes the family buried may contain a small metal disc with an ID number on it, which could lead to identifying the remains.
But the presence of that ID number may be the only way to find out who they originally buried back in 2018.
“I want to believe that what they're telling me is true, that they do in fact have our father's remains,” says Carey. “But it will be very difficult to find out who is the person that was buried.”
The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating.

articles.title: 'Just plain panic': Fears mount as N.B. considers restricting U.S. hunters, anglers
articles.summary: Hunters and anglers from the United States as well as New Brunswick outfitters say they were caught off guard by the province's move to possibly "restrict" hunting and fishing licences in response to…

image.caption: Bradford Burns looks out at his fishing pools from his camp property alongside the Main Southwest Miramichi River. (Shane Fowler/CBC)

blocks.text: Bradford Burns grew up in Friendship, Maine, a town south of Augusta made up of just over 1,000 people. It rests on a peninsula and hosts a public wharf used by dozens of lobster fishers.

That included his grandfather. He’d spend time with him on the boat helping to place bait in lobster traps. But, as he grew up, his taste for fishing brought him inland. First for brook trout. Then he hooked his first salmon.

“There's just a lot of things that scratched a lot of itches for me,” said Burns. “I really got into it, and I really sort of abandoned saltwater fishing after I came here and started making this the focus of my fishing.”
"Here" is New Brunswick. For the last 25 years, Burns has made the six-hour drive from Friendship to Blackville multiple times a year.
This year, he stayed in New Brunswick from mid-June to mid-July, fishing the early salmon run before returning home to his wife, June.
This fall, he’ll spend another five weeks in the province fishing with companions he’s invited from the U.S. and reconnecting with locals.
He loves the wilderness and the people. But mostly he just loves a big fish.
“Every day it's a little different. Some of them pass up the river through the pool," Burns said.
"Those will stay here for a few days, and you'll see them jumping. You'll even get to recognize your particular fish for a few days, and then they're gone.
“It's just interesting to me and exciting and very natural and wild. And so I just like everything about it.”
At 75, Burns is very invested in salmon fishing. He’s bought multiple fishing camps on the shores of the Cains River and the Miramichi.
He owns the rights to Campbells and Keenans fishing pools in front of his fishing camp just outside of Blackville. He owns Doctor's Island in the town that hosts multiple fishing camps.

“I've spent over a million dollars in buying these camps up here and, you know, I don't know if I'll ever get it back,” said Burns, who made his money in the copy business. “But I figured, whatever I spent on it was for my hobby.”
That’s why the idea of not being allowed to obtain a New Brunswick fishing licence is unthinkable.
Hunters on both sides of border react to possible curb on hunting, fishing licences
On Sept. 10, Premier Susan Holt detailed responses to new tariffs from the U.S.

In the aftermath of President Donald Trump imposing new 50 per cent tariffs on select Canadian goods and blocking the import of Canadian alcohol, the province stated it would work to eliminate U.S. goods for government contracts. It would prioritize Canadian goods and work to develop supports for moving away from American markets.
But Holt stated hunting and fishing allowances for Americans could also be targeted.

A following news release from the province states that “the provincial government will continue to pursue additional measures, including undertaking a legislative review to explore giving the minister of natural resources the authority to restrict the issue of fishing and hunting licenses and mining claims based on certain criteria.”

CBC News called and emailed New Brunswick’s Department of Natural Resources communications officer Nick Brown for clarification on what that could mean for U.S. hunters and anglers. CBC News did not receive a response.
But Burns said he believes that could eventually mean hunting and fishing licences will not be available to Americans.

“What good would it do in New Brunswick to take [from] people like me or other people that live along the river; that own property?” asked Burns. “To say, 'Well, you can't come and spend your money here anymore because we're mad at the country, at these officials that have nothing to do with us.'"
Burns described himself as a "Trump Republican." He compared the province's threat of restricting American access to New Brunswick’s fish and wildlife to something his president would do.

“I think, just like Trump has done, is famous for doing, is to come out with these statements that are a little far-fetched, you know, sometimes to get people's attention,” said Burns. “I certainly hope that it's along those lines. I mean that it's not really a serious thought.”
Burns’s sentiment is shared among several New Brunswick outfitters and anglers.
“Putting this industry into that trade war is completely asinine,” said Larry Adair.

He owns Adair's Wilderness Lodge near Poley Mountain. He’s been guiding Americans on hunts since the 70s. Today, he said about 30 per cent of his business comes from the States. But he knows other outfitters, particularly those that cater to bear hunters, where Americans make up nearly 100 per cent of the clientele.
“A lot of our small outfitters, it would devastate them.”
He said his business is only starting to recover from the last time Americans were banned from hunting and fishing the province during the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to Adair, the typical American hunter pays between $3,000 and $5,000 a week to hunt at his outfitting business. That’s on top of paying the province significantly more for a non-resident hunting licence.

New Brunswick’s annual big game harvest reports do not break down sales of hunting licences to Americans. It categorizes them as resident and non-resident licenses. And for the last five years, the number of non-resident licences has been growing.

In 2021, there were 1,954 non-resident moose licences sold. Last year, there were 3,247 sold. In 2021, the province sold 198 deer non-resident licences. In 2025, it sold 363. The report does not tally black bear licences sold.
The cost of a non-resident licences is significantly more for non-residents.

A licence for hunting black bear costs $37 for a New Brunswicker, or $18 if you’re a senior. For non-residents, that same licence costs nearly four times as much — $143, plus a $26.25 application fee.

For a moose licence, New Brunswickers pay $72, or $37 for seniors, plus a $6.30 application fee. Non-residents pay more than seven times as much — $548 for that same licence plus a $26.25 application fee.
For an antlered deer licence, locals pay $34, or $19 for seniors. But non-residents pay five times more for a total of $183.
Adair said a significant portion of those non-resident licences are sold to Americans.
“They have to pay more than your average New Brunswicker or they pay a premium rate,” said Adair.

Those paying Americans have been coming to Upper Oxbow Adventures for more than a century. Co-owner Debbie Norton said her family has guided hunting and fishing guides for five generations now. Her family has lived on the same property alongside the Little Southwest Miramichi River for 203 years.

As an outfitter and the president of the New Brunswick Professional Outfitter Guide Association, she said restricting American hunters from purchasing licences for hunting and fishing would be “crippling.”
“I was a bit astonished and scared,” said Norton about her reaction to hearing about the possibility of restricting American hunters.
Norton said the amount of business the province's outfitters rely on from the States is massive.
"I would have to say that probably over 90 per cent of business in the hunting and fishing outfitting industry in the province comes from Americans," said Norton.
What she’s hearing from the provinces collective of hunting and fishing guides is dire.
“Panic; I think that sums it up the best,” said Norton. “Just plain panic.”
Norton said she and her husband host “hundreds” of Americans each year. She estimated that around 90 per cent of them are repeat customers.
“If somebody is your customer for 40 years, you develop a real friendship with them,” said Norton. “So it sounds a little silly maybe, but sometimes they come just to visit us.”

Norton said she and the association understand that “everything needs to be on the table” regarding Canada’s response to American tariffs. But she argued that American hunting and fishing parties bring in a lot of “new” money to the province, especially in rural areas.

“It's not the hugest industry in the province, but it is a real industry," she said. "It has a tremendous impact, particularly in rural New Brunswick because that's where the industry operates and it will have, should it go forward, it would have a very negative economic outcome for rural New Brunswick in my opinion.”

For Burns, he knows he’ll be able to continue fishing for salmon in the Miramichi and the Cains River throughout the fall until the end of the season. Until then he’s expecting a revolving door for friends coming up for a few days at a time to join him, most of them American. But after Oct. 15, he’ll pack up his fishing gear and head home to Friendship.
What happens over the winter months with New Brunswick’s legislative review will weigh on his mind while he waits to return to his camp for the fishing season to start again.
He said he’ll be at a loss if New Brunswick does move to restrict him from obtaining an angler's licence. It may mark the end of his time coming back to his riverside properties.
“I don't know what I would do,” said Burns. “I guess I'd have to sell it, especially if it was going to be a long-term thing.”

articles.title: Police officer and man injured in shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue
articles.summary: A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized…

image.caption: Belleville police officers stand outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue Sunday night. The incident occurred on the street in front of the synagogue. Last night, the synagogue was taped off as part of the crime scene. (CBC)

blocks.text: Canada

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.
Shooting occurred as members of Jewish community gathered for Yom Kippur

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in the southern Ontario community of Belleville as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, about 175 kilometres east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. and that both were taken to a hospital.

Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.

items: 'Canada's civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians,' Carney says in speech addressing antisemitism

blocks.text: Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway.

I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur.

My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to…—fordnation
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.

"I'm disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur," Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear" and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
"My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones," Ford said.
Surge in antisemitism
York Regional Police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Sunday's shooting comes months after Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.

Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.

Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

articles.title: SEC witness: VP Sara a member of corporation’s board while in office
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte remains a shareholder and member of the board of directors of a Davao-based corporation despite having already assumed office as vice president.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 4:55pm
MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte remains a shareholder and member of the board of directors of a Davao-based corporation despite having already assumed office as vice president.

This was revealed by documents presented before the Senate impeachment court on Monday, September 21, which showed that Duterte remained a member of the board of directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation even after she was elected vice president.

Upon presentation of the corporation’s general information sheet, Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo del Rosario confirmed that Duterte had both subscribed shares in and served as a member of the board of directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation.

According to Article 7, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution, provides that the president, vice President, members of the Cabinet and their deputies or assistants shall not “hold any other office or employment during their tenure,” in order to avoid conflicts of interest.

It also prohibits these officials, during their tenure, from “directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries.”
Duterte was elected in 2022 and assumed office on June 30 of that year.

According to the documents presented by the prosecution, Duterte was an incorporator of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation in 2016, holding a 20% ownership stake. She subscribed to P50,000 worth of shares, of which only P12,500 had been paid.
However, Duterte continued to serve on the corporation's board of directors and remained a shareholder from 2022 to 2025, during which she retained her 20% ownership stake.
The General Information Sheet of Metro Chow Foods Corporation also shows that Duterte was the corporation's second-largest shareholder, with 500 shares subscribed and P50,000 in subcribed capital.
The prosecution also presented documents showing Duterte's previous dealings with City Hall Chow Foods Corporation, where she served as a member of the board of directors in 2018.
The documents indicate that Metro Chow had not declared any dividents because it had no unrestricted retained earnings.

Under the Revised Corporation Code, the board of directors of a stock corporation may declare dividends only out of its unrestricted retained earnings. These dividends may be paid in “cash, property, or in stock to all stockholders on the basis of an outstanding stock held by them.”
However, despite the absence of dividends, Del Rosario explained that a shareholder or a director may receive “reasonable per diems” or a salary if the member is also an employee of the corporation.

“Ngayon kung shareholder na ito at ay director, maaari po siyang makatanggap ng additional let's say yung kanilang reasonable per diem o kung ang shareholder na to ay empleyado pa ng kumpanya maaring meron po siyang sweldo,” Dela Rosario said.

(Now, if this individual is a shareholder and at the same time a director, they may receive additional compensation, such as a reasonable per diem. Or, if this shareholder is also an employee of the company, they may be entitled to a salary.)
On Monday, the prosecution tackled Article II of the Articles of Impeachment against Duterte.

The article covers allegations of unexplained wealth, failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth from 2022 to 2024 and failure to divest from and willful continue business interests.

articles.title: NCMH: Suicide-related hotline calls rise to 35%; callers getting younger
articles.summary: The number of suicide-related calls to the government's mental health hotline has increased to 35%, with callers increasingly getting younger, the National Center for Mental Health (NCMH) said Monday.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 4:52pm

The number of suicide-related calls to the government's mental health hotline has increased to 35%, with callers increasingly getting younger, the National Center for Mental Health (NCMH) said Monday.

“On our 24/7 crisis hotline, the number of callers has quadrupled. Before the pandemic, 10% of callers were suicide-related, but now they account for 35% of all callers,” NCMH Medical Center Chief Dr. Noel Reyes said on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon.
“The number of callers experiencing problems related to self-harm has increased. The callers are also getting younger,” he added.
Reyes stressed that seeking mental health support is not a sign of weakness but an indication of self-awareness, courage and responsible decision-making.
The NCMH urged young people not to wait until their emotional burden becomes unbearable before seeking help or support.

“We must tell our young people that seeking help is not a sign of weakness but a form of self-protection. Protecting yourself is a sign of courage, self-awareness and, of course, responsible decision-making,” Reyes said.

The agency also urged adults to be more understanding of young people and avoid comparing their experiences with those of previous generations, noting that children are growing up in different environments.

Adults should listen to young people's feelings and emotional distress without judgment and avoid dismissing their concerns as being “dramatic” or telling them that they should be grateful because “others have it worse.”
Reyes said the neglect or invalidation of children's feelings is among the common reasons they refrain from seeking help even when experiencing severe emotional distress.
“Remember that this child is exposed to a different environment. The pressures they face are different from those we experienced while growing up,” Reyes said.
He said adults should respond with reassurance when a child opens up about emotional difficulties.

““Thank you for telling me. Thank you for opening up to me. Don't worry. I know you shouldn't have to face this alone. I will help and support you. I'll try to help you find the right support.' These are appropriate responses when a student opens up,” he said.
The NCMH issued the statement following another fatal school shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato.

The agency called on parents, teachers and peers to closely monitor children and friends for significant physical or behavioral changes that interfere with normal functioning, as these may indicate emotional distress.
Among the warning signs identified by the NCMH are an intense fear of going to school, intrusive thoughts and nightmares.
Adults should also watch for physical complaints such as headaches, stomachaches, constipation, cold hands and feet, tremors and palpitations, which may indicate anxiety or nervousness.

The NCMH said some children may exhibit more explicit warning signs, including expressing feelings of hopelessness or guilt, abusing alcohol or showing evidence of self-harm. These require immediate intervention from parents or mental health professionals.
Individuals who need mental health support can call the 24/7 crisis hotlines at 1553 or 0919-057-1553.
Free online psychosocial support is also available via video call. Sessions can be scheduled through www.ncmhusaptayo.com.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Ed Davey rejects claims party is ‘sleepwalking into irrelevance’ under his leadership – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Lib Dem leader says he is proud of party’s record at Brighton conference

Ed Davey has urged Andy Burnham to deliver some “home truths” to Donald Trump when they meet at the…

blocks.text: Ed Davey rejects claims party is 'sleepwalking into irrelevance' under his leadership

Good morning. Ed Davey became Lib Dem leader in 2020, which means he is technically the longest-serving leader of a national party in the UK. (“Technically” because, while Nigel Farage only became leader of Reform UK in his current incumbency in 2024, he had led it before when it was called the Brexit party and, if you include Ukip, he has been leader of the anti-migrant, anti-EU right in British politics for more than 20 years.) After six years in charge, it is inevitable that some Lib Dems are starting to complain and, with the Lib Dem conference taking place in Brighton, Davey has been giving interviews this morning where he has had to respond to complaints from his critics.
The most vocal has been Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, who told the BBC yesterday that the Lib Dems were “sleepwalking into irrelevance” with Davey at the helm.
Not surprisingly, Davey does not agree.
Asked about Brazil’s comments, the Lib Dem leader told BBC Breakfast:

double quotation markWe’ve grown really fast in recent years under my leadership. Record number of MPs. We’re running more councils than the Conservatives – councils up and down the country. [I’m] really proud of that record and it means when you have a bigger party, you can’t please everyone all the time.
And Davey was a bit more blunt when asked the same question on Sky News.

double quotation markI would say to the Devon councillor, we’ve now got six Liberal Democrat MPs in Devon. That’s not happened since the 1920s. We have a huge number of councillors across Devon and are leading the way in Devon, and I could go around the rest of the country. I happen to know Brazil. We’ve rarely seen eye to eye. So, all I would say is, we’re going to build on the success we’ve had.
I will post more from Davey’s interviews shortly.
There is more coverage here of what was happening at the Lib Dem conference at the weekend.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9am: The Liberal Democrat conference proceedings resume in Brighton. The main speech this morning is from Max Wilkinson, the home affairs spokesperson, at 11,50am. Here is the agenda.

blocks.text: Davey urges Burnham to 'take a stand' when PM meets Trump in New York tomorrow
Ed Davey has urged Andy Burnham to deliver some “home truths” to Donald Trump when they meet at the UN tomorrow.
Asked how Burnham should treat the US president, Davey told Sky News:
double quotation markTake a stand, please. And the cosying up to him that was done by Keir Starmer absolutely failed miserably.
Davey praised Mark Carney, the Liberal Canadian PM for “standing up to Trump with success” and, referring to what he wanted to see from Burnham, he said:

double quotation markYou have to stand up to them. And this is a man who’s ruining our world. He’s ruining his own country, but he’s hitting people in our country. His disastrous war in Iran is leading to the hike in oil and gas prices, which means people are paying more for petrol and diesel. So if Andy Burnham is going to represent Britain’s interests and the interests of British people, he needs to tell Donald Trump some home truths, whether it’s on the economy and defence, whether it’s on Iran, whether it’s on NATO. I’m afraid, under President Trump, we no longer have a reliable ally in the White House ... You can’t trust this man. And I think, while he may want to choose his words slightly more diplomatically than I’m giving to you, he needs to stand up for Britain and British interests.

With Trump deeply unpopular in the UK, it is easy to see why Davey criticises him harshly. But prime ministers who have had to negotiate with Trump have tended to be more tactful and, in her preview of what is likely to happen when Burnham meets Trump tomorrow, Pippa Crerar, the Guardian’s political editor, says Burnham is not angling for a fight. She says:

double quotation markDowning Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful [than Keir Starmer was] when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister. Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 11m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll start in Germany after a bruising night for Friedrich Merz’s party.

The German chancellor is staring down pressure over his leadership and authority after the CDU suffered heavy losses in two regional elections. For the first time in 77 years, it’s failed to enter a state parliament, in the former East German state of Mecklenburg- Vorpommern.
This was the home state of former CDU chancellor Angela Merkel; the party there last night pulled just 4.9% of the vote, losing more than half of its support.

Many of its voters have flocked to Alternative for Germany (AfD). The far-right, anti-migrant party gained 38% of the vote, doubling its share to now become the largest party in the state. This result comes just a fortnight after AfD romped to a majority in Saxony-Anhalt.
Merz called it a “disaster” last night in a public address, but vowed to stay the course and press on with his government’s reforms.

articles.title: Sara trial bares possible constitutional violation that SEC did not probe
articles.summary: Did Sara Duterte violate the constitutional ban on a vice president participating in business?

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 4:48pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Securities and Exchange Commission has not concluded on its own whether Vice President Sara Duterte violated the 1987 Constitution by sitting on a company's board while in office, one of its officials said at her impeachment trial on Monday, September 21.
SEC Director Gerardo del Rosario said company filings list Duterte as a director of Metro City Chow Foods Corp. from 2018 through 2025. Duterte was elected vice president in 2022.
Del Rosario believes it is for the Senate, not the SEC, to decide whether her role breached the constitutional ban on the vice president participating in any business.

The SEC director was testifying as one of the prosecution's witnesses for Article II, which accuses Duterte of amassing wealth disproportionate to her lawful income and of having undeclared business interests.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian raised the issue after Del Rosario confirmed that the filings for Metro City Chow Foods also list Duterte as a member of the company's compensation committee.
Gatchalian asked whether this meant Duterte had "direct participation" in the management of the corporation.
"Ayon po sa report ng corporate secretary (Yes, according to the report of the corporate secretary)," Del Rosario replied.

Gatchalian then asked whether he can say it was a possible violation of the Constitution. "Kasi nakasulat ho dito bawal po 'yung participate in any business (Because it's written here that you're not allowed to participate in any business," Gatchalian said.
Del Rosario answered, "Opo (Yes)."

When Gatchalian asked again whether there was a violation, Del Rosario did not answer directly and carefully restated the provision instead: "Ang sinasabi po kasi ay 'wag kang magkaroon ng ibang opisina, you should not hold office, employment, and engage in other profession during the term of office, even to participate."

Asked whether the SEC had looked into the matter as an actual potential violation by Duterte, Del Rosario said they have not, as the SEC's investigative powers cover securities violations, not breaches of the Constitution by public officials.
"Siguro po it's the Senate po ang bahalang maghusga kung talagang meron violation (Maybe it's the Senate who can judge if there is a violation)," Del Rosario said.
'They should have flagged it'

The issue first came up in the morning, when prosecution counsel Erwin Matib asked Del Rosario whether a vice president may sit on a company's board. The defense, represented by counsel Justin Nicol Gular, objected that the question called for an opinion from "a witness that is clearly incompetent."
Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero allowed the question, saying: "Because if it's indeed illegal, they should have flagged it."

Del Rosario first described the constitutional ban as covering business interests, not just businesses. After Matib read Article VII, Section 13 into the record, Escudero noted that the term does not appear in it.
"Wala po akong napakinggan sa binasa ni Attorney Erwin na business interest," Escudero said.
"Siguro po mali lang po 'yung aking pag-interpret in Tagalog po," Del Rosario replied.
Del Rosario earlier testified that Duterte was one of the company's incorporators and sat on its board from its founding in 2016.

She holds 20% of its subscribed shares, worth P50,000. She initially paid P12,500, and filings from 2022 to 2024 show her subscription fully paid. The company's amended 2025 filing, however, shows her paid-up amount back at P12,500.
Del Rosario said the SEC only reflects what companies report.
He said the company posted a combined net loss of P3,154,676 from 2017 to 2025 and declared no dividends from 2018 to 2025.

articles.title: Taliban says three killed in new Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan
articles.summary: The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were reportedly struck. Pakistan last carried out deadly strikes on Afghanistan in June.

image.caption: Taliban officials accused Pakistan of targeting civiliansImage: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistani security officials described as militant hideouts, resulting in some deaths.
The two neighbors reported conflicting casualty tolls.

The Taliban government in Kabul claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes," while the Associated Press news agency cited two unnamed Pakistani security officials as saying that 28 suspected militants were killed.
Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.

Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.
He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.
There has yet to be an official statement from Pakistan on the strikes.

blocks.caption: The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calmImage: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan

The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.
At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.
Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict
Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.
Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.
Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.
Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.
Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.
Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.
The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.
Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war?

articles.title: The eyesore next door: N.L. man fighting for action on derelict grocery store
articles.summary: Derelict and abandoned buildings are common throughout the province, as municipalities struggle with how to best deal with the eyesores. One in Musgrave Harbour, however, is causing increased…

image.caption: The basement of the old grocery store is exposed as a portion of the floor has rotted away. (Troy Turner/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

Derelict and abandoned buildings are common throughout the province, as municipalities struggle with how to best deal with the eyesores. One in Musgrave Harbour, however, is causing increased headaches for a neighbour.
Newly elected Coun. Steve Butler says it's a safety risk and environmental hazard
A derelict building in the way means this man can't get his house insured
It’s now part of his regular routine. Steve Butler scans his lawn and picks up shingles that have blown off the roof next door.
He’s built a shed around his heat pump to protect it from flying debris. Sometimes it’s a sheet of metal siding, other times scraps of building material.
Living about four metres away from a derelict, abandoned grocery store hasn’t been easy for the Musgrave Harbour, N.L., man.
“I’ve had damages done over the past. The eaves got torn off last winter in the storm because shingles blew off the porch there. The siding is blown off the back."
"Every time there's a bad storm, you don't know the minute the roof is going to come off.”

His neighbour is the once-thriving Foodex grocery store. It closed in 2009, and a year later Butler moved in next door. In the early days, he expected the business to sell and possibly open again. But that didn’t happen. Instead, it started a steady decline to dilapidation.
Now, it’s practically unusable.

“If a little child goes inside, that place is wide open and, God forbid, goes through the floor, who’s going to be responsible at the end of the day?” Butler said. “I got no interest in that building at all, other than to get it cleaned up.”
To amplify the issue, given the state of the building, he says he cannot get house insurance.

“I got insurance on the car and truck and my motorcycle … every time I renew my insurance at the end of the year, this comes up. ‘Well, why don't you get house insurance?’ I explain it to them. ‘Oh, well, that's a different situation.’"
For many years, Butler has been looking to municipal, provincial and federal governments for help, but he says nothing has worked.
Early in September, he successfully ran in a byelection to become a member of Musgrave Harbour town council.

“By being on there, I can push more with certain people … because every time that I have contacted somebody in government, the first thing they will ask is, ‘Well, are you with the town council or anyone?’”

Jason Chaulk has been mayor of Musgrave Harbour for the past five years. He and council have fielded many complaints about the state of the old Foodex. The mayor says the Business Development Bank of Canada owns the building and it’s the bank’s responsibility to clean it up.
“Come and accept ownership and clean it up and not to expect the town of Musgrave [Harbour] to live with it or have to clean it up,” he said.

In a written statement, the BDC says the loan to the business ended in 2012 and the file was written off. The bank said it has not been involved with the property since the mortgage was discharged in 2012.
“As a result, we are not in a position to comment on the property's current status, ownership or maintenance responsibilities.”
For larger communities, removal of buildings may be possible, but the mayor says cleanup would run hundreds of thousands of dollars, and they just don’t have the means.
"I feel bad for the people that's living in the immediate area around there," he said.
"It would be a significant cost to the town of Musgrave Harbour — we would not be able to be in that financial situation to take care of that."
The problem of derelict and abandoned buildings goes far beyond Musgrave Harbour.
Municipalities Newfoundland and Labrador, a non-profit advocacy group, says many towns are struggling with how to best deal with these community eyesores.
Recent changes to the Municipalities Act allow communities to pass bylaws to give them more power in how to best deal with issues such as derelict buildings.
However, those usually require a means of enforcement, says MNL president Amy Coady.
Even with staff to enforce, that doesn’t solve the issues of having enough in the town purse to cover the demolition work.

“The affordability to be able to do the cleanup ourselves, or take down buildings, can be very costly. We can apply a lien on the property and recoup those costs when the property or the building or the land gets sold, we would recoup it at that point. But again, there's no guarantees as to how much we would get back.”

Back in Musgrave Harbour, Butler peers into the old Foodex. It’s gone from a hangout for youth who broke in, to being stripped over all the copper wire, to now, a building where the stench of mould meets you at the entrance, and of which gaping holes expose the rot in the basement.

Butler has been putting up signs warning of danger, and pleas for people to stay away. He says he will continue to “rattle the cages” of provincial and federal governments to take action and force the owner of the building to clean up what he considers to be an environmental and safety risk.
“Something’s got to be done … I don't know who and I don't care, but somebody's got to come out and assess the situation and figure out what they're going to do.”

articles.title: Universal early childhood education better than baby bonus to increase Australia’s birthrate, Labor says
articles.summary:
Intergenerational report predicts that in four decades’ time, more Australians will be dying than being born each year

Labor says better investment in early childhood education and care,…

blocks.text: Labor says better investment in early childhood education and care, such as a possible move to universal access for families, is a better way to address Australia’s declining birthrate, rejecting the need for a new “baby bonus”.

Monday’s intergenerational report showed that more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time, a milestone already experienced by countries including South Korea, Italy, Germany and Japan.
It is the first time the three-yearly report has forecast more deaths than births.

Lower fertility rates will drive slower population growth, according to Treasury’s report. Australia’s fertility rate is projected to decline to 1.34 by 2065–66, down from 1.5 children per woman in 2030–31.

Fertility rates have been below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman for 50 years, contributing to a projected drop in population of 1.7 million people and an increase in the projected median age by 1.7 years in 2065–66.

The report says a complex mix of economic, social and cultural factors is to blame, including greater access to contraception, more time spent in education, career development, longer periods living with parents, and delays in forming partnerships and having children.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said fewer families with more than three children was part of the drop.
“When it comes to fertility rates, I do not and will not give people free advice about these very personal decisions that they make about whether to start a family and when to start family,” he said.
He said federal Labor was making it easier for adults to choose to have more children if they wished, citing expanded paid parental leave, superannuation settings and access to childcare.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, wants universal childcare to be part of his political legacy, and the government has commissioned consulting giant Deloitte to help design a universal system. Its report on the policy “pathway” is due in time for the next election.
The assistant minister for productivity, Andrew Leigh, said the government would “prefer that it were otherwise, but that’s the norm around the world.”

“My read of the evidence, as an economist, is that the biggest impact you have is around childcare, and that’s why we made it such a priority upon coming to government, improving access to childcare, ensuring that it is affordable for Australians.”
But, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he was “open minded” about an economic incentive, like a return to the Howard government’s baby bonus payment.
“The real problem is of course that family formation is being delayed because people can’t get into home soon enough, and families are having less children,” he told ABC TV.
“We want Australians to have a better chance of getting into a home, forming a family and having children of their own.”
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said families should have more support, but a baby bonus payment was not the right approach.
He has previously called for a “hyper” Australia and “more Australian babies”. He said solutions should be designed around helping families working for their own advancement.
“The baby bonus, it was just ‘Here’s some cash’, without you having to put in the effort as well.”

Research by the e61 thinktank found that the baby bonus, introduced by then treasurer Peter Costello in 2004, led to births increasing by 6.5%. Births increased by 10% among mothers with no taxable income, by 8% among below-median income mothers, while there was no change among high-income mothers. It also found that births of a third child increased by 9%, and that mothers who received the baby bonus, as a group, had 6.8% more children in total by 2022.
The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, said the government would not revisit the baby bonus.
“Our government doesn’t get into promoting choices for individual families, but we recognise that people making those choices should be supported.”

articles.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
articles.summary: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on…

image.caption: Germany's auto industry is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the countryImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.
Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.
"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.
Labor costs too high in Germany?
Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.
Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.
To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.
The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.
It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."
Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.
IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.
VW is bringing out the axe
Can longer working hours save jobs?
The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.
The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.
"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.
On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.
"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.
How can Germany's auto industry recover?
Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.
"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.
"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.
At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.
Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production?
Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.
"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.
And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."
