articles.title: DILG's Remulla seeks limits on children's social media use, access to violent sites
articles.summary: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said he is seeking tighter restrictions on children's access to social media and websites promoting violence following the deadly shooting at Banga…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 4:09pm

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said he is seeking tighter restrictions on children's access to social media and websites promoting violence following the deadly shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato.
At a press conference, Remulla said he would ask Congress to consider measures limiting social media use among children and blocking access to websites that promote nihilism and violence.
“Tomorrow I will go to Congress to ask for the following things. One, to limit the use of social media of children 16 years old and below. Two, to regulate firearms, legal and loose,” he said.

“Three, the opportunity for the PNP to inspect the safety of all licensed firearms in their homes with due notice but without need for a warrant. Four, the total abolition of the access of anyone in the Philippines of these nihilistic sites through the DICT,” he added.

The proposals came after investigators found that the Banga school shooter had allegedly been influenced by online groups and websites promoting satanism, fascism, nihilism, anti-LGBT views, and hate.
According to the DILG head, the student came from a stable family, had friends and a relationship, and aspired to become a doctor. He was also not known to be a bully or a victim of bullying.
However, authorities said information recovered from the student's phone showed his exposure to online groups and content that allegedly influenced his thinking and behavior.
The Philippine National Police said the investigation is continuing to determine who or what influenced the student and how he accessed the online content.
On Sept.18, three students were killed and eight others were wounded following the shooting inside the Banga school.

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Sunday asked IT communities to "come forward" and help the government amid the recent incident of school violence in South Cotabato that is being linked to the dark web. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: US proposes AI safety mechanism in talks with China
articles.summary: US Treasury chief Scott Bessent said there had been "successful" talks with China on trade and AI. The talks come amid growing fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

image.caption: Hopes of finding common ground on concerns over AI safety comes amid fierce competition between the two countriesImage: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Top officials fro the United States and China have discussed a communication mechanism dealing with AI concerns between the two countries.
The talks on Sunday evening come ahead of a summit this week between US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping and amid growing fears that AI poses an existential threat to humanity.
The discussion with a team led by China's Vice Premier He Lifeng also involved top US trade official Jamieson Greer and took place at JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters.
What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy?
What did US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent say about the AI talks with China?
"We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters.
Bessent said the delegations spoke about a mechanism to communicate about AI issues, calling it the "US-China AI dialogue."
"The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries," Bessent said.

The US Treasury chief said that these notifications would be for potential "incidents" or an instance "that rises up to a national security level from AI," he said, adding that both sides have agreed to meet again.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said at the conclusion of the talks.
What has been reported in China?
Chinese state news agency Xinhua described the talks as "candid, in-depth, and constructive" on Monday.

"The two sides engaged in... discussions on key economic and trade issues of mutual interest, such as implementing the consensus from previous consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment," Xinhua reported in a brief readout.
Xinhua added that Chinese and US officials also held a dialogue on "issues related to AI", with no further details provided.
AI fear machine?
Concern over the threat posed by AI
In recent weeks, leading AI firms have warned of the threat posed by unbridled AI development and the pace at which these threats could become a reality.
They have begun working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers.

Late in August, more than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats.

That came after it emerged that OpenAI models had gone rogue and had hacked into a digital repository of AI technology. Anthropic conducted investigations to see if its own models had carried out similar attacks and found three incidents in which a Claude model and later identified a fourth incident.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
AI experts sound the alarm
Earlier this month, researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."
Former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."
Trump has dismissed calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."
Trump's stance has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.

articles.title: Loren Legarda extended medical leave to October 9 -- Senate Secretary Bantug
articles.summary: Senator Loren Legarda has extended her medical leave to October 9, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. said Monday.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 4:04pm
Senator Loren Legarda has extended her medical leave to October 9, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. said Monday.
Bantug said Legarda will be on leave from September 21 to 23; September 28 to October 2; and October 5 to 9.
Legarda has been on medical leave beginning August 3. The last time she was seen at the Senate was on July 29, during the plenary session.
Senator Juan Miguel Zubiri earlier said Legarda is receiving medical treatment for a serious lung illness but could not give a definite date for her return to the Senate.
He added his colleague wants to return to the Philippines as soon as possible but still needs to complete medical tests.
Senator Panfilo Lacson, meanwhile, said Legarda sought moral support from her fellow senators.
“Nagkausap kami ni Senator Loren. Twice na kaming nagkakausap. Wala naman siyang nabanggit kung siya ay babalik o hindi,” Lacson told Super Radyo dzBB on Sunday.
(Legarda and I talked twice. She has not mentioned whether she will return to the country or not.)
“Ang appeal niya sa amin, bilang kasamahan sa Senado, parang humingi lang siya ng moral support,” he added.
(Her appeal to us, as her fellow senators, was simply for moral support.)

Legarda and her son Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste are facing complaints for plunder and graft in connection with the alleged failure of the latter’s renewable energy firm to provide solar power, as mandated in its congressional franchise.—Sandra Aguinaldo/AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Legarda extends medical leave for sixth time until October 9
articles.summary: If she remains absent until then, she will have been away from the chamber for 72 days since her last plenary appearance on July 29.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 4:01pm
Loren Legarda speaks as a senator-judge in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Loren Legarda has extended her medical leave for a sixth consecutive time, with her absence from the Senate expected to reach until at least October 9.
Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. confirmed on Monday, September 21, that Legarda filed leave covering September 21 to 23, September 28 to October 2, and October 5 to 9.
It is her longest filing yet, spanning three weeks, since she was last seen attending the Senate's plenary session on July 29. Her earlier notices covered one or two blocks of days at a time.
Legarda has been absent from the Senate for nearly two months. If she remains absent through October 9, her absence will reach 72 days, or more than 10 weeks.

Aside from having missed plenary sessions and budget hearings, Legarda has also largely missed out on the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, where she sits as a senator-judge.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and other senators have all said Legarda is being treated for lung problems.
Gatchalian told reporters on August 27 that Legarda had gone without her salary while on leave.
Sen. Ping Lacson said in a radio interview in August that Legarda had called him and promised to return to the Philippines once her medical tests were completed.

Legarda left the Philippines on August 2, a day before her first medical leave took effect. National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag said she traveled via Hong Kong with France as her final destination, while her son, Rep. Leandro Leviste (Batangas, 1st District), took a separate flight to Hong Kong on the same day.
According to Senate rules, senators need no permission from the Senate president for personal trips abroad

Legarda left two days after Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla ordered a preliminary investigation into her, Leviste and former Energy Secretary Alfonso Cusi on complaints of non-bailable plunder and several counts of graft.
Investigators have accused the Legarda, Leviste and Cusi of allegedly conspiring to corner exclusive government rights over the country's solar energy resources.

Legarda has called the accusations "utterly false and baseless" and has said her leaves comply with Senate rules. Her spokesperson, Tony La Viña, has argued that the complaints against her and Leviste are political persecution.

articles.title: Canada faces questions over treatment of Iranian conscripts as U.K, Australia take different approach

image.caption: Mostafa Tasbandi, 44, is one of what are believed to be hundreds of Iranians who received letters from the federal government informing them they may not be able to stay in Canada because of mandatory military service they completed in Iran as young men. (Submitted by Mostafa Tasbandi)

blocks.text: Mostafa Tasbandi lost his job last Thursday.

It's just one of the many ways his life has taken a turn since he and hundreds of other Iranians living in Canada received letters on Aug. 6 and 7 informing them they may be inadmissible to stay in the country because of mandatory military service they were forced to complete in Iran as young men.
"I don't have a future right now," Tasbandi, who lives in Halifax, told CBC News this week.

For years, Tasbandi, who arrived in December 2023, had been waiting for a work permit renewal, a situation that prevented his wife from getting a work permit of her own. His 11-year-old daughter has had serious trouble at school since she discovered her father's immigration troubles, he said.

Tasbandi, a computer engineer, isn't sure he will be able to renew his own work permit following his dismissal at work. His boss told him he was letting him go because the company didn't have enough work for him, but Tasbandi suspects a sudden decrease in his productivity due to the stress of his immigration situation had something to do with the dismissal.

"If I can't get another work permit, I don't have money to pay my bills and I cannot go back to my country because I am afraid. I'm stuck. What shall I do?" said the 44-year-old who has participated in several protests against the Iranian regime while in Canada. Iran has since undertaken campaigns to identify and punish citizens demonstrating abroad.

CBC reported last week that former conscripts of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and their family members increasingly face inadmissibility to Canada because of Ottawa’s designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization. Men across the country who were forced into that military service now tell CBC they feel branded as terrorists by the country they sought refuge in.

They are calling on federal Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab to publish guidance distinguishing conscripts who were forced into service and didn’t commit any terrorist acts from full-fledged, regime-supporting members — similar to what the United Kingdom and Australia have done.

"Canada has a very aggressive policy vis-a-vis national security issues that leads to some decisions which I would say are absurd," said Lorne Waldman, a Toronto-based immigration lawyer representing nearly 40 former Iranian former conscripts targeted by the procedural fairness letters (PFLs).
'Why is Canada doing this?'

Tasbandi and five other Iranians who were forced into mandatory IRGC service in their late teens and early 20s tell CBC they self-disclosed the mandatory military service in their permanent residency applications and now feel penalized for their honesty.
"Why is Canada doing this? We trusted them. They’re treating us differently than other countries [would]," Tasbandi said.

In response to questions from CBC, a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) said the department recognizes "that some individuals may have served as a result of conscription."

The department "cannot disclose details of our screening processes," spokesperson Mary Rose Sabater wrote in an email, adding the procedural fairness letters sent out in August provide "applicants with an opportunity to respond before a decision is made."

items: They came to Canada for safety. Now they’re suspected of supporting the regime they fled
They fled Iran after years of fear and protest. Canada's new asylum law has put them in limbo

blocks.text: But Yalda Ghani, an Iranian immigration consultant in Toronto, says several of her clients were deemed inadmissible before the August wave of procedural letters was sent out, despite having been conscripted and performing only menial tasks for the IRGC and are challenging the decisions in Federal Court.

"I have many clients who are scared to death, honestly," Ghani said. "They are afraid that if they become inadmissible in Canada, they will lose their chances for other countries, too, because this is a very serious thing to be labelled inadmissible under security and being a ‘member’ of a terrorist organization."
Canada designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps a terrorist organization in 2024, following the lead of the United States.
Every conscript CBC spoke with say they agree with the designation itself.
"I want Canadian immigration to … understand that we are not members of them and we were not members of them," Tasbandi said.
U.K., Australia recommend examining cases closely

The United Kingdom and Australian appear to have taken different approaches, where conscripts are not automatically considered "members" of an organization. In March, Australia's Parliament published guidance on the matter, saying authorities should distinguish involuntary conscripts from supporting members.

The U.K. government published similar guidance in August, stating military service is compulsory for men and that conscripts are unlikely to be required to commit acts "contrary to the basic rules of human conduct."

The six Iranians CBC spoke with for this story, who received PFLs in August, say they or their family members were randomly assigned to IRGC service among Iran's military and security organizations and were tasked with menial or administrative work. None were in a combat role, nor did they carry weapons, they said.

Tasbandi said that when he completed his service in 2008 and 2009, he was appointed to the guard's sports office, due to its substantial involvement in state sports, and was tasked with printing posters and booking appointments. He also briefly worked in a library. After he finished the service, he got an unrelated job in a refrigerator factory in his hometown of Mashhad.
The impact of the letters has extended beyond former conscripts themselves. In some cases, family members have also received procedural fairness letters because of a relative's past IRGC service.
Reza Rajaei, who came to Canada with his wife and daughter in 2022, said his wife and four-year-old daughter also received PFLs because they are part of his permanent residency application.
"What should I respond for her?" Rajaei said of his daughter. "She is four years old."
Samira Chahargoli, who lives outside Toronto with her family, said she also received a PFL because of her husband's compulsory military service in 2002, when he was 18 years old.
"We built a life in Canada. Canada is our home right now," Chahargoli said.
Iranian told he may have to leave Canada over past IRGC service

Without a specific policy, immigration officers and some Federal Court judges appear to be basing their decisions on a recent Federal Court ruling that upheld the inadmissibility of Mohammedreza Vadiati, an Iranian former IRGC conscript, according to Ghani and Waldman.
The Federal Court ruled in Vadiati v. Canada that mandatory service with Iran's IRGC can still count as "membership" for Canadian immigration purposes.
"That's the albatross hanging around our neck," said Waldman.

"The problem is now the immigration officers are relying on Vadiati and they're saying, 'Well, based on Vadiati, if you're a conscript, you're still inadmissible,'" Waldman said. "But the answer to that is there are a whole series of other legal arguments that should have been made that were not made in Vadiati."

Waldman says immigration officers should instead be basing their decisions on the Supreme Court's 2023 Mason decision, which requires immigration decision-makers to meaningfully consider the evidence and circumstances of each case.
Federal Court backlog
What remains unclear is why such a large number of people received letters advising them of their potential inadmissibility over the same two days in August.
Tasbandi belongs to a Telegram messaging group with 19,000 people in it. He says nearly 2,000 members of the group said they received one.
Waldman believes it may have been an attempt by immigration officials to clear a massive backlog in immigration-related Federal Court applications.

In June, the Federal Court published a news bulletin stating immigration proceedings could exceed 30,000 files in 2026, representing nearly five times the volume it handled before the pandemic caused "significant and sustained operational pressures" on the court.

articles.title: His Hyundai Santa Fe burst into flames on busy highway after repairs at dealership
articles.summary: Jason Pelletier was driving to work in June when his car suddenly caught fire. He managed to escape seconds before an explosion blew up its front end and, three months later, he's still waiting for…

image.caption: Jason Pelletier's Hyundai Santa Fe went up in flames in June, while on the road just north of Toronto. The car was a writeoff after the blaze, the cause of which is still under investigation. (Submitted by Jason Pelletier)

blocks.text: Three months after a "traumatizing" vehicle fire, Jason Pelletier is still waiting for answers — and hoping for more compensation — from automaker Hyundai.

On June 9, during the morning commute to work, the school principal was driving on a busy highway, just north of Toronto, when his Santa Fe suddenly caught fire. He saw thick black smoke and flames billowing from the hood. He says the engine and brakes were no longer responsive.
"I'm trying to cross five lanes of traffic on the 401 in morning traffic," Pelletier said. He says he initially struggled to open the door, but finally made it out of the vehicle.
"I got out and, 20 seconds later, there was an explosion," he said. "The whole front end blew up."

What Pelletier finds even more unsettling is that he had just taken his SUV to the dealership the day before. He had to replace a head gasket, a critical seal located between an engine's block and cylinder head that maintains combustion pressure and prevents coolant and oil from mixing.
He says he noticed a burning smell shortly after leaving the downtown Toronto dealership, but wasn’t too worried because the service manager said it might be from residue after the service.
He later sent text messages to the service manager, asking whether he should be concerned about the light smoke coming out from the hood.
Santa Fe catches fire on busy highway
The next morning, on his way to work, a message popped up on his vehicle’s touchscreen, warning of a "potential condition" with the engine control system and recommending a "full system check."
Pelletier sent a few more text messages — but the service manager did not reply before the engine burst into flames.
"They reached out and made sure I was alive essentially," he said.
Safety is 'top priority'
Hyundai Canada declined our request for an interview, but told CBC News in an emailed statement that safety is its "top priority."
"The circumstances surrounding this matter are still under review and we cannot comment further at this time," said Nitish Bissonauth, senior manager of corporate communications.

Joe Hakim, general manager of the dealership, stated in an email to Pelletier that Hycay Consulting Engineering had been commissioned to conduct a joint investigation with the insurance company to determine the cause of the fire.
Hyundai Canada did not respond to questions regarding other vehicle fires reported to the company or the preventive measures put in place in recent years.

Over the past decade — from Jan. 1, 2016 to Sept. 8, 2026 — Transport Canada received 1,140 reports of vehicle fires, across all makes and models. But it says there is no obligation to report these incidents to the ministry, so this number could be higher.
"Fires are about one in 2,500 cars in Canada," according to Murray Thomson, a combustion specialist and professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Toronto
"If you add it up across all of Canada, you have 10,000 vehicle fires per year. That is significant."

With 168 of the 1,140 reported fires, Hyundai accounted for roughly 15 per cent of incidents during this period. The Korean automaker ranks second, behind Ford. The ministry did not provide year-by-year data for each automaker.
A joint investigation by CBC Marketplace and Go Public, published in 2021, focused on seven cases involving Hyundai and Kia vehicles when engines had stalled or caught fire.
"If a car has recurring issues, that's obviously a concern," Murray said.

In 2023, Hyundai recalled more than 320,000 vehicles in Canada linked to a potential fault in the anti-lock braking system that could cause a fire. Pelletier’s Santa Fe was not affected by that recall but it was impacted by two others.

It was fitted with a Knock Sensor Detection System, which warns the driver if their engine is about to fail, in 2020 and, three years later, was fixed again because of a fire risk "even when the vehicle is stationary and the engine is switched off," as Hyundai warned in its safety recall.

items: 'My car's on fire': Drivers fear for their safety as years-long recall rollout drags on

blocks.text: Thomson says automakers remain responsible for the safe operation throughout a vehicle’s lifetime, but admits that it can be difficult when cars change hands. "There could be a system to track ownership more clearly, to link the current owner to the manufacturer directly," he said.

"That's what the whole recall system is about. Transport Canada plays a role too, because it tracks, collects information, and sometimes requests recalls or identifies issues that the manufacturer should respond to."

Transport Canada has conducted several investigations into parts and components of Hyundai vehicles, many of which have led to safety recalls. The federal ministry is currently investigating the trailer lighting module in 2019 to 2023 Santa Fe models, saying two reported fires may be linked to that part.

"In the majority of vehicle fires, the damage caused is significant, making it difficult to determine the exact origin and cause of the fire," the ministry stated in an email to Radio-Canada, adding that vehicle fires can result from various factors, such as inadequate maintenance, improper repairs or manufacturing defects. Arson is also included in its figures.
"Transport Canada does not have data that would allow it to reliably assign a specific percentage to the various potential causes of vehicle fires."
Lengthy claims process
Pelletier’s insurer paid him nearly $22,000 — the estimated value of the vehicle before the fire — on top of the cost of a rental car for one month.
But according to his own estimates, he has lost more than $5,000 worth of personal belongings, including AirPods, pairs of glasses, sportswear and accessories for his dogs.

That’s not to mention the many drag outfits, accessories and make up products that were in his SUV when it burned. The fire happened during Pride Month, a particularly busy time of year for his alter ego, Jezebel Bardot.
"I’m not trying to become a millionaire out of this. I just don’t want to be worse off than I was when I handed them the keys on Monday June 8th to have my car repaired," he said.

Three months later, the Toronto resident is astounded that his Santa Fe, currently stored in distant Oshawa, is still under forensic investigation. He wonders whether yet another recall could have prevented this ordeal.
"I'm certainly hoping that they're not knowingly gambling with people's lives."
In the meantime, he has decided to buy a new SUV — opting for a different brand. "I don't think you could pay me to drive a Hyundai at this point. And it's too bad from a guy who was a longtime fan."

articles.title: Rental rules in Ontario change today. Here’s what tenants and landlords need to know
articles.summary: A batch of changes to Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act comes into force on Monday, including shorter deadlines for tenants who landlords say have fallen behind on rent payments.

image.caption: Kayla Andrade, founder of Ontario Landlords Watch, argues that the only way to speed things up at the LTB is to streamline common applications. (Submitted by Kayla Andrade)

blocks.text: Toronto
A batch of changes to Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act comes into force on Monday, including shorter deadlines for tenants who landlords say have fallen behind on rent payments.
The Residential Tenancies Act is updated with tighter deadlines for late rent repayment
Do you rent in Ontario? Here's what you need to know about new rental rules
A batch of changes to Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) comes into force on Monday, including shorter deadlines for tenants who landlords say have fallen behind on rent payments.
The RTA amendments, some of which were brought into force on July 1, come out of two bills — Bill 60 and Bill 97.
Earlier in the summer, they were described by a spokesperson for Ontario’s housing minister as being necessary to “restore balance and rebuild confidence in Ontario’s rental housing market.”
As of Monday, Sept. 21, here are the major changes that will impact both tenants and landlords:

items: If a tenant falls behind on rent and is issued what’s called an N4 eviction notice (a legal document demanding the money) the tenant now has seven days instead of 14 days to pay. If they don’t, the landlord can apply for an eviction.

Tenants who want to raise their own issues at an eviction hearing at the Landlord and Tenant Board, such as problems with their unit, now have to pay half of the rent they allegedly owe in order to do so.

The RTA now has a formal definition of “persistent late payment,” instead of leaving it open. It’s defined as rent being paid more than seven days late on at least three different occasions over any six-month period.

A landlord who evicts a tenant for their own or their family’s personal use with at least 120 days of notice no longer has to provide that tenant with compensation or the offer of an alternative unit.
Finally, if a landlord evicts a tenant for personal use, the intended new occupant has to move in within 60 days, or the eviction is presumed to be in bad faith.

blocks.text: Will this lead to faster evictions?

Ontario has billed the changes to the RTA as a way to address delays and backlogs at Ontario’s Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB), where non-urgent applications have been known to sit for months before being considered.
A spokesperson for Tribunals Ontario, which oversees the LTB, told CBC News it's been preparing for the RTA updates with “no impact anticipated on caseload or application processing times.”
But both landlord groups and some tenant advocates have questioned whether the changes will mean fewer LTB delays.
The halved deadline to pay back late rent “just means you can file the paperwork a little sooner at the LTB,” said Kayla Andrade, founder of the landlord advocacy group Ontario Landlords Watch.
“It doesn’t mean that you’re going to get your hearing any faster.”

The Small Ownership Landlords of Ontario group has raised similar concerns, arguing that the LTB should allow landlords to skip a hearing altogether for non-payment of rent disputes and instead be able to use a faster-moving mediation process.

Andrade is supportive of the formalizing of the definition of “persistent non-payment of rent,” telling CBC News that previously, “you didn’t know… exactly what the [adjudicator] would consider as persistent late payments. It’s good to have something concrete.”
Tenant advocates call changes a ‘smokescreen’
Tenant organizations have also argued that the RTA updates fail to address the cause of bottlenecks at the LTB.
In a release, the Federation of Metro Tenants' Associations said efficiency was merely a “smokescreen” for “eroding tenants' rights.”

Dania Majid, director of duty counsel for the Advocacy Centre for Tenants Ontario, told CBC News that her legal clinic is deeply concerned that the changes make it easier for tenants to be evicted. But that wouldn't necessarily happen faster, she said.
The switch from 14 to seven days to repay rent will “trigger more hearings. And that’s going to trigger a backlog,” she said.
New tenant union launches across Toronto
Majid says she expects a similar outcome from one of the earlier July 1 RTA updates, which halves the amount of time for tenants and landlords to request a review of an LTB decision.
“If you're not able to provide your materials in time at the LTB to request a review there, people are going to end up at the divisional court and that's going to create a backlog there,” she said.
Then there’s the requirement that tenants pay 50 per cent of the unpaid rent they allegedly owe in order to raise other complaints at their eviction hearing.
“Now the tenant has to file a separate application to raise these issues… when the entire matter could have just been handled at the same hearing,” said Majid
CBC News asked the Ministry of Housing how tenants can recover the money they paid before a hearing if it's found they don’t actually owe it. The ministry did not reply by publication time.

Kate McGillivray is a writer and newsreader in Toronto. She's worked for the CBC in Montreal, Sherbrooke and St. John's, and she always wants to hear your feedback and story ideas. Get in touch here: kate.mcgillivray@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 11 things we learned from the Neil Peart documentary
articles.summary: The documentary Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple celebrates late Rush drummer's extraordinary musicianship, intellectual curiosity, resilience and lasting influence on rock music.

image.caption: Rush drummer and Canadian rock icon Neil Peart performs in Las Vegas in May 2007. The CBC documentary Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple documents his tough start as a young artist and rise to fame, featuring heart-to-heart interviews with bandmates Geddy Lee, Alex Lifeson and others. (Ethan Miller/Getty

blocks.text: Drummers often get short shrift. Hidden behind the kit, they remain mysterious, even anonymous.
Not so for Neil Peart, who was a tour-de-force for the Canadian rock band Rush and is widely considered one of the best drummers of all time.
In Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple, co-directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn celebrate Peart's life, extraordinary musicianship and lasting influence through interviews and musical performances.

Bandmates Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, along with Peart’s fellow drummers and friends — including Stewart Copeland of the Police and Chad Smith of Red Hot Chili Peppers — share insights into the wizard behind the kit and perform Rush songs together as a tribute to his enduring legacy. The film debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sept. 16. Here are 11 things we learned:
1. His name is pronounced 'Peert'
"It's not 'Pert' like the shampoo," says Dunn, correcting a mispronunciation that has even appeared in films such as School of Rock and I Love You, Man.
2. He moved to London at 18 to pursue music

After leaving high school, Peart moved from St. Catharines, Ont., to England determined to become a musician. He lived in cheap rooms and shared flats, experiencing what he later described as "anonymity and poverty" — an early test of the focus and stubbornness that would define his career.
3. He was an enthusiastic reader
When his bandmates first met Peart, he was reading "five or six books a day," according to Lee, who said it soon became obvious that their new drummer should also be writing lyrics.
4. He loved The Lord of the Rings

Peart’s imagination was shaped by fantasy, mythology, science fiction, comedy and classical music — influences that found their way into Rush’s songs and lyrics. His love of J.R.R. Tolkien influenced songs such as The Necromancer and Rivendell.
5. He rehearsed before rehearsal
Peart studied, practised and took lessons throughout his career, always approaching the drums as a student.
"I think it matters for me to play better all the time," he says in archival footage, "to play my best all the time, to keep it fresh and changing. It’s kind of my responsibility."

He would rehearse for at least an hour by himself before rehearsing with the rest of the band. As the filmmakers put it, he was continuously trying to get better — even after becoming one of the best in the world.
6. He helped build Rush’s big, theatrical sound
Peart played a major role in shaping Rush’s intricate arrangements and dramatic instrumental passages, which became central to the band’s sound.
His influence is especially evident in 2112, the 20-minute title suite from the band’s 1976 album.

"It was Neil’s idea to do an overture," says Lifeson, to "take all these pieces and put them together in one really cool opening." The movement weaves together themes that return throughout the piece, reflecting Peart’s operatic and orchestral approach to percussion.
7. His whisky pours got bigger

During studio mixing sessions, Peart reportedly enjoyed a glass of Macallan whisky at 5 p.m. — a pour of about "two fat fingers," according to Lee. Over their 40-year friendship, Lee jokes, Peart’s "fingers got fatter."
8. He was an air drummer's drummer
Copeland notes Peart’s solos were so intricate, physical and theatrical that audiences didn’t just watch — they played along in the air.
"I asked him one time, how do you get the air drummers? I want that," Copeland said. "It's amazing at a Rush show to see them."
"The middle part of Tom Sawyer is every air drummer’s fantasy section," adds Smith. "If you hear Tom Sawyer, they’re all air drumming."
9. He was intensely private
Peart was uncomfortable with fame and fiercely protective of his personal life.
"If I go off to do my job, I’m a professional," he says in an archival interview. "If I’m not doing my job, then I’m a person, so don’t get that mixed up."
10. He took bikes very seriously
Lee recalls Peart riding his bicycle from Milwaukee to Chicago, some 150 kilometres, on his day off and then performing a three-hour concert.
He later became a devoted motorcyclist, chronicling his travels, which followed devastating personal losses, in his memoir Ghost Rider: Travels on the Healing Road.
11. He nearly walked away from Rush

After the deaths of his 19-year-old daughter in a car accident in August 1997, and his wife, from cancer 10 months later, Peart took an extended sabbatical and travelled by motorcycle. Although he considered leaving Rush permanently, Lifeson convinced him to return for a final tour in 2015.
Rush members honour late drummer Neil Peart at TIFF
'Respect the drummer'
"Drummers are the backbone," of bands, Dunn told CBC News, "and Neil was taking drumming to a whole other level."

That appreciation drives the film, which serves as the tribute Peart never received: a proper farewell concert or memorial, made impossible by the pandemic after his death from brain cancer in January 2020.
Instead, Lee and Lifeson reunite with four of Peart’s musical "brothers" for a musical, funny and emotional tribute.
"It’s a very joyous celebration of a complex individual," McFadyen said.

items: The 9 best of a TIFF grappling with a world coming apart
IN PHOTOS | Run Terry Run, Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend close out TIFF

blocks.text: Lee jokes that Peart "would say we were idiots" and might be "a little embarrassed" by the attention. He adds that he remembers him as "a very wise, quick thinker, philosopher" and gifted lyricist.
The film ultimately asks audiences to do exactly what Dunn recommends: "respect the drummer."
Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple will air on CBC’s The Passionate Eye, on Sept. 23 at 8 p.m. (8:30 NT) on CBC and CBC Gem.

articles.title: Psychological horror Silent Hill: Townfall ratchets up the scares — and frustrations
articles.summary: Silent Hill: Townfall has a grab bag of mechanics that seem at odds with one another, making it likely you'll love one part of the experience, but loathe the next.

image.caption: Simon, voiced by Jovan Adepo, is the main character in the psychological horror game Silent Hill: Townfall, out Sept. 24. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Silent Hill: Townfall has a grab bag of mechanics that seem at odds with one another, making it likely you'll love one part of the experience, but loathe the next.
The long-running series moves to a Scottish town with fleshy monsters and vintage tech
Resident Evil and Silent Hill, two foundational series in video game horror that continue to release new games today, both emerged in the late 1990s on the first Sony PlayStation.
But Silent Hill's psychological take on the genre has found a relatively niche audience compared to the crowd-pleasing Resident Evil.

Instead of police officers and secret agents cracking wise in the face of a zombie outbreak, Silent Hill threw civilians into oppressive settings, dripping with unreliable narrators and metaphors for facing past trauma or sins.

Silent Hill: Townfall, published by Konami and developed by Glasgow-based Screen Burn Interactive, has moments that reach the pinnacle of horror in gaming today. But with a grab bag of mechanics that at times seem at odds with one another, it's likely you'll love one part of the experience, but loathe the next.
Welcome to St. Amelia

Townfall's first note is an odd one. The year is 1996, and we see American Simon Ordell (voiced by The Leftovers' Jovan Adepo) wash up ashore in St. Amelia, an abandoned Scottish fishing village, with no idea of how he got there. He's got an IV bag strapped to his arm, its tubing plugged into his left hand.

Protest signs cover the town's square, hinting that a corporation is behind some kind of disaster. Simon answers a ringing payphone and speaks to a man named Richard (Lost's Terry O'Quinn), who tells him to search for a nurse named Zoe Ellis (Kezia Burrows). She knows Simon, though he has no memory of her.
The fishing town, once bustling with everyday folk, is now populated by fleshy, humanoid monsters that moan and growl despite lacking facial features.

Key to Simon's survival is the CRTV — a handheld portable television that resembles Sony's Sport Watchman. Tuning the device shows enemies' shivering silhouettes amidst a scratchy red screen, allowing him to hide and skulk past them unscathed.

Cryptic messages come through the fuzzy screen — glimpses of your intended destination like Zoe's house, or clues to help you open a rusty locker in a pharmacy's back room, sometimes with snippets of messages from Zoe or Richard playing through its low-fi speaker.

Your other tools for dealing with enemies are meagre at best: tossing a bottle can distract their attention; a rotting wooden plank can withstand one melee, but cracks in half before long. A handgun is a powerful last resort, but you'll rarely have enough bullets to fill its six chambers.
All of this evokes a feeling of dread and helplessness, forcing you to avoid fights whenever possible.
First-person stumbles
In a series first, Townfall is played entirely in first-person perspective, meaning you see everything through the eyes of Simon (though a few chapters put you in Zoe or Richard's shoes).
Since you can only see what's immediately in front of you, you'll constantly dart your gaze left and right and use sound cues, as well as your CRTV to follow the threats around you.

That change has come with some growing pains, though; button prompts will appear when you approach an interactable object or item you can pick up, but the symbols and text that appear onscreen are often too small to read very quickly.

Too often while scrambling to find a closet to hide from a monster's hunt, I lost critical seconds panning around for the "X" button prompt to show up. Sometimes, while trying to avoid an enemy in a cramped hallway, I jammed on the button thinking I was picking up a first-aid item — only to slam a door shut in my face, leading to my demise.
Masters of unlocking
Silent Hill: Townfall is at its best when you're exploring a chunk of the town like it's a giant puzzle box, searching through spooky homes and alleyways to reach the next destination.

You'll consult your paper map, marked in red to denote locked doors and areas you've already searched, planning your next route, making a mental note of enemies and taking a deep breath before setting out for the next trinket or clue. Each step is just close enough that you're compelled to follow the crumb trail for up to hours at a time.
You'll also spend a lot of time staring at '90s-era computer screens, checking answering machines for messages next to landline phones or searching for floppy disks and cassette tapes along the way.

This fascination with vintage tech is a signature of developer Screen Burn, formerly known as No Code, who have used the unease you might feel from hearing a monitor's low capacitor hum to great effect in 2017's sleeper hit Stories Untold.
The Weight of it all

Things get really dangerous (and metaphysical) when St. Amelia is plunged into an alternate world, possibly manifesting a part of Simon's psyche. This world is bathed in a blood-red light. Black iron pipes block pathways that were once clear and enemies stalk you in greater numbers.
This is a signature of Silent Hill games, made even more menacing by the introduction of The Weight — a larger grotesque that can kill you the instant it catches you.
The "hide from the big bad" element is common in horror video games, and Screen Burn's team includes people who have worked on Alien: Isolation, one of that subgenre's high points.
Here, though, it's an exercise in frustration, as The Weight moves too erratically and can sometimes park itself in front of your hiding spot, leaving you stuck for minutes at a time.
Most frustratingly, if it catches you, the game will often respawn you right where you died — with The Weight still standing in front of you, setting off a frustrating loop of death.
And while the sights in St. Amelia's nightmare version are initially impressive, as time goes on the dreary visuals become tiresome.

It's especially a shame because some parts of "normal" St. Amelia stand out in their novelty. A flat in a block of corporate housing shifts and transforms seemingly at the whim of a series of haunted cassette tapes. Later, Richard attempts to climb an office tower infested with monsters, snatching precious shotgun shells dropped by the bodies of those who unsuccessfully came before him.
Another attempt? For die-hards, maybe

After a gruelling 18-plus hours in Silent Hill: Townfall, I reached the story's conclusion — or one of them, anyways. The game has at least five alternate endings, each (hopefully) shedding light on the tragedy of St. Amelia — and Richard, Zoe and Simon's part in it.

The series is known to focus on vibes more than a coherent plot, but even then I felt frustrated by how few questions were satisfyingly answered — or how many more times I'd have to play it to uncover new details.

The excitement I felt exploring the town was at odds with the agony I felt hiding from The Weight — to the point where it might be only the most die-hard Silent Hill fans, or those who truly love every contradictory flavour of horror in video games, who will have the stomach to finish the entire journey once, let alone many times over.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jonathan Ore is a writer and editor for CBC Radio Digital in Toronto. He regularly covers the video games industry for CBC Radio programs across the country and has also covered arts & entertainment, technology and the games industry for CBC News. You can reach him at jonathan.ore@cbc.ca

articles.title: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance
articles.summary: The groups have been active in Ethiopia's most populous regions for years and now say they will work together.

blocks.text: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa and push for a transitional administration.

The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival.
The groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction, and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration.
Federal authorities have not yet responded.
Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country.
There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions.
An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement.
Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Ogaden, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states.
Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces during the Tigray war.
It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm.
The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018.
The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea.
Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities".
"Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July.

The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties.
The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results.
The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll.

Search and rescue authorities in the southern state of Kerala found three more dead bodies on Monday morning, taking the death toll from a flash flood to at least five.

Floods and rain-triggered landslides are a common occurrence in Kerala during the monsoon months, between June and November.

articles.title: Who is private prosecutor Erwin Matib?
articles.summary: On Day 27 of Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial, private prosecutor Erwin Matib led the direct examination of a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) witness.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 3:29pm
On Day 27 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, private prosecutor Erwin Matib led the direct examination of a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) witness.
Matib’s examination focused on Duterte’s alleged corporate shareholdings under Article 2 of the impeachment complaint, which accuses her of accumulating unexplained wealth.

Matib is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel on a pro bono basis, or voluntarily and without charge. The House prosecution panel initially named 10 private lawyers to assist in the impeachment trial.
He is a partner at PECABAR Law, a firm founded in 1983 by former Senator Juan Ponce Enrile and former Senator Rene Cayetano.
Matib joined the firm as an associate shortly after his admission to the Philippine Bar in 2010 and was admitted to the partnership in 2016.
He currently heads PECABAR Law’s Special Projects and Tax Department and co-heads its Corporate, Intellectual Property, and Immigration Department.
In addition to being a lawyer, Matib is a certified public accountant.
He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Accountancy from Saint Louis University in 2003 and passed the CPA licensure examination that same year.
He obtained his Juris Doctor degree from the University of the Philippines College of Law in 2009.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Sydney policeman allegedly disguised himself as Uber Eats rider before murders
articles.summary: Beaumont Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to the 2024 murder of his ex-partner and his new boyfriend.

blocks.text: A former police officer accused of using his work gun to kill a Sydney couple was driven by a "jealous infatuation" with his ex, a court has heard.
Beaumont Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two charges of domestic violence-related murder and one of aggravated break and enter.

Prosecutors allege Lamarre-Condon shot his ex-partner, 26-year-old TV presenter Jesse Baird, and Baird's new partner Luke Davies, a 29-year-old Qantas flight attendant, at a home in the Sydney suburb of Paddington in 2024.
The couple's bodies were found in a rural area 200km away, hidden in surfboard bags. The trial is expected to run for three months.
In his opening address on Monday, prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC described how Lamarre-Condon had developed an "obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Baird after a brief romantic relationship.
It manifested itself in a "range of compulsive behaviour", Hatfield said, which escalated when Baird ended all contact in November 2023.
The barrister said Lamarre-Condon used a friend's phone to message Baird and claim he had cancer, stalked his ex-lover, and tampered with his car in the weeks after their break-up.

On the day of the alleged murders, Lamarre-Condon had set his alarm for 04.30 local time, Hatfield claimed, and sent a text to a friend which read: "I'll try to call you tonight and update you... there's no sign I'm doing it".

Lamarre-Condon then switched to a burner phone, picked up a rental car and waited outside Baird's home for three hours dressed as an Uber driver, the prosecution alleged. He had previously bought a surfboard bag to dispose of Baird's body, Hatfield said.

After entering Baird's home with a key he had previously obtained, Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in the kitchen and then killed Davies in the bedroom as he was trying to call emergency services for help, the court was told.
Hatfield said that the accused had planned Baird's murder, and killed Davies so as to "eliminate him as a witness".
In the hours and days after the alleged killings, Lamarre-Condon tried to cover up the murder, Hatfield said, including sending messages from Baird's mobile phone.
The aggravated break and enter charge that Lamarre-Condon is facing refers to an incident in August 2023 where it's alleged he broke into Baird's home and stole his phone and wallet.
Hatfield also told the court that Lamarre-Condon had earlier offered to plead guilty to a single charge of manslaughter relating to Baird's death but this was rejected.
Police were first alerted to the alleged murders after bloodied items belonging to Baird and Davies were found in a bin in Sydney's south.
Later that week, Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to a police station and was charged.
Eight days after the alleged killings took place, authorities found the couple's bodies.
Lamarre-Condon was sacked by New South Wales Police in the weeks after he was charged with the alleged murders.

Before the opening address on Monday, a 15-member jury was selected, with the judge, Justice Natalie Adams, explaining that three extra people were chosen - a jury is typically made up of 12 people - as a contingency for sickness and other unforeseen circumstances.

articles.title: Angara: PH schools focused on academics, unprepared for shootings
articles.summary: Education Secretary Juan Edgardo "Sonny" Angara said the country's schools need stronger security, adding that the agency has focused on the academic performance of Filipino learners. Angara said…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 3:15pm
Education Secretary Juan Edgardo "Sonny" Angara said the country's schools need stronger security, adding that the agency has focused on the academic performance of Filipino learners.
Angara said this in an interview in Banga, South Cotabato, over the weekend, in the wake of the third school shooting in 2026 that led to multiple deaths.
The Tacloban shooting saw the deaths of three students, while the Zamboanga shooting led to the deaths of two students, including the shooter.
He added that the DepEd would seek the help of other agencies to investigate the “true crime community” aspect following reports that the Banga National High School shooter was involved in it.
Angara said that the agency planned to roll out enhanced safety measures following the third case of deadly school shootings since June.
“'Yong security measures, talaga kailangang paigtingin dahil hindi talaga kami handa sa mga ganitong shootings eh. Na-concentrate tayo sa academic performance ng mga bata,” Angara said.
(The security measures, we really need to strengthen those because we are not ready for these types of shootings. We concentrated on the academic performance of children.)

Angara said the DepEd agency will seek the help of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) to investigate "true crime community."

“’Yon talaga ang gusto nating imbestigahin dahil hindi natin kabisado 'yan. Hihingi tayo ng tulong sa DICT, DILG, at siguro talagang dapat imbestigahan nang maigi itong mga… dahil mukhang naimpluwensiyahan siya,” Angara said.

(That is what we want to investigate because we are not familiar with that yet. We will ask for help from the DICT, DILG, and that is really what we want to investigate well… because it seemed like he was influenced.)
The DepEd secretary said that the agency has already purchased more metal detectors, but did not specify when they would be distributed.
He also clarified that while police may be present outside schools, officers are usually no longer allowed inside the premises because they are zones of peace.
Angara said that the DepEd is looking into how to improve mental health among the students, adding that the agency is hiring more school counselor associates. –Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Presley Gerber, Cindy Crawford's son, dies aged 27
articles.summary: His family asked for privacy during a "very difficult and painful time" following the model's death.

blocks.text: Presley Gerber, the son of supermodel Cindy Crawford, has died at the age of 27.
Gerber, a model, passed away at a rehab facility on Sunday, according to records filed by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. The cause of death was not listed.
Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and her husband Rande Gerber, told the BBC's US news partner CBS: "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."
Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his runway debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.
He went on to model for brands including Burberry, Dolce & Gabbana, and Bottega Veneta.
His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.
In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use.

In 2023, he told the Studio 22 podcast: "Having struggled with mental health, depression and some other things that come along with that, I think that whether I help one person or a hundred people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that's all I need to do."
And in this month's American Vogue, Kaia discussed her brother's struggles with addiction. She said: "When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone.
"I think that's also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help."

Gerber had previously spoken of his close relationship with his family, including sister Kaia, who he appeared alongside in a campaign for Calvin Klein in 2018, and whose name he had tattooed on his arm.
He told People Magazine that year: "We're a close family, especially me and my sister, so it's definitely cool.
"We get to travel together half of the time, so it makes it a lot less lonely."
Gerber also starred alongside his mother in Pepsi's 2018 Super Bowl commercial, 26 years after Crawford first appeared in her famous 1992 advertisement for the brand.
"We're a really tight family, so it was just like going to work with one of your friends. It was so fun, and easy," he told People Magazine at the time.
In July, Crawford shared two childhood photographs of her son on Instagram to mark his 27th birthday.
"I'm so proud of the man you've become, but I'll always see you as my little boy! Love you," she wrote.

articles.summary: Five matches into the league season, which teams in the Premier League have impressed so far and who have disappointed?

blocks.text: There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October.
We are five matches into the league season and there is a long way to go in the campaign, but which teams have impressed so far and who have disappointed?
You can have your say in the comments at the bottom of the page.
Arsenal: Solid start to their title defence until they were ripped apart by Brighton having survived a penalty scare at Sunderland. 7
Aston Villa: Signs they are beginning to move in the right direction after losing so many key players during the transfer window. 6
Bournemouth: If games lasted 80 minutes the Cherries would be near the top of the table. Need to cut out conceding so late. 6
Brentford: Demolished Spurs and Chelsea without fuss during a highly impressive unbeaten start. Can they keep it up and challenge for Europe? 8
Brighton: Kings of entertainment after hitting 16 goals in five top-flight games, including three against champions Arsenal. A joy to watch. 9
Chelsea: After a strong start under Xabi Alonso, the Blues have lost two of their past three - and were picked apart by Brentford. Are they really moving in the right direction? 6
Coventry City: You could hear the sighs of relief in the away end at Nottingham Forest on Saturday. Will Frank Lampard's side kick on after that win? 6
Crystal Palace: Room for improvement after one win and three defeats. 5
Everton: Despite a transfer window to forget, David Moyes has made the Toffees hard to beat. 6

Fulham: Decent draws against Liverpool and Manchester United but need a win. Ipswich (away) followed by Hull (home), Coventry (away) and Crystal Palace (home) offer hope when they return from the international break. 5
Hull City: To have eight points from a tough opening five fixtures is an excellent return, including beating Manchester United and drawing with Aston Villa and Chelsea. 8
Ipswich Town: Defensively vulnerable but two late winners, against Sunderland and Crystal Palace, have earned them six points and shown their fighting spirit. 5
Leeds United: Fifth in the league, unbeaten and with the joint-best defensive record. They showed what they are capable of with a superb 4-1 win over Newcastle. 7
Liverpool: Unbeaten but have been far from their best. Three clean sheets in their past three games, but more is expected from Andoni Iraola's side. 6

Manchester City: Five league games, five victories. Managed to win at Manchester United despite going down to 10 men midway through the first half. With Erling Haaland already top scorer, City fans will expect a real push to win the league. 9

Manchester United: Disappointing performances to lose at Hull and draw at a Fulham side who were bottom of the league. Their only win so far came against Ipswich and they were denied a victory at Everton by a late equaliser. 4

Newcastle United: A mixed bag under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They impressed in a draw against Liverpool, won comfortably at Tottenham, but were also terrible in a loss at Leeds, although they responded well to beat Hull. 6

Nottingham Forest: Their best results have come away, drawing at Liverpool and winning at Aston Villa. But their home form will be a huge worry - yet to score a goal and with only one point from three matches at the City Ground. 5

Sunderland: After coming seventh in 2025-26, Sunderland fans will have wanted a better start to this season. The Black Cats gave good accounts of themselves against Arsenal and Manchester City, but lost both matches. 5

Tottenham Hotspur: After spending more than £300m in the summer, Spurs have been poor, failing to score in their opening four league matches. Supporters will be demanding an instant improvement after the international break. 2

articles.title: Japan: Typhoon Dujuan sparks flood, landslide warnings
articles.summary: At least 275 flights have been canceled in Japan, which is in the middle of a five-day holiday. The storm could dump record levels of rain on the country.

image.caption: Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture, near Tokyo, already saw heavy rains this weekendImage: Takuya Matsumoto/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A powerful typhoon was nearing Japan's eastern coast on Monday, triggering warnings of floods and landslides and prompting hundreds of flights to be canceled.
Dujuan is forecast to pass close to the Tokyo metropolitan area later in the day.
What do we know about Typhoon Dujuan?
Typhoon Dujuan was packing winds at speeds of 144 kilometers (89 miles) per hour as it lingered some 110 kilometres from Hachijojima, one of Tokyo's most remote islands.
Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture near Tokyo already saw heavy rainfall over the weekend.
The ⁠Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has cautioned that weather conditions could worsen rapidly.
"The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the JMA said.

Authorities have also warned of a possibility of ⁠linear ​rain bands forming over central Japan and the Kanto region — which includes Tokyo and surrounding prefectures — that could raise the risk of rain-related disasters like flash floods and landslides.
Linear ‌bands cause heavy torrential rainfall ​over a narrow area for several hours.

blocks.caption: Dujuan is Japan's 25th typhoon of the yearImage: Ichiro Ohara/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How have Japan's regions been affected by the incoming storm?
Over 4,000 households in Chiba were without power.
In the central prefecture of Aichi, which is currently hosting the Asian Games, an equestrian eventing competition was postponed until Tuesday.
The Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs, was shut down ahead of its final day on Monday.
Dujuan could also scupper travel plans during Japan's "Silver Week" holiday, which has just begun and which normally sees a surge in domestic travel.
On Monday, Japan Airlines canceled 120 domestic and 15 international flights, while All Nippon Airways canceled 140 domestic flights.
Some railway services were suspended on some lines in Tokyo and its neighboring areas.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband explains why he forgave her over children's killings
articles.summary: The husband of the US mother who strangled her three young children discusses his grief in an interview with CBS News.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide
Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of a US mother accused of murdering their three children, has said he would have been "eaten up inside forever" had he not forgiven her for their deaths.
In an interview with CBS, he also said he did the best he could as his then-wife Lindsay Clancy struggled with mental illness in the months leading up to the day she strangled their children.
Lindsay has not disputed that she killed them but her lawyers argued she should not be held legally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness.
A judge declared a mistrial in the case earlier this month after the jury said it could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty of murder.
The prosecution had alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.
Clancy, now 36, was then left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. She attended the trial in a wheelchair.
Patrick Clancy testified during the trial about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth.
Clancy's team said she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both.
"I didn't know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he told CBS, the BBC's US news partner.
It was her mental health that led to Patrick Clancy deciding later to forgive her.
"I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom', and 'Baby Murderer', 'Monster'. And none of them were accurate," he said in the interview.

"I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever."

Asked if he felt he had failed in some way in this period leading up to the killings, he said: "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day."
Living with his grief in the weeks after the tragedy became a struggle and he admitted having suicidal thoughts.
"I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it," he said.
During the seven week trial, Patrick was singled out online for wild vitriol and cover-up accusations.
There were claims he was to blame for the murders in some way. Thrust into the limelight, tabloids snapped photos of him travelling and with his new wife Rachel Danis.
The 36-year-old said the speculation was "deeply harmful to the legacy of my children. It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health".
It was also "painful to see" for him personally.
"And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said.
The intense scrutiny prompted him to move from Duxbury to New York City in a bid to seek anonymity.
Now he is starting a family with Danis and looking forward to telling his future children about their siblings.
"I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids. And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister."
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.
A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

articles.title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
articles.summary: Top US and Chinese officials held talks in New York on Sunday ahead of a Trump-Xi summit this week.

blocks.text: Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday.
Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.
The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week.

AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks.
He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade.
A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November.
The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment.
Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI.
Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people."
The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries.
In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity.
Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China.
He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins."
In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed.
Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs.

articles.title: PNP: No group applied for permit to protest on Martial Law anniversary
articles.summary: No group has applied for a permit to protest in Metro Manila on the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law, the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) said.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 1:15pm
Personnel from the Philippine National Police in Manila behind the barricade on Sept. 21, 2026.
The STAR / Edd Gumban
MANILA, Philippines — No group has applied for a permit to protest in Metro Manila on the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law, the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) said.
This was confirmed by NCRPO spokesperson Major Hazel Asilo in a message to Philstar.com on Monday, September 21.
This means that progressive groups that wish to stage protests are not allowed to hold them across Metro Manila unless they do so in designated freedom parks.
Some groups have announced anti-corruption protests today, including the Kilusang Bayan Kontra Kurakot, which will hold a program at 3 p.m. at Liwasang Bonifacio, a designated freedom park in Manila.
According to the Philippine National Police (PNP), more than 17,000 police personnel have been deployed across Metro Manila in anticipation of the protests.
This is higher than the 15,000 personnel the PNP initially said would be deployed in Metro Manila.

The PNP said the personnel include 8,553 from the NCRPO, 465 from the Regional Support Unit, 1,000 from the Reactionary Standby Support Force, 1,000 from Police the Regional Office (PRO) CAR, 1,000 from PRO1, 2,000 from PRO3, 2,000 from PRO4A and 1,000 personnel from the Philippine Coast Guard.
Police also barricaded portions of roads in Manila. Manila Mayor Isko Moreno Domagoso earlier suspended face-to-face classes in the capital in anticipation of the protests.
On the eve of the anniversary, Sunday, September 20, several groups marched to the Supreme Court and the EDSA Shrine to commemorate the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law.
