articles.title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals
articles.summary: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy…

blocks.text: Nika’s story

blocks.caption: Silhouette of an Iranian woman, DHS officers wrestle a detainee to the ground

blocks.text: No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.
Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.

Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.

Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.

After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.
“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”

The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?

Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.

It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.

The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.

A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.

A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.
The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.

Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.
The rug pull

blocks.caption: Trump’s deportation drive is being led by Stephen Miller (left)

blocks.text: Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.

Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.
Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.
Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.

This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.

Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.

For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.

Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”
African deals

blocks.caption: Montage of images, including one of Rabbiatu Kuyateh, government papers and maps

blocks.text: When Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.

A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going”.

blocks.caption: Rabbiatu Kuyateh being forcibly removed from her temporary accommodation in Ghana

blocks.text: Kuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.

She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.
In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.

“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”

The drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire to end most migration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.

Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its name incorporating a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.

Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 38 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.

They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.

The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.

Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.

On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.
“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.

During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”
Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.

The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”

He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”
Malaria

blocks.caption: Montage of images including one of a man in handcuffs and one of a persons hand in a hospital bed

blocks.text: Onboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.

blocks.caption: Deportation plane arriving in Bangui on 11 June

blocks.text: For several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.
Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.

US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.

When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”

Back in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.
The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.
The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”

blocks.caption: Montage of images including a cityscape and a woman silhouetted against a window

blocks.text: As the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.
Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.

In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.

According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.

Nika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”

The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.

An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”
Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.

“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”
Life in the shadows

blocks.caption: Montage of images, including of a woman and a man and official US documents

blocks.text: People who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”

She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”
She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.

Annan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.

In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.

It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”
Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.

He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.

In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.
Exhaustion

blocks.caption: Montage of images including men walking towards a plane and people sitting in a large room

blocks.text: In Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.
Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”

Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.

When a client is detained, avenues of accountability have largely been shut, including the office of an independent ombudsman for immigration detention, which was responsible for investigating abuses and misconduct.

In court, immigration lawyers can face hostile judges after the Trump administration purged some of those deemed insufficiently loyal to the deportation agenda. Meanwhile, the cost of even filing a case has risen steeply, under the terms of a bill passed through Congress in July last year.

Jalili, like many others, spent much of the first Trump administration mounting legal challenges against a policy of separating children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Knowing that what would follow might be worse, she decided on the eve of Trump’s re-election to start her own firm to fight the coming storm
It was not uncommon for calls from the desperate families of new ICE detainees to wake her in the night.
One of the biggest challenges, said Erica Reilly, an immigration attorney based in Washington DC, was basic communication with ICE officers.

“You send all these emails to deportation officers, and you’re like: ‘Hi, just following up again on the email I sent you last week, and the week before that, and the week before that, and the week before that, that you haven’t responded to,’” she said. “And they know they don’t have to because there’s no accountability.”
The worst thing, she said, was the powerlessness. But the cruelty and the lack of access, she had come to believe, “that’s all the point”.
“I think that the administration is doing what they can to get enough people to say, well, the alternative is too scary or too uncertain or too bad. I’ll just leave on my own.”
Getting through the day meant reformulating the wins, Reilly said. “Getting a call back from a deportation officer shouldn’t be a win, but in this environment it is.”

Jalili said she did her best to focus on the battles she could win. When she heard Nika’s flight had left for Bangui, she sank to the floor, called her mother, and began to cry. “It’s not a situation where you can just say: ‘Oh, I did my best.’”
Nika had lost the life she knew in Iran. The US offered little better. Jalili listed the cost.

“Being detained for 17 months. Being released from the federal judge’s order for 10 days. Being stripped away from her uncle’s hands. Being put in a car and then on a flight in shackles, and for 24 hours, sitting on that flight. She must have felt so lonely.”
Additional reporting by Alice Speri

articles.title: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister tells BBC
articles.summary: It comes after European Commission President proposed "opening the door" for Canada to become an associate member of the EU.

blocks.text: The UK should "team up" with a proposed economic alliance between Canada and Europe, Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said.
"This is all about the substance, to build an alliance of the future," he told the BBC. "The world has changed. America has changed. So we need to change."

Champagne also gave a frank assessment of the Canada-US trade war after a deal collapsed last month, saying the country had "stood up for our industries, our workers, our country" by imposing tariffs.
His comments come after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to an associate EU membership for Canada, an unprecedented move for the bloc.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to address the EU in Strasbourg, shortly after von der Leyen's proposal was made, was "to build the alliance of the future", Champagne said.
Carney, the former governor of the Bank of England, has previously talked about an alliance of "middle powers" working together on economic growth, resilience and security.
Champagne told the BBC that the UK and Canada had shared values.

"We need to look at partnership in a different way and the great thing is that when you look at Canada - and I would say the United Kingdom - we share the same values. We are very aligned in our vision of the world. Why don't we team up?" he said.
"We are independent and sovereign, but we are stronger together."
After his return to the White House last year, US President Donald Trump imposed sweeping global tariffs, including on long-standing trade allies such as the UK.

While the UK renegotiated a trade deal with the US in June last year, the new Canada-EU alliance does raise questions for the UK's post-Brexit positioning with Europe, as well as its position with the US, after some changes of presidential rhetoric over the Falklands and Irish unity in recent weeks.

Carney met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool in the middle of his trip to Brussels and Strasbourg last week, while Champagne attended a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday, alongside Chancellor John Healey.

The developing discussions around closer ties between the EU and Canada come as Ottawa remains locked in an escalating trade war with the US, with both sides imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after talks broke down at the last moment in August.
Trump has also threatened further tariffs on the EU if the associate membership plan proved "hostile" to the US, calling the idea laughable and labelling Canada a "terrible trading partner".
Champagne said the trade war was not a conflict chosen by Canada.
"We responded because at some stage you have to say 'enough is enough'. No one can infringe on our economic sovereignty... the world took notice," he said.

The minister said Canada did not seek escalation after its "measured, targeted and strategic... dollar-for-dollar, tariff-for-tariff" response and the country would "re-engage at the right time" with its southern neighbour.
Affected industries would be supported "as long as it takes and whatever it takes", he added.
Champagne argued that Canada's strong fiscal position helped underpin its resilience, and that the dispute with the US provided a "golden opportunity" to diversify.
This is the backdrop to the promise of an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the EU, and the idea of "teaming up" with the UK too.
Burnham will meet Trump for the first time this week, in New York at the UN General Assembly.

Last year, after his election, Carney invited King Charles to open the Canadian Parliament in Ottawa, a move widely seen as a rebuff to Trump's repeated suggestion that Commonwealth Canada could become part of the US.
The detail of the offer made by the EU to negotiate "associate membership" for Canada is yet to be formalised.
Champagne said this was "a moment of great opportunities" and to strengthen the existing relationship between Canada and the EU.

Carney last week pointed to Canadian membership of EU university, scientific research, AI and defence funding schemes, as well as for young Canadians and Europeans to "cross the ocean and be able to study and live".
He said Canada could supply critical minerals and gas and would seek access to European advanced technologies.
It is understood that both Canada and the EU see the opportunity for a process for like-minded nations which might not ever be full members, for example Australia.

articles.title: ‘It’s unrecognisable’: How being a tax haven has changed Jersey
articles.summary:
While global billionaires and multinational companies have been lured to its shores, many islanders feel left behind and priced out, with food bank use increasing

On a late Friday afternoon…

blocks.text: On a late Friday afternoon on the Channel Island of Jersey, tourists and locals are flocking to St Helier’s waterfront where the town’s sprawling beach has emerged at low tide.
In one direction, they face the calm waters of St Aubin’s Bay, ringed by a seaside promenade and punctuated with a tidal island hosting the 16th century Elizabeth Castle.

Back on shore, however, it is all business. Gleaming glass buildings hosting global accountancy firms and and international banks hint at the £4bn offshore finance industry dominating this nine-by-five-mile island’s economy.

For decades, low taxes and corporate secrecy have lured the wealth of global billionaires and multinational companies to Jersey’s shores, requiring a high-paid cadre of bankers, accountants and lawyers who now make up more than half of the island’s economic output, and two in every five jobs.
It has also made Jersey one of the world’s richest economies, giving its 104,500 population a GDP per head that is nearly 60% higher than the UK.

But those tactics have come at a cost, not least to Jersey’s international reputation, with the island consistently securing a top-10 slot in the Tax Justice Network’s international tax haven rankings. It also came under fire after the Panama and Paradise papers data leaks, which shone a light on how elites were hiding wealth in offshore hubs such as Jersey.
But Jersey isn’t the only place chasing global wealth, and foreign governments that have built on and replicated the island’s model are now threatening to eat its lunch.

“Without urgent intervention, Jersey’s future success as a financial centre is at risk, with inevitable repercussions for the Jersey way of life,” a government-backed review, led by NatWest Group’s former chair Howard Davies, warned in March.

blocks.caption: Jersey cows waiting to be shipped to Denmark from St Helier harbour around 1880. Photograph: Philip Godfray/Societe Jersiaise Photographic Archive

blocks.text: In response, Jersey’s government is charging ahead with a £31m four-year plan aimed at slashing red tape, boosting the British crown dependency’s global profile and diversifying into popular crypto assets, all to keep it relevant in a rapidly changing world. “The risk of complacency is real,” the report warns. “Standing still means falling behind.”
This is not the first time Jersey has faced an economic crossroads.

Its boom and bust history stretches back to the 1700s, when it was home to a lucrative fine knitting industry. Once knitting was killed off by machines, oyster catching and shipbuilding took over, until overfishing and steam power closed shipyards.

Entrepreneurial farmers then discovered and bred new exports: the docile and milk-rich Jersey cow, followed by a blight-resistant potato that still bears the island’s name, requiring a swathe of migrant workers to support farmers. “The cycle of Jersey’s industries has tended to see everyone getting involved where there’s a lot of money to be made,” says Lucy Layton, outreach curator at Jersey Heritage.

blocks.caption: Lucy Layton, outreach curator at Jersey Heritage. Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: A century later, as postwar Jersey tried to recover from Nazi occupation, tourism boomed, aided by the popularity of the Bergerac detective series. That industry was eventually ruined by discount airlines offering cheap holidays to sunnier European destinations, ushering in a new economic era focused on billionaires and corporations looking for a low-tax home for their wealth.

Jersey has crafted an alluring package to draw in global wealth, involving zero inheritance or capital gains tax, and no corporation tax – outside of financial services firms, which are charged just 10% on their earnings. Meanwhile, an army of high-earning bankers, lawyers and accountants face a maximum of 20% income tax on the island, compared with 45% in London.

But wealthy Britons have been choosing the glass towers of Dubai over Jersey’s low-rise seaside towns, while rich families overseas are hedging their bets and spreading cash across a number of offshore hubs.

The Panama and Paradise papers data leaks have also influenced money flows. “People now are much more selective about the jurisdictions that they deal with,” says Joe Moynihan, chief executive of the sector’s promotional body, Jersey Finance. “They don’t want their organisation, or indeed their family, to be associated with a jurisdiction that could potentially damage their reputation.”

However, Moynihan says Jersey’s reputation is strong: “We’re well regulated, with plenty of expertise, good legislation and an independent judiciary, which is becoming increasingly important in the crazy world that we live in.”

blocks.caption: Joe Moynihan, the chief executive of Jersey Finance. Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: But Jersey is still losing ground. Authorities say they need to regain a competitive edge, including by diversifying into crypto assets – such as stablecoins and tokens – to draw a younger wealthy client. Ian Gorst, the island’s finance minister, says it is also looking to cut back on “regulatory friction”.

To some, that may sound like an opportunity to cut corners, but Gorst insists this is not about watering down rules meant to stop financial crime, corruption or sanctions evasion. Jersey’s ongoing battle with the Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich over his frozen assets is a case in point, he says. “What I think it shows is that Jersey can stand alongside the UK in fighting these issues.”

Cooperation with the UK, though, only goes so far. Gorst has so far resisted pressure from Westminster’s anti-corruption champion Margaret Hodge to publicly release its beneficial ownership register, showing who ultimately owns Jersey-based companies. “I don’t intend to make our register public, and I’ve been clear to the UK about that,” he says.
But not everyone is on board with the government’s finance-first agenda.

Laura Craig, the owner of the Little Wren gift shop in St Helier, has lived in Jersey for 45 years. “For me personally, I would like to see Jersey have more of a balance in industry,” she says, including a return to more tourism.

blocks.caption: Laura Craig, the owner of Little Wren gift shop. Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: St Helier itself has changed over Craig’s lifetime, with the old granite-frontage that once dominated the town’s waterfront having been reclaimed and built up for the finance industry. “It’s unrecognisable to when I was a little girl,” Craig adds. “All the big buildings on there now are banks and finance houses.”

Many say the influx of wealthy bankers has pushed up house prices across the tiny island, just 14 miles off the coast of France. “They just increase the cost of living for everybody,” says Antonio De’Lemos, co-owner of the La Topaze D’or antiques shop in St Helier market.

blocks.caption: Antonio De’Lemos, co-owner of the La Topaze D’or antiques shop in St Helier market. Photograph: Gary Grimshaw

blocks.text: He fears Jersey’s reputation has also taken a blow. “I don’t like to be in Jersey, knowing this is a tax paradise. And let’s be honest, it is,” he says. However, he acknowledges that it has become taboo to criticise the sector. “The establishment don’t like when you speak up.”

While Jersey’s authorities are panicked about losing billionaires to Singapore and Dubai, many islanders are struggling to make ends meet. The number of food bank users tripled in the three years to 2024, and demand has continued.

Just streets away from St Helier’s financial district, Vini Jones, the general manager of the Grace Trust charity, is helping prepare a free weekly meal at St Paul’s Church for dozens of locals. “You can move here, you can get a job, you could send your kids to school, you can go to your office at the weekends, you go to the beach, and you can have absolutely no idea or concept of what it’s actually like for a lot of people who live in Jersey,” he says.

blocks.caption: Vini Jones, the general manager of the Grace Trust charity, which works with struggling islanders. Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: Jones, who moved to Jersey from London in 2000, doesn’t blame the finance industry, which he says helps fund the charity’s work. If the finance sector took a blow “it would be a bit of an earthquake but I think that people can get pretty resourceful”, he says. “We may see a little bit less coming our way in donations if that was the case, but I think there’s still a good community spirit in Jersey that people will rise to.”

That community spirit is palpable across the island, including in Gorey, a 15-minute drive up the coast from St Helier. There, 76-year-old Liz Viney is manning a ticket table at the Saturday car boot sale. She says that while some islanders would like to see the bankers go, it would be more painful than they expect.

“There’s a large part of the community here who would be quite pleased to revert back to being agricultural and fisheries and everything. But I don’t think we can go back there … who would support [the economy]? Who would pay the taxes? I think we have to live the life that, well, God gives us. And at the moment we are paid by the finance community. That’s what keeps us going.”

articles.title: US: Man wounded in Texas after being shot by ICE agent
articles.summary: An ICE agent shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas. The city's mayor has called for an independent investigation into the shooting.

image.caption: Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers stand at the scene where a man was shot by an ICE officerImage: Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A man has been hospitalized in Austin, Texas after being shot by an officer of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), local officials said Sunday.
Austin's Mayor Kirk Watson expressed his anger over the shooting, calling for the involvement of the local police in a "clear-eyed" investigation into the incident.
What do we know about the ICE shooting in Austin?
The man suffered one gunshot wound in his torso during a brief foot pursuit in the Texan capital's north side shortly before 1 pm local time, Austin officials said at a press briefing.
He is at a local hospital in a serious but stable condition, the officials said, adding that the information on the incident was "very preliminary."
City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said.
Who is the man wounded by ICE agent?
The officials did not name the man or release his age and nationality but an immigration lawyer, representing his family, identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan.
Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video published on her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and had no final order to be removed from the country.
The Associated Press later cited Goldfinch as saying that she did not know his current immigration status.
There is yet to be a statement on the shooting from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security that oversees the immigration agency.
Meanwhile, a group of about 100 protesters gathered at the site of the shooting and demonstrated against ICE's actions.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators protest at the scene of the shootingImage: Kaylee Greenlee/REUTERS

blocks.text: The protest was held across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla which had damage to its ​passenger-side door, news agency Reuters reported citing local TV, as ICE agents stood nearby.

blocks.caption: The damaged car was towed awayImage: Jesse Bedayn/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Austin Mayor rails against 'rogue' ICE, calls for independent probe
Sunday's shooting is the latest in a slew of incidents involving ICE, which has become the face of an immigration clampdown by US President Donald Trump's Republican administration.
Watson, a Democrat, told the media that the shooting occurred amid a "significant increase, almost overnight" of ICE operations in Austin.

"While I'm angry and disappointed, I'm not surprised. This has happened in other cities. With the rogue nature of ICE and the chaos we're seeing fomented by ICE, there's no reason to be surprised," the Austin mayor wrote on X.
He called for an independent investigation into the shooting, with the Austin Police Department (APD) having a role in the probe.
He said that the people of Austin had a "right to know what happened" and "a right to feel safe in their community".
"Though APD was not involved in the shooting, I believe that there needs to be an investigation that APD assures is clear-eyed, as complete as possible, and independent," Watson said.
He added that police chief Davis had deployed the APD's Special Investigation Unit at the scene, elaborating that the unit is the one responsible for probing Austin's officer-involved shootings.
Watson said that Davis has also asked the Texas Rangers to help out in the investigation.
'Horror has come to our doorstep,' says Congressman
On Sunday, US Representative Greg Casar — a Texas Democrat — called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.
He accused ICE of not being "truthful" in shooting in other cities.
"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar said.
"A few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come ... I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot," he told the media.

articles.title: DMW: No OFWs affected in Riyadh explosions
articles.summary: The DMW urged Filipinos in Saudi Arabia to remain vigilant and follow local authorities' advisories.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 11:40am

This video grab taken from UGC images posted on social media on September 19, 2026, shows smoke rising near Riyadh airport. Black smoke and flames rose near Riyadh's international airport on September 19, as Yemen's Houthis announced they had carried out strikes on targets in the Saudi capital and coastal oil facilities.
@Hey_Itsmyturn / X / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) assured the public on Monday, September 21 that no overseas Filipino workers in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia were affected by the explosions that occurred over the weekend.
The agency’s statement came following reports of explosions in Riyadh, the capital and largest city in Saudi Arabia, on Friday night, September 18 and Saturday morning, September 19.
The explosions were allegedly linked to Houthis drone and ballistic missile attacks that targeted Riyadh and energy sites along the Red Sea coasts.
Based on reports from international media, Saudi Arabia has confirmed that Yemen’s Houthi militants tried to attack Riyadh with a ballistic missile, but were intercepted.
Residents heard explosions and saw thick smoke near the airport late on. Authorities recorded no casualties or damage.
The Houthi’s claimed the attacks were their response to Saudi’s attempts to target Sanaa, the capital of Yemen that they currently control.
Based on DMW’s initial data from January to July 2026, Saudi Arabia remains the top destination for land-based OFWs with 147,021 workers.
It was also the top destination in 2025, with 333,487 workers.
The DMW said they continue to coordinate with the migrant workers offices in Saudi Arabia, and the Philippine Embassy and Consulate to monitor the situation.
The agency also provided the contact details of the labor attaché in the migrant workers offices.

“The DMW advises OFWs to remain vigilant and to follow guidance and advisories issued by Saudi authorities. OFWs who need assistance should immediately coordinate with the Migrant Workers Offices of the Philippine Embassy and Consulates,” the agency said.

articles.title: LTO summons van driver seen in road rage, gun-brandishing incident
articles.summary: His license is under 90-day preventive suspension after a viral road incident.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 11:08am
Photo from the Land Transportation Office showing the show-cause order and the driver who brandished a gun in a road rage incident.
Land Transportation Office

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has issued a show-cause order and placed a van driver's license under a 90-day preventive suspension following a viral road incident in which he was seen driving dangerously and pointing a gun at another motorist.

In a statement on Sunday, September 20, the agency said it is summoning the driver and the vehicle's registered owner to appear before the Intelligence and Investigation Division at the LTO Central Office in Quezon City on September 25.
They are required to submit sworn statements or explanations and supporting documents on the incident.
Footage of the incident showed the van driver maneuvering dangerously while pointing a firearm at another motorist.
Investigators also observed that the driver was not wearing a seatbelt, in violation of road safety regulations.

Under the show-cause order, the driver faces allegations of reckless driving, violation of the seatbelt law and being an "Improper Person to Operate a Motor Vehicle," alongside other potential administrative liabilities.
Pending the investigation, the driver's license was placed under a 90-day preventive suspension, with instructions to immediately surrender the physical card to the IID.
The vehicle involved has also been placed on alarm status while the investigation and administrative proceedings remain ongoing.

articles.title: Carney touts Arctic alliance with Norway during PM's visit to Ottawa, amid Russia threat
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting deeper defence ties with Norway, as well as investment from its massive, petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, meets with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Sunday. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
Prime Minister Mark Carney is courting deeper defence ties with Norway, as well as investment from its massive, petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre warns of 'real threats' from the Kremlin
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his focus on building international relationships, including with Norway, is part of the answer to renewed threats from Russia.

During a news conference with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre in Ottawa on Sunday, both leaders were asked about warnings from the Polish prime minister that Russia may be planning attacks on European countries that support Ukraine.
Støre said those warnings should be taken seriously and that Norway's intelligence has concluded there are "real threats coming from hybrid activity, ranging all the way to potential sabotage."
Carney didn't comment on the credibility of the threats but said he agreed with Støre's statements.

"One of the advantages of this relationship and deepening across a broad range of relationships is, yes, greater intelligence sharing, greater perspective, greater capacities that are built together," he said.
Arctic security on Carney's agenda during Norway visit
Carney said that includes having the "right partners" among Arctic nations working together. "The phrase that always sticks with me ... is 'High North, low tension,'" he said.
The way to accomplish that, he said, includes submarine and space capacity.

items: Zelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters

blocks.text: In July, Carney chose to buy a dozen submarines from a European shipbuilder instead of a Korean firm, after a months-long, hotly contested bidding process. The chosen partnership involves a German company but partners with Norway, with the three nations collaborating to produce and maintain the submarines.

Carney said the "time spent, whether it's in the high north in Norway, a meeting with the French president who's directly implicated in a number of these decisions, our meeting today and beyond, it's all connected."
Russia accuses NATO of creating "direct threat" as tension rise over Arctic military activity
Before his meeting with Støre in Ottawa, Carney travelled to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron earlier in the day.
Støre's visit comes as Carney looks for closer ties with Europe, including potential "associate membership" in the European Union.

Norway is not a member of the EU, but for three decades the country has had a deal with the political and economic bloc that gives both sides free access to each other's markets for goods and services — and gives Norway access to most EU programs.
Carney pledges deeper ties in EU speech but offers few details
Carney is courting deeper defence ties with Norway, as well as investment from its massive petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.
Carney was in Norway in March — the first sitting Canadian prime minister since 1980 to visit the Nordic country.

During that visit, the two leaders pledged to advance collaboration in fields ranging from Arctic security and space to critical minerals and energy. Carney and Støre also touted their reputations as low-risk global oil producers, amid supply shocks emanating from conflicts like U.S. President Donald Trump's war on Iran.

items: No longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight

blocks.text: Norwegian officials have often described Canada as a similar country, given that both seek to balance a large oil sector with a push for green energy and respect for Indigenous people.

They both put an emphasis on using multilateral institutions to resolve disputes while identifying as strong proponents of NATO and deeply tied with the EU, without being members. Both countries have put support for Ukraine at the forefront of foreign policy, amid Russia's full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Since late 2024, Canada has had an Arctic foreign policy that calls for more intense ties with Nordic countries in defence, strategic sectors and environmental issues.

articles.title: Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response
articles.summary: In response to the Iranian authorities' decision to close a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, France vowed to take appropriate measures.

image.caption: The language center that was closed by Iranian prosecutors was affiliated with the French embassy in TehranImage: Fatemeh Bahrami/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paris will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities closed a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the French Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.

"This new attack against France's cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and ​unacceptable," the ministry's spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement.
What do we know about the center's closure?
Earlier on Sunday, Iranian authorities announced the closure of a French language center in Tehran following a judicial order from the prosecutor's office.

"The illegal center affiliated with the French embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, was closed," the judiciary's Mizan news website said, referring to the French Language Center (CLF).
The Iranian judiciary accused the center of conducting "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions".

It also accused the center of having "abused its status as a language training facility" and of having sought to "identify and build networks among the country's elite figures while facilitating their departure."
Tensions between Paris and Tehran

France has previously dismissed such allegations. The country claims that there has been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as it has sought to increase support for and contact with Iran's civil society following the crackdown on protests at the beginning of this year.

Tensions between Tehran and Paris have been escalating in recent years. Last month, France expelled two Iranian diplomats in response to the brief detention and prohibition of two French envoys to the Islamic Republic. Tehran accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs.

Diplomats said Iran was also upset by a recent social media post from French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot commemorating the fourth anniversary of Mahsa Amini's death, which sparked protests nationwide.
In response, on Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi called the post "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of slaughtering 1.5 million Algerians during Algeria's war of independence.
The two ministers are scheduled to meet on Tuesday at the United Nations' annual gathering of world leaders.

articles.title: Macron and Carney announce closer France-Canada ties amid Trump tensions
articles.summary:
Two leaders meet in French territory off Canada as Ottawa seeks stronger relations with EU while fighting trade war with US

The leaders of France and Canada have pledged closer ties to…

blocks.text: The leaders of France and Canada have pledged closer ties to grapple with rising geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values, after ⁠they met in a ⁠French territory off Canada’s Atlantic coast.

The two leaders’ visit to Saint-Pierre ​and Miquelon – the first by a French president since 2014 and the first by a Canadian prime minister – came just weeks ⁠after Donald Trump posted an image showing the islands, as well as all of Canada and other countries in North America, covered by the US flag.
Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the ⁠EU amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war with the US.

“Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate ​change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to ‌our sovereignty,” Canada’s Mark Carney said in a statement ‌alongside France’s Emmanuel Macron on Sunday. “The time has come to strengthen our ties.”
Macron added that the two allies agreed to forge closer ties in sectors ranging ‌from space and climate to energy.

“We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions, and the strategic autonomy that we defend,” the French president said.
Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual UN general assembly of world leaders, had a symbolic weight following Trump’s social media post.

The image Trump shared showed the US flag draped over a map of the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, and was labelled “United States of America”. It included Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories.

Responding to questions on Trump’s post, Macron dismissed any notion that the territories ​could not be French and said he did not need to reaffirm that point every day just because “people have strange ideas or say strange things”.
For France, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic.
The territory also occupies a key place in France’s cooperation with Canada, including over energy.
Macron, whose government is facing increased pressure at home over rising fuel ⁠prices, said the talks had opened the door for bilateral discussions aimed at sealing concrete deals. ​
Paris hopes Canada will broaden its exports of ​liquefied natural gas to Europe rather than primarily ​to Asia.
“Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,” Macron said.
The two leaders ​also discussed Canada’s relationship with the ‌EU after the bloc ​proposed ​that Ottawa become its first associate member, something Macron said France supported.
Trump threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the proposal – an idea he derided as “laughable”.

Any move towards deeper integration is likely to face hurdles. More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

articles.title: Patrick Clancy gives first TV interview after Lindsay Clancy mistrial
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy 's former husband said he forgave her for killing their three young children in his first televised interview Sunday on CBS News' 60 Minutes since a jury deadlocked in her trial for…

image.caption: Patrick Clancy, seen in court July 29, did an interview with 60 Minutes that was televised Sunday. (David L. Ryan/Pool/The Boston Globe)

blocks.text: World·New

Lindsay Clancy 's former husband said he forgave her for killing their three young children in his first televised interview Sunday on CBS News' 60 Minutes since a jury deadlocked in her trial for the children's deaths.
Lindsay Clancy's former husband spoke with 60 Minutes in a Sunday episode on CBS
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

Lindsay Clancy's former husband said he forgave her for killing their three young children in his first televised interview Sunday on CBS News' 60 Minutes since a jury deadlocked in her trial for the children's deaths.

Patrick Clancy talked about his grief, saying he battled suicidal thoughts after the killings and experienced a panic attack while testifying at Lindsay Clancy's trial when attorneys played to jurors his 911 call to report the children's deaths.
At trial, the anguished 911 call included Patrick howling and crying after he discovered the bodies of his children in the family's basement as a confused dispatcher repeatedly asked what happened.

Earlier this month, 11 of 12 jurors were ready to clear Lindsay Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that the Massachusetts mom was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids in 2023.
But a lone juror sided with prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing. The deadlock forced a judge to declare a mistrial on Sept. 4.
The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health
Clancy says son died in his arms
Patrick Clancy also said his youngest son, Callan, didn't die immediately that fatal day on Jan. 24, 2023, but lived four more days before dying in his arms.
While holding his 8-month-old son, he said he typed with one hand tributes to his other children, Cora, 5, and Dawson, 2, and also forgave his wife.
"I saw headlines that say 'killer mom' and 'baby murderer monster' and none of them were accurate," he said. "I believed that it was her mental illness that caused that."
Calls conspiracy theories a 'distraction'
Clancy said stress from the murders and trial took a toll.
"There was a time I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday, and I was completely fine with it," he said.
He also addressed social media conspiracy theories surrounding the case, which have included unfounded claims he was connected to the death of his children.

items: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror breaks silence, says he didn't have 'any doubts' of her guilt
Will Lindsay Clancy face a new trial? What's next after mistrial declared

blocks.text: "It's deeply harmful to the legacy of my children," Patrick Clancy said. "It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health."
His new wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, joined him in the interview, describing Patrick Clancy as the "most selfless and supportive partner."

"I don't understand how the story has been so twisted," she said. "I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday. And I don't think there's anything wrong with that."
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
